The reject closure still needs per-index since it writes its error
into the correct slot of `errors_arr` for the eventual AggregateError;
sharing would require switching to a different ABI for the rejection
path (e.g. storing the index in a thread-local slot before invoking),
which isn't worth the spec complexity for the minor extra savings.

perf(runtime): fix O(N²) object key insert — 4680× speedup on dict building

The build-then-fill pattern (`for (i=0; i<N; i++) obj["k_"+i] = i;`)
was paying O(N²) per insert because `transition_cache_insert` eagerly
stamped `GC_FLAG_SHAPE_SHARED` on every new keys_array — which then
forced `js_object_set_field_by_name` to CLONE the entire keys_array
on every subsequent insert (the shape-shared guard at line ~4359).

For a single-owner object building 10k keys: 10k clones of growing
size = ~50M total array entries copied. Probe `obj["k_"+i] = i × 10k`
went from 9359 ms → 2 ms — 4680× speedup, Perry now faster than Bun.

**Fix**: move the SHAPE_SHARED stamp from `transition_cache_insert`
(eager, fires on every new shape — even single-owner ones) to
`transition_cache_lookup` (lazy, fires only when a SECOND object
actually reuses the shape via a cache hit). Single-owner build
patterns now extend their keys_array in place; the moment a second
object joins the shape via cache hit, both observe the stamp and
future extensions clone.

**Sidecar hash index** (`KEYS_INDEX`): added a thread-local
`obj_ptr → key_hash → slot` map that kicks in when keys_array grows
past `KEYS_INDEX_THRESHOLD` (32 entries). Replaces the O(N) linear
scan in `js_object_set_field_by_name`'s slow path with O(1) hashmap
lookup. FNV-1a hash for collision-free probing; byte-for-byte compare
on hit for hash-collision safety. Sidecar rebuilds lazily on lookup
when stale (length-mismatch detection); incremental updates on append
keep it in sync when the keys_array doesn't reallocate.

Together these two changes turn `Object[stringKey] = value` from
~quadratic into amortized constant time. The combined effect on the
benchmark probe:

- 100k keys: Perry 15 ms vs Bun 25 ms — Perry 1.67× FASTER

perf(runtime): reuse in-flight `next` Promise across async-step iterations (5.11x of Bun on promise_all_chains)

Each `await` inside an async function used to allocate one fresh `next` Promise
per iteration: `js_async_step_chain` either called `js_promise_new` (primitive
fast path) or `js_promise_then` (slow path with a Fulfilled/Rejected inner from
`Promise.resolve(...)` — the dominant kernel shape). On
`benchmarks/app-patterns/kernels/promise_all_chains.ts` (1000 batches × 50
inputs × 3 awaits) that was ~150k Promise allocs and ~150k thunk-pair allocs
purely to bridge consecutive AsyncStep iterations.

Reuse hook: when AsyncStepChain is invoked from inside a microtask whose step
closure matches the one currently being dispatched, reuse the runner's
`INLINE_TRAP_NEXT` as this iteration's `next` and return it back. The runner
detects the self-chain marker (`result == next`) and skips the propagate hop
that `js_promise_resolve_with_promise` would otherwise do.

Gating is critical: a NESTED `await` whose step body's `__next` runs user TS
that calls another async function would, without the gate, see the parent's
`INLINE_TRAP_NEXT` and return it as the nested function's user-visible Promise
— collapsing all of `Promise.all([unit(), unit(), ...])`'s inputs onto one
Promise. The new `CURRENT_STEP_CLOSURE` TLS holds the step closure that the
runner just dispatched; reuse fires only when AsyncStepChain's step_closure arg
matches. Nested calls receive a different step closure (allocated by the
nested function's own outer wrapper), miss the gate, and fall through to a
fresh `js_promise_new` — keeping the user-facing Promise distinct.

The slow path is also rewritten: instead of allocating fulfill/reject thunks
and going through `js_promise_then` for an already-Fulfilled/Rejected inner
(the steady-state shape — `Promise.resolve(<primitive>)` returns Fulfilled),
we unwrap the inner's value/reason and enqueue `Task::AsyncStep` directly. The
thunk path remains for genuinely Pending inners (rare in this kernel shape).
This eliminates 100k of the 150k slow-path `js_promise_then` calls and the
matching thunk-pair allocations.

INLINE_TRAP_NEXT is lifted from `js_promise_run_microtasks`'s function-local
`thread_local!` to module scope (`pub(crate)`) so AsyncStepChain can read it.
Behavior of the existing throw-trap routing is unchanged.

**Numbers (M-series ARM64, hyperfine --runs 15 --warmup 3):**

|----------------------------------|--------:|--------:|--------:|

| `promise_all_chains` min         | 312 ms  | 192 ms  | -38.5%  |
| `promise_all_chains` ratio / Bun | 13.37×  |  5.11×  | -62%    |
| per-await steady (200k probe)    | 670 ns  | 535 ns  | -20.1%  |

|--------------------|---------:|---------:|
| microtasks (runs)  |  301,999 |  201,999 |
| Promise allocs     |  352,001 |  252,001 |
| `js_promise_then`  |  151,000 |    1,000 |
| closure allocs     |  503,003 |  201,005 |

fix(hir,cjs-wrap): refs #488 drizzle-sqlite — cross-file class inheritance (v0.5.797)

Two coordinated fixes so `class B extends import_X.Y { ... }` correctly
inherits methods across module boundaries — the load-bearing shape for
drizzle-orm's column-builder class chain.

HIR fix (crates/perry-hir/src/lower_decl.rs:673 + :1584): both
class-lowering paths' `extends Member` arms (`extends import_X.Y` shape)
now call `ctx.lookup_class(&parent_name)` to populate `extends`
alongside the existing `extends_name`, matching the `extends Identifier`
arm above. Pre-fix the Member arm set `extends_name = Some("Y")` but
`extends = None`, so the class had no parent link in HIR and inherited
methods were unreachable on instances.

CJS-wrap fix (crates/perry/src/commands/compile/cjs_wrap.rs): Issue
#652's class-hoist moved `class B extends import_dep.A {...}` to
module scope so consumers' named imports resolve to the real class,
but `import_dep` was only bound INSIDE the IIFE — the hoisted
`extends import_dep.A` saw `undefined.A` at class-decl time, the class
lost its parent, and inherited methods came back `undefined`. Fix:

1. Surface each `var import_X = require("Y")` as a module-scope
   `const import_X = _req_N;` BEFORE the hoisted class block.

2. Blank the original `var import_X = require(...)` from the IIFE
   body — otherwise the inner re-binding shadows the module-scope
   alias under function scope (perry's resolver hits the inner var
   first), and the hoisted class re-loses its parent.

IIFE-body code that references `import_X.Y` continues to resolve via
the outer `const` through closure scope, so non-hoisted paths are
unaffected. New helper `extract_require_aliases_with_ranges` returns
each match's byte range so the inner var can be blanked precisely
(newlines preserved for line-number stability).

entry.ts): `integer("id").setName` was `undefined` (the load-bearing
symptom — drizzle's `sqliteTableBase` calls `colBuilder.setName(name2)`
for each column and threw `TypeError: setName is not a function`);
now resolves to `function`. The 4-level inheritance chain
`SQLiteIntegerBuilder → SQLiteBaseIntegerBuilder → SQLiteColumnBuilder
→ ColumnBuilder` (spread across 3 .cjs files) now correctly walks the
parent chain. `sqliteTable("users", {...})` succeeds, `db.insert(...)

of undefined (reading 'tableName')` on `db.select().from(users).all()`

fix(runtime): Object.entries/values silently returned only first 8 entries for >8-key objects

Bug: `js_object_entries` and `js_object_values` iterated `field_count`
instead of `keys_array.length`. For dict-built or parser-built objects
with ≥9 fields, `field_count` caps at the inline alloc_limit (8) — the
overflow values live in `OVERFLOW_FIELDS` (see object.rs:32). The result:
`Object.entries(obj)` silently returned only the FIRST 8 entries
regardless of how many properties the object actually had. Major silent
correctness bug for any code that uses Object.entries / Object.values
on real-world objects.

Bisect: 50-key obj returned `entries.length === 8` (was 8) instead of 50.
1000-key obj returned 8 entries. 10k-key obj returned 8 entries.

Fix: iterate up to `keys_array.length` (the logical property count),
matching the same fix already applied in `js_object_keys` and
`json.rs::stringify_object` (which already iterate `keys_len`).
`js_object_get_field` already handles the inline-vs-overflow split
internally (inline if `i < field_count`, `overflow_get` otherwise), so
no further changes needed.

fix(codegen,runtime): refs #488 drizzle-sqlite — `arr.push(...src)` on property receiver (v0.5.803)

Symptom: drizzle's mergeQueries does `result.params.push(...query.params)`
for each chunk. The push silently failed — every iteration showed
`result.params.length: 0 → 0` even when `query.params.length: 1`.
Rendered SQL `insert into "users" (...) values (?,?,?),(?,?,?),(?,?,?)`
went to better-sqlite3 with 0 bound params, 0 rows inserted, SELECT
returned `count=0`. This was the v0.5.767-documented "this.client
small-handle preservation" symptom mis-diagnosed — the real root
cause is missing codegen.

Root cause: the HIR at `crates/perry-hir/src/lower/expr_call.rs:4810`
correctly lowered `arr.push(...src)` (where `arr` is a property-access
receiver) to `NativeMethodCall { module: "array", method: "push_spread",
... }`. But `crates/perry-codegen/src/lower_call/native.rs` only had
arms for `"push_single"` / `"push"` — no arm for `"push_spread"`. The
call fell through to the "Unknown native method" catch-all at the end
of `lower_native_method_call` which lowered receiver+args for side
effects and returned the `0.0` sentinel. The actual push never
happened.

(Direct `LocalGet` receivers — `arr.push(...src)` where `arr` is a
local — already worked because a different HIR path lowers them to
`Expr::ArrayPushSpread { array_id, source }` with its own codegen.

fix(runtime): \`delete obj.key\` now properly removes the key (not just zeroes the value)

Pre-fix, `js_object_delete_field` just called `js_object_set_field(obj, i,
undefined)` and left the key in place in `keys_array`. Three problems:

1. **Property still enumerable**: `Object.keys(obj)`, `Object.entries(obj)`,
   `Object.values(obj)`, `for...in`, `for...of Object.entries(...)` etc. all
   still showed the deleted key (with value `undefined`). Bun and Node
   remove the key entirely.
2. **Overflow keys not deleted at all**: `js_object_set_field` has its own
   OOB guard at `field_index >= alloc_limit` and returns with a `[PERRY
   WARN] OOB write` log line — so deleting an overflow-stored key (i ≥ 8)
   silently didn't even touch the value.
3. **`hasOwnProperty` mismatch**: after the broken delete the property
   stayed in keys_array, so `hasOwnProperty` returned true for it.

Fix: clone the keys_array (must clone since the array can be shared
via the transition cache — mutating in place would corrupt OTHER
objects that picked up this shape), with the deleted key omitted.
Then shift the per-slot VALUES down by one using `js_object_get_field`
+ inline-or-overflow write, so slot positions stay aligned with the
shifted keys. Adjust `field_count` to track. Invalidate the keys-index
sidecar for this object since slot positions changed.

The keys_array clone is the load-bearing part — the prior in-place
mutation would have left other objects sharing the same keys_array
with corrupted lengths.

Sanity:
- 5-key obj `delete o.b; delete o.d`: now returns ['a','c','e']
  (length 3), was returning ['a','b','c','d','e'] (length 5).
- 50-key obj `delete big.k25; delete big.k30`: Object.keys.length =
  48, "k25" in big = false (matches Bun byte-for-byte; was 50, true).
- After delete on one obj, OTHER objs built from the same transition
  chain still have all their keys (the clone fix).
- 26/28 gap parity tests pass byte-identical to Node — same as before,
  no regressions.

fix(codegen): closes #685 — nested-class static-field init no longer crashes Schema.ts__init (v0.5.814)

Effect's `Schema.ts__init` throws `TypeError: (number).slice is not a
function` 309 modules into Effect's init chain, before any user code
runs. Root cause: HIR hoists every class declaration into
`module.classes`, including class EXPRESSIONS returned from a factory
function. Schema.ts:923's `TemplateLiteralParser = (...params) => {
return class TemplateLiteralParserClass extends transformOrFail(...) {
static params = params.slice() }}` hoists the inner class with its
`static params = params.slice()` initializer keeping a LocalGet
pointing at the factory's `params` parameter.

`init_static_fields` (codegen.rs) runs at the top of `<module>__init`
and lowers every class's `sf.init` there. At module-init scope the
factory's `params_id` is in neither `ctx.locals` nor
`ctx.module_globals`, so `Expr::LocalGet`'s soft fallback returns
`double_literal(0.0)`. The init compiles to
`js_native_call_method(0.0, "slice", null, 0)`, and the runtime's
Issue #510 primitive-receiver catch-all throws.

it with `collect_ref_ids_in_expr` (made `pub(crate)`) and check every
collected LocalId against the union of `ctx.module_globals` and
top-level `Stmt::Let` ids. When any reference is out of module scope,
skip the emit — the slot stays at the zero default. Symmetric guard
on the computed-key (`js_class_register_static_symbol`) arm.

rather than the intended value. A full fix would emit the init AT the
class-expression evaluation site inside the factory body (where the
param IS in scope), but that requires restructuring how class
expressions lower (they emit as `Expr::New { class_name }` with no
per-evaluation slot). For #321's goal of letting Schema.ts finish,
having `static params` be `undefined` is fine — module init completes
and the program runs into user code.

perf(transform): fuse __next body directly into async step closure (P1)

Each `await` inside an async function previously went through two
closure dispatches: the runtime invoked the step closure via
`js_async_step_chain`, and the step closure's body then called
`__next(value)` via a separate closure dispatch. Each call to __next
also did a captures-box re-lookup (cap_singleton_miss when consecutive
microtasks belonged to different async-function activations — common in
Promise.all kernels).

This commit inlines the entire __next body directly into the step
closure. The step closure's captures grow to include the hoisted
state-machine vars (state, done, sent, params, hoisted, extras), and
the __next closure is no longer built at all. Iter-result Returns
inside the inlined body are rewritten to `Expr(IterResultSet(...))` +
`LabeledBreak("__step_done")` so they fall through to step's post-
dispatch logic (IterResultGetDone check + AsyncStepChain) instead of
exiting step early. The __throw closure stays separate (cold path —
fusing it would tangle the state-machine catch routing).

Profile delta on benchmarks/app-patterns/kernels/promise_all_chains.ts:

| counter            |   before |    after |
|--------------------|---------:|---------:|
| closure allocs     |  201,005 |  151,004 |
| cap_singleton_miss |  150,003 |  100,002 |
| microtasks         |  201,999 |  201,999 |
| Promise allocs     |  252,001 |  252,001 |

Mechanically: 50k fewer closure allocations per kernel run and 50k
fewer cap_singleton misses on the closure-call path — one __next
closure was being allocated per unitOfWork call and dispatched 3× per
call. Sanity sweep (test_async, test_async_chain, test_async2,
test_simple_class, test_inheritance, test_break_continue,
test_array_methods, test_set, test_map, test_edge_promises,
test_gap_async_advanced, test_stress_promises,
test_issue_256_microtask_ordering — 13 tests) byte-identical to Node.
Kernel checksum stays 2500050000.

Hyperfine wall-clock impact on the kernel itself is within noise (run-
to-run variance on this kernel dominates the small per-microtask save
— 50k×~80ns = ~4ms on a 200ms run). The simpler 200k-iter per-await
probe shows the expected modest ~3% improvement post-fix. The
remaining gap to Bun (still ~8×) lives outside the closure-dispatch
path this commit attacks; see report for next-session targets.

perf(runtime+transform): reuse in-flight `next` for done-case Promise (P2)

Builds on P1 (commit bc02754). The async-step driver's done branch
previously emitted `return Promise.resolve(IterResultGetValue)` —
allocating one fresh fulfilled Promise per async function call.
The runner then propagated that Promise's value into `next` via
`propagate_callback_result`, settling `next` with the same value
and discarding the fresh wrapper.

Reuse hook: when step's done branch is hit from inside a microtask
dispatched by the runner, INLINE_TRAP_NEXT holds the in-flight `next`
Promise. New `Expr::AsyncStepDone { value, step_closure }` lowers to a
runtime helper `js_async_step_done(value, step_closure)` which (gated
by CURRENT_STEP_CLOSURE matching `step_closure`) resolves `trap_next`
with `value` in-place and returns it. Step returns that Promise; the
runner's self-chain check (`result == next`) skips the redundant
propagate hop. Net effect: zero new Promise allocations on the done
path in the steady state.

Fallback (initial entry to a no-await async function, or nested
async-fn call where outer activation owns INLINE_TRAP_NEXT): allocate
via `js_promise_resolved` exactly as before.

Profile delta on benchmarks/app-patterns/kernels/promise_all_chains.ts
(P1 → P1+P2):

perf(runtime+codegen): swap setjmp(3) → _setjmp(3) on Apple + gate profile counters (P4 + P5)

Two independent wins for async-heavy workloads on macOS, applied together
since both target the same hot path (per-microtask overhead in
`js_promise_run_microtasks` + every async-fn's setjmp/longjmp exception
trap).

## P5 (dominant) — setjmp signal-mask save was 43% of CPU on `promise_all_chains.ts`

Samply profile of the kernel showed:
  - `sigprocmask` (libsystem_kernel): 28.27% self time
  - `__sigaltstack` (libsystem_kernel): 15.02% self time
  - `setjmp -> sigprocmask` edge: 28.27% inclusive
  - `setjmp -> __sigaltstack` edge: 15.02% inclusive

Root cause: on Apple platforms the C `setjmp(3)` saves the signal mask
via a `sigprocmask` syscall and the alt-signal-stack via
`__sigaltstack`. Each pair is ~500 ns of kernel time on arm64. Perry
calls setjmp in three places, every one of them in the async fast path:

  1. `js_promise_run_microtasks` — the outer "throw out of a microtask
     body" trap (once per drain).
  2. `mark_stack_roots` in the GC — register-capture for the
     conservative stack scan (once per GC cycle).
  3. The async-to-generator transform wraps every async function's
     `__async_step` closure body in a `try { ... } catch { ... }`,
     and `try/catch` codegen emits a setjmp around the body. That
     fires once **per microtask** — 200k times on the kernel.

Switch to `_setjmp(3)` (linker symbol `__setjmp` on Mach-O = the same
function minus the sigprocmask/sigaltstack round-trips). Perry never
longjmps out of a signal handler — `js_throw` runs in normal user
context — so the signal mask doesn't need to be saved/restored across
setjmp/longjmp pairs. POSIX explicitly allows this; macOS, FreeBSD,
NetBSD, OpenBSD all ship `_setjmp/_longjmp` as the no-signal-state
variant.

  - `crates/perry-runtime/src/promise.rs`: cfg-gated extern declaration
    in `js_promise_run_microtasks` — Apple uses `#[link_name = "_setjmp"]`
    (which the Mach-O linker resolves to `__setjmp`, the fast variant).
  - `crates/perry-runtime/src/gc.rs`: same swap for the conservative
    stack scan.
  - `crates/perry-codegen/src/runtime_decls.rs`: Apple now declares
    `_setjmp` (1-arg) instead of `setjmp`.
  - `crates/perry-codegen/src/stmt.rs`: Apple now emits
    `call i32 @_setjmp(ptr %buf) #0` for `try/catch` blocks. The IR
    name `_setjmp` maps to linker `__setjmp` via the C ABI prefix.
  - `crates/perry-codegen/src/module.rs`: the `attributes #0 =
    { returns_twice }` block was guarded on `setjmp` being declared;
    now matches either `setjmp` OR `_setjmp` so the attribute group
    still gets emitted on Apple.

Linux glibc's `setjmp(3)` already does NOT save the signal mask
(POSIX leaves it implementation-defined; glibc opted for the fast
path). So Linux declarations stay on `setjmp` — no swap needed.

## P4 — gate atomic instrumentation counters on a cached runtime flag

The `MT_RUN_COUNT`, `MT_FAST_PATH_HIT/MISS`, `MT_STEP_CHAIN_REUSE_HIT/MISS`,
`MT_STEP_DONE_REUSE_HIT/MISS`, `MT_PROMISE_NEW_COUNT`,
`MT_PROMISE_THEN_COUNT`, `MT_PROMISE_RESOLVED_COUNT`,
`CLOSURE_ALLOC_COUNT`, etc. fired 3–5 unconditional
`fetch_add(1, Relaxed)`s per microtask body whether the user set
`PERRY_MT_PROFILE` or not. On Apple Silicon a relaxed atomic add is
~4-5 ns; conditional-on-flag-load is ~1 ns.

Introduce `bump(&COUNTER)` helper that checks a process-startup-cached
`AtomicBool MT_PROFILE_ENABLED` before fetching. When the flag is off
(the common production case) the body of `bump` compiles down to a
load + branch — atomically free for the steady-state hot path.

`mt_profile_register()` (called once via `std::sync::Once` from
`js_promise_run_microtasks`) reads `PERRY_MT_PROFILE` once and stores
into the flag. The `atexit` printer is only registered when profiling
is enabled — so non-profile runs don't pay an extra `atexit` hook
either.

Also replaces the per-call `std::env::var_os("PERRY_MT_PROFILE")` read
inside `js_promise_run_microtasks` with `mt_profile_enabled()` —
env-var lookup is ~30 ns; the cached load is ~1 ns.

  - `crates/perry-runtime/src/promise.rs`: define MT_PROFILE_ENABLED +
    `bump()`, replace 23 `XXX.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed)` sites
    with `bump(&XXX)`.
  - `crates/perry-runtime/src/closure.rs`: replace 3 closure-counter
    bumps in `js_closure_alloc` and the singleton-capture cache.

perf(runtime/gc): hashset-backed valid-pointer contains() — cuts try_mark_value from 28% → 8% self-time

`ValidPointerSet::contains` was the GC-mark phase's hottest call —
~28% of CPU on `promise_all_chains` (1000 batches × 50 promises × 3
awaits). With ~100k live pointers in the set, each call paid ~17 cache
misses through a 1.2 MB sorted Vec via binary search, called millions
of times per cycle while scanning closure captures + promise fields.

multiplicative hash on the pointer bits — same `PtrHasher` already
used for the malloc-state registry, no SipHash overhead). The sorted
Vec stays around for `enclosing_object`'s interior-pointer floor-
search, which can't be answered by a hash set; `contains` and its hot
callers (`try_mark_value`, `try_mark_value_or_raw`, `trace_promise`,
`trace_object`, …) flip over to the hashset.

perf(runtime): switch closure + box thread-local maps to PtrHasher, pre-size MallocState

hash cost dominated `hash_one` (4–6 % self-time on
`promise_all_chains`).

  - `DISPATCH_CACHE` (per-`func_ptr` dispatch strategy)

perf(runtime/gc): lazy MallocState lookup-set — 21% kernel improvement on promise_all_chains

`MallocState.set` was eagerly inserted/removed on every `gc_malloc`
and every sweep-freed object. With ~200 k allocations per
`promise_all_chains` kernel run, those hashbrown group-probe inserts
dominated `gc_malloc`'s caller chain (~17 % CPU after the prior
hasher fix landed).

The set's only real consumer is `gc_realloc`, which validates that an
incoming pointer is still tracked before dereferencing it. Profiling
shows that promise/closure-heavy kernels (the entire app-patterns
suite) never call `gc_realloc` at all — string concat goes through
custom paths in `string.rs` that avoid `gc_realloc` deliberately
(see the comment around `js_string_concat`). So we're paying ~17 %
CPU to maintain a data structure that almost never gets read.

Switch the set to a lazy view of `MallocState.objects`:
  - `gc_malloc` / `gc_malloc_batch` just push to `objects` and flip a
    `set_dirty` flag (one bool store vs a 50 ns hashbrown insert).
  - `sweep_with_age_bump` skips the per-object `set.remove` calls;
    flips `set_dirty` once at the end if anything was freed.
  - `gc_realloc` and the test helpers call `ensure_set_built(&mut s)`
    before any `set.contains`, which clears + extends the set from
    `objects` if dirty. Idempotent — repeated calls without dirtying
    in between are O(1).

The set's hashbrown backing storage is still pre-sized to 256 k
buckets at startup so the lazy build (when it does fire) doesn't
have to rehash. Memory pages don't fault until first written, so
workloads that never trip the rebuild path pay essentially zero.

perf(runtime/gc): specialize trace-phase field mark — bypass MARK_SEEDS and interior-ptr fallback

The trace-phase callers (`trace_closure`, `trace_array`, `trace_object`,
`trace_promise.value/.reason`, `trace_map`) all share one hot loop:

    if try_mark_value_or_raw(val_bits, ...) {
        // re-decode NaN tag to extract pointer
        let ptr_val = if tag == POINTER_TAG | STRING_TAG | BIGINT_TAG {
            (val_bits & POINTER_MASK) as usize
        } else { val_bits as usize };
        worklist.push(header_from_user_ptr(ptr_val ...));
    }

The generic `try_mark_value_or_raw` is general enough to also handle
conservative stack scans (raw interior pointers via `enclosing_object`)
and root scans (push to MARK_SEEDS so trace-marked-objects picks them
up), but BOTH features are pure overhead inside the trace drain:

1. Field words never hold interior pointers — they're written via
   `arr[i] = x` / `obj.f = x` / closure capture stores, all of which
   use the object-start user pointer. Skipping `enclosing_object`
   saves a binary-search lookup per field.

2. The MARK_SEEDS push happens once per newly-marked object, but the
   same header is immediately pushed onto the local worklist by the
   trace function. The MARK_SEEDS push is consumed at the *next*
   cycle (via `take_mark_seeds`) — extra entries during trace are
   pure waste.

3. The caller re-decodes the NaN tag a second time to extract the
   pointer. Folding the extraction and mark-and-enqueue into one
   inlined helper avoids the redundant switch.

fix(runtime): NaN equality semantics — indexOf(NaN) returns -1 (v0.5.823)

Pre-fix `[1, NaN, 3].indexOf(NaN)` returned 1 (the NaN's index).
Per ECMA-262, strict equality (===) follows IEEE 754 where NaN !== NaN,
but SameValueZero (used by includes/Map/Set keys) considers NaN === NaN.
Perry used one helper for both and got the strict-equality side wrong.

The fast path `if abits == bbits { return 1; }` matched two identical
NaN bit patterns (0x7FF8000000000000). The fast-path comment assumed
"Perry doesn't produce raw IEEE NaN as a user value" but a literal
`NaN` in source lowers to exactly f64::NAN.

Fix:
- js_jsvalue_equals: check top16 == 0x7FF8 BEFORE the bits-match
  fast path and return 0 for NaN-vs-NaN.
- New js_jsvalue_same_value_zero that returns 1 for both-NaN.
- js_array_includes_jsvalue routed through SameValueZero so
  [NaN].includes(NaN) keeps returning true.

perf(runtime/gc): malloc walk inserts directly into lookup_set — skip per-cycle 2.1M sort + merge

`build_valid_pointer_set` previously staged every malloc user pointer
into `malloc_sorted: Vec<usize>`, then `finalize()` ran
`malloc_sorted.sort_unstable()` (pdqsort) and merged it with
`arena_sorted` into `merged_sorted`, finally extending `lookup_set`
with the merged contents. On `promise_all_chains` that meant
~2.1 M Vec pushes + a 2.1M-item sort + a 2.1M-item merge + 2.1M
hashset inserts per GC cycle — `build_valid_pointer_set` inclusive
was 14.5 % of total kernel time, of which the `quicksort` alone
was 5.78 %.

Most of that work was redundant. `merged_sorted` only exists for
`enclosing_object`'s interior-pointer floor-search, and every
Perry runtime function known to hold an interior pointer across
user callbacks (`js_array_reduce`'s `elements_ptr = arr + 8`,
`js_buffer_data = buf + 8`, etc.) does so against an
*arena-allocated* array/buffer. Malloc-tracked types (Closure,
Promise, String, Map, Error, BigInt, Symbol) are accessed
exclusively at their user pointer (object start) — they never
give rise to interior-pointer probes.

So: drop `malloc_sorted` and `push_malloc()` entirely; insert
malloc user pointers *directly* into `lookup_set` during the
build walk; track the malloc address range via a cheap
`record_malloc_for_range` min/max update so `maybe_contains`'s
`[range_min, range_max]` prefilter still rejects out-of-range
candidates correctly. `merged_sorted` is now arena-only,
populated by a single `std::mem::swap` from `arena_sorted`.

Numbers on promise_all_chains × 10 (10000 batches × 50 inputs,
hyperfine --warmup 5 --runs 20):
  before: min 576 ms / mean 588 ms
  after:  min 517 ms / mean 589 ms      -10.2 % min, -0 % mean
Total samples (samply, sample-count): `build_valid_pointer_set`
inclusive 14.52 % -> 7.95 %; `quicksort` (was `malloc_sorted.sort_unstable`)
5.78 % -> ~0 %; `hashbrown::insert` 6.60 % -> 7.76 % (same total
inserts, just no longer behind the sort+merge).

checksums; 1M-closure+promise stress probe (1000×1000 batches)

test: microtask ordering invariant probe suite (7 probes)

Pre-work for an upcoming structural change that may bypass the
microtask queue for synchronously-resolved inner Promises. These
probes pin down the ordering invariants that change MUST preserve.

Each probe tests one specific Promise/await/then interleaving
pattern against Node. All 7 currently pass byte-identical to
`node --experimental-strip-types`:

  01_two_fn_interleave        — 2 async fns alternate on each await
  02_then_vs_await_fifo       — .then + await share the same FIFO queue
  03_chained_then_interleave  — 2 .then chains interleave step-by-step
  04_await_caller_callee      — outer await(inner) preserves sibling
                                ordering across inner's own awaits
  05_nested_promise_unwrap    — `await Promise.resolve(Promise<v>)`
                                takes 2 microtask hops; sibling lands
                                between them
  06_finally_after_await      — try/finally preserves microtask
                                boundaries around finally body
  07_promise_all_mixed        — Promise.all of mixed async + resolved
                                inputs; result-order = input-order

Notes on dropped probes (existing Perry/Node divergences, separate
issues — not relevant to this suite's purpose):

  - queueMicrotask + await/then FIFO ordering: Perry batches qm
    callbacks together; Node interleaves them with then/await
  - try/catch around `await Promise.reject(...)`: Perry inserts an
    extra microtask hop between catch body and post-catch code
  - deep async recursion: Perry drops the final result line entirely

perf(transform): #691 skip __async_throw alloc when no awaiting try/catch (v0.5.843)

Phase 1 of issue #691 (Bun-gap on promise_all_chains). Re-profiled the
~84% callback bucket with PERRY_MT_PROFILE=1 across a 0/1/2/3-await
sweep — the gap is per-invocation state-machine setup, not per-state
dispatch (perry's first-await delta over bun is +12 ms; additional
awaits roughly even). The dominant per-invocation cost is closure
allocation (3 per call, 2 of which carry user captures and miss the
captured-singleton cache).

When linearize_body reports no awaiting try/catch (catches.is_empty()),
the throw closure body collapses to a single Stmt::Throw(__throw_val)
rethrow that references zero captures. build_async_step_driver_direct
now accepts Option<Expr> for the throw closure and, when None, emits
Stmt::Throw(value) inline in the dispatch's is-error arm — the outer
try/catch then re-enters __step(e, true) which short-circuits to
Promise.reject (semantics identical). Skips the let __async_throw =
... outer stmt and drops throw_id from step's captures.

min-runs=50): perry 41.7 -> 37.1 ms (-11%, min 40.5 -> 35.5), perry/bun

invocation), cap_singleton_miss 999,000 -> 499,500, callback bucket
37.5 -> 32.1 ms (-14%).

perf(transform): #691 Phase 3 strip await Promise.resolve(<non-Promise>) (v0.5.855)

Pre-pass in `transform_async_to_generator` (before `hoist_awaits_in_stmts`)
rewrites `Await(Call(PropertyGet(GlobalGet(0) /* Promise */, "resolve"), [arg]))`
to `Await(arg)` whenever `arg` is statically provable to be non-Promise.

Discovered via a manually-stripped variant of `promise_all_chains.ts`
showing -20% wall-time on perry while remaining byte-equal in
checksum. Profile diff confirms the lever: callback bucket 63.5 ->
23.8 ms (-63%), `new` Promise allocations 201,899 -> 51,949 (-150k,
exactly 3 per `unitOfWork` invocation), `resolved=149,951 -> 1`,
`fast_path: hit=0 -> 149,950` — the `is_definitely_primitive` branch
in `js_async_step_chain` now hits 100% of the time instead of going
through the unwrap-Fulfilled-inner code path.

Result on promise_all_chains: 41.7 -> 28.5 ms min (perry was 1.77x
slower than bun -> roughly on par on min; today's bun system was noisy
so the precise ratio jitters). The lever wasn't reachable via per-
state-transition or per-invocation closure work (the Phase 1/2 levers)
because the dominant cost was per-await **Promise allocation**
wrapping a primitive that was about to be unwrapped on the next line.

Spec-equivalence: for non-Promise arg, `await arg` and
`await Promise.resolve(arg)` both take exactly one microtask hop,
resolve to the same value, and don't trigger thenable resolution. The
analyzer's `is_non_promise_expr` returns false for any expression that
could carry a Promise (Calls, locals with Type::Any/Unknown/Object/
Function/Promise/Named/Generic, etc.) — probe 05's
`await Promise.resolve(<Promise>)` shape is NOT stripped because its
inner is a `Call` (Promise.resolve(42)) bound to a const with
inferred Type::Any.

Implementation: HashSet<LocalId> seeded from func params with
non-Promise types (Number, Int32, Boolean, String, Void, Null,
BigInt, Symbol), propagated through Stmt::Let inits — a let whose
init is a non-Promise expression (literal, arithmetic/compare/logical
op of non-Promise children, LocalGet of a non-Promise local, or
Await of a non-Promise — recursive: the Await's resolved value is
its inner when inner is non-Promise) adds its id to the set. So
chains like:

  async function unitOfWork(i: number) {
    const a = await Promise.resolve(i);       // i: Number -> strip
    const b = await Promise.resolve(a + 1);   // a: non-Promise, 1: literal -> strip
    const c = await Promise.resolve(b * 2);   // b: non-Promise, 2: literal -> strip
    return c;
  }

get all three awaits stripped. Closure-typed expr children aren't
traversed (`Expr::Closure { .. }` is its own scope; nested closures
are handled by the outer pipeline independently).

Validation: 26/28 gap tests (same 2 pre-existing failures:
console_methods, regexp_advanced), all 7 microtask_inv_* probes
byte-equal to Node (including probe 05 which is not a strip target),
test_issue_256_microtask_ordering passes, `cargo test --release
--workspace` clean.

fix(hir,runtime): #665 accessor mis-categorised as field + Object.keys mutation (v0.5.862)

Two fixes in one. Both surfaced from the user's residual rate-limiter-flexible
bisect on issue #665 after the v0.5.848 class-expression rewrite + v0.5.839
super()-no-op fixes landed.

Primary (#665): when a class declares `get X` / `set X` AND the constructor
body writes `this.X = ...`, lower_decl.rs's "infer fields from ctor body
`this.x = ...`" pass mis-categorised `X` as an own data field. The spurious
slot surfaced via Object.keys and shadowed the inherited getter at read time
(runtime getter dispatch only fires when no own slot is present), so
`m.points` returned 0 instead of going through `get points()` even though
the setter had literally run and stored `_points = 7` correctly.

Fix in `crates/perry-hir/src/lower_decl.rs`: before the bare-`this.X = Y`
field-inference loop, collect the union of own + inherited accessor names
and skip the `fields.push` when the candidate matches. New
`class_accessor_names` registry on LoweringContext mirrors the existing
`class_field_names` (own+inherited union, single-hop lookup from child).

Side bug uncovered and fixed (Object.keys mutation): while writing a
regression test that called `Object.keys(m).sort()` to get deterministic
key ordering, the sort scrambled subsequent property reads —
`m._points` returned `60` instead of `7`. Root cause:
`js_object_keys`'s no-descriptor fast path returned the object's internal
`keys_array` pointer directly. That array is the source of truth for
both Object.keys AND the runtime's key-name → slot-index mapping.
`.sort()` mutated keys_array in place, and the next `obj.foo` lookup
walked a now-reordered key list against an unchanged `obj.fields[]`
slot vector. Per ECMA-262 §7.3.23 Object.keys must return a fresh array.
Fix mirrors the slow path's existing emit: alloc new array, copy bits.

Validation: single-file accessor repro, user's exact rlfshape cross-module
bisect (both declaration + expression form), Object.keys.sort probe all
byte-identical to Node. New `test-files/test_issue_665_accessor_field_inference.ts`
covers the subclass + inherited-accessor case. Full workspace test suite

fix(codegen): closure mutation across await/.then/.finally propagates (v0.5.866)

Three sibling boxing-analysis walkers in `boxed_vars.rs` had silent `_ => {}`
catch-alls that never recursed into Expr::Await, Yield, TypeOf, Void, etc.

was therefore invisible — `closure_refs`/`closure_writes` came back empty,
the captured-and-mutated id was excluded from `boxed_vars`, and both ends
compiled non-box paths. The closure mutated its own capture slot while the
outer post-await read saw the initial value.

Fix: replace the catch-all with a delegating fallback to
`perry_hir::walker::walk_expr_children` (the project's single source of truth
for child traversal) in all three walkers. Walker skips Closure body by
design, matching each caller's "stop at closure boundary" semantics — refs
inside nested closures still picked up via the explicit Closure arm.

fix(codegen): throw / await-reject in is_async fn rejects promise instead of crashing (v0.5.869)

`async function f() { throw new Error("x"); }; f().then(_, e=>...)` printed
the error to stderr and exited 1 instead of running the rejection handler.
Same for `await Promise.reject(...)` with no enclosing try.

Root cause: Stmt::Throw and the Await reject-branch unconditionally lowered
to js_throw → longjmp → setjmp frame, but transform_async_to_generator bails
out of the state-machine rewrite when (a) the body contains any capturing
closure (very common — any `.then(cb)` / `forEach` / etc.) or (b) the body
has no await. Those bail-outs leave the function as `is_async: true` at
codegen time with no implicit try-catch wrapper, so a literal throw or
awaited rejection had no setjmp frame to land in and the runtime aborted.
ECMA-262 §15.8 says any abrupt completion of an async function must reject
its returned promise.

Fix: at both lowering sites, when `ctx.is_async_fn && ctx.try_depth == 0`,
emit `return js_promise_rejected(value)` (NaN-boxed) instead. Two-condition
guard: is_async_fn rules out sync fns (unwind is correct); try_depth==0
rules out throws inside a user try-block (the existing setjmp catch fires).
State-machined async fns have is_async_fn=false at codegen time, so the
guard naturally doesn't apply and their existing AsyncStepDone driver
keeps handling abrupt completions.

`try { await inner_async_that_rejects() } catch` (state-machine bug)
captured as follow-up. Gap parity 26/28 unchanged.

fix(transform): try { await reject } catch { return X } no longer hangs (v0.5.870)

State-machine async-to-generator's `__async_throw` closure inlined the
user catch body verbatim. When the catch body contained `return X`, the
literal `Stmt::Return(X)` exited `__async_throw` with X — but the calling
step body discards that return value. The iter-result scratch slots
retained the awaited-promise's stale data (the rejected promise, done=false),
so the step's post-dispatch chained the same rejected promise → infinite
loop, outer promise never settled.

Fix: before inlining the catch body, walk it with a new
`rewrite_catch_returns_to_iter_result` helper that rewrites every
`Stmt::Return(Some(X))` to `Stmt::Return(Some(make_iter_result(X, true)))`
and `Stmt::Return(None)` to the equivalent with `undefined`. Recurses
through If/While/For/Try/Switch/Labeled but NOT nested closures
(those returns belong to their own closure). The existing
`rewrite_iter_results_to_scratch` pass then converts the iter-result
into scratch-slot writes + actual return value, so the catch body's
`return X` now properly hands back (value=X, done=true) to the step
driver and the outer promise resolves with X.

Pre-fix bug masked by the fact that most async catches don't `return X`
(`catch (e) { console.error(e) }` falls through and the post-catch
state-dispatch path works fine). 5-case probe_catch_return.ts: 4/5 match
Bun (t4 await-inside-catch still broken — separate state-machine gap,
captured as follow-up). All earlier fixes preserved; gap parity 26/28
unchanged.

fix(compile): force `crypto` feature in auto-optimized stdlib (v0.5.871)

perry-stdlib unconditionally re-bundles perry-updater (so user code
calling `perry/updater` resolves at link time). perry-updater's
`perry_updater_verify_signature_v2` references the extern symbol
`js_crypto_ed25519_verify`, which only exists when perry-stdlib is
built with `feature = "crypto"`. The auto-optimize path passes
`--no-default-features` and only adds features inferred from user
imports, so `crypto` is off for any user binary that doesn't
explicitly import a crypto API — and the link fails on
`undefined reference to js_crypto_ed25519_verify` from the bundled
updater object.

Surfaced when v0.5.868 re-enabled the gtk4 doc-tests entry; the
gtk4 link path triggers the auto-optimize rebuild, the rebuilt
stdlib didn't include crypto, and every doc-test failed to link.

Forces `crypto` on always (mirrors how `async-runtime` is forced
when `ctx.needs_ui` for the same reason — bundled object code
that needs a symbol gated behind a feature).

fix(transform,runtime): await inside catch handlers returns the right value (v0.5.872)

Two coordinated fixes for the realistic try/catch+await shape.

Bug 1 (transform): the blanket `await→yield` rewrite in
transform_async_to_generator ran on the whole function body before
linearize_body classified states. Catch bodies get inlined into the
`__async_throw` closure verbatim, but that closure is is_async=false
is_generator=false, so an `Expr::Yield` in its body hit
`Expr::Yield => double_literal(0.0)` in codegen. The await operand was
evaluated for side effects, the result discarded, `const r = await ...`
inside a catch silently bound `r = 0`.

Fix 1: before inlining the catch body, walk it with a new
`rewrite_yield_to_await_in_stmts` helper that flips every
`Expr::Yield(v)` back to `Expr::Await(v)` recursively, stopping at
nested closure boundaries. Catch-body awaits now route through the
busy-wait codegen path which works correctly inside __async_throw
(invoked from Task::AsyncStep dispatch; re-entrant drains are
no-ops on empty queues).

Bug 2 (runtime, surfaced by fix 1): once awaits inside catches
executed, the OUTER promise still resolved with the inner's value
("helpC" instead of "got: helpC"). `js_async_first_call` preserved
the outer trap_next, so the inner step's AsyncStepChain satisfied
can_reuse and resolved the outer's trap_next with the inner's
intermediate value. Top-level `await innerAsync()` coincidentally
worked because outer continuation overwrote it; busy-wait path
inside __async_throw doesn't have that overwrite.

Fix 2: clear trap_next to null in js_async_first_call (preserving
prev for restore). Inner async fns now allocate their own next
promise. Outer's trap_next is untouched.

fix(transform): break/continue inside loops containing await no longer hang (v0.5.875)

`for (let i ...) { await ...; if (cond) break; }` hung forever — the
state-machine emitted by linearize_body left user `Stmt::Break` and
`Stmt::Continue` as raw HIR nodes that exited the dispatch loop
without setting a proper exit state. Post-dispatch read the scratch
iter-result set by the in-flight await (done=false), returned
AsyncStepChain on a stale promise, and the chain looped forever.

Two coordinated additions in For/While arms of linearize_body:

(1) Pre-walk the body before recursing and rewrite top-level
    `Stmt::Break` to `[LocalSet(state_id, BREAK_SENTINEL); Continue]`
    and `Stmt::Continue` to the equivalent with CONTINUE_SENTINEL.
    Walker recurses through If/Try/Switch/Labeled but stops at
    nested loop / closure boundaries (their break/continue belong
    to those constructs).

(2) For for-loops, restructure into TWO post-body states: a
    `tail_state` (residual post-yield body, exits to update_state)
    and an `update_state` (update expression only, exits to
    cond_state). User `continue` jumps to update_state (the
    update-only state); body's natural fall-through goes
    tail → update. Without this split, conflating tail+update
    causes `continue` to re-execute the body residual and loop
    forever on the same iteration.

(3) After body linearization, walk new states and replace sentinels
    with the loop's real targets. Inner loops fix their own
    sentinels first via recursive call, so outer-loop fix-up only
    sees outer-loop sentinels.

feat(cache): closes #686 — HIR-addressable per-module object cache (Plan C) (#688)

* feat(cache): closes #686 — HIR-addressable per-module object cache (Plan C)

Replace the V2.2 source-bytes hash in the per-module object cache key
with a deterministic fingerprint of the post-transform HIR that
`perry_codegen::compile_module` actually consumes. Formatter-only
edits, comment changes, quote-style rewrites, and any other source
change that lowers to identical final HIR now hit the cached `.o`.

New `perry_hir::stable_hash` module walks the HIR with an exhaustive
match (no wildcards) over every variant, so adding a new HIR variant
breaks the build and forces the author to assign a stable tag and
walk children. The only HashMap reachable from `Module`
(`ObjectType.properties`) is sorted by key before emit.

Hash is computed inside the rayon per-module job, after every
HIR-mutating pass has run. `compile_module(&Module, ...)` is
documented as load-bearing — switching to `&mut` would have to also
move the hash to AFTER codegen.

Diagnostics: `PERRY_DEV_VERBOSE=1` now prints per-miss `hir=<...>
key=<...>` lines; `PERRY_CACHE_DEBUG_HIR=1` dumps the post-transform
HIR of every miss to `.perry-cache/debug/<key>.txt` so two miss-dumps
can be diffed.

Tests: new `stable_hash` unit tests (5) cover insertion-order
independence, behavior-vs-cosmetic differentiation, and per-field
metadata sensitivity. New `cross_process.rs` integration test spawns
an example binary twice via `cargo run --example` and asserts
byte-identical stdout — the only way to catch a forgotten HashMap
sort, since Rust's RandomState only randomizes between processes.
`scripts/run_cache_tests.sh` gains cosmetic-edit and behavior-edit
steps end-to-end.

* fix(stable_hash): cover Expr::AsyncStepDone variant + minor fmt

Rebased onto upstream main (v0.5.811 → v0.5.818). Upstream added
`Expr::AsyncStepDone { value, step_closure }` (#688 P2 work, commit
b216cef1) which the exhaustive match in `stable_hash.rs` did not
cover, breaking CI with E0004. Added the variant with tag 442 and
walked both children. Other small rustfmt-driven whitespace fixes
on touched files.

* fix(stable_hash): cover 4 new Expr variants from upstream merges

Two `main` merges into this branch (v0.5.818 → v0.5.867) added four
HIR variants the exhaustive walker did not yet cover, breaking the
build with E0004:

- Expr::CurrentStepClosure (tag 443) — #691 Phase 2 async-step opt
- Expr::AsyncFirstCall { step_closure } (tag 444) — same series
- Expr::TaggedTemplateStrings { cooked, raw } (tag 445) — tagged
  template literals

perf(ci): PERRY_NO_AUTO_OPTIMIZE skips per-test cargo rebuild (v0.5.885)

Each doc-test runs `perry compile`, which calls `build_optimized_libs`
to rebuild runtime+stdlib with a feature-set hashed from the user's
imports. Different tests → different feature sets → different
`target/perry-auto-<hash>/` cache dirs → cargo starts from scratch
for each. We saw `stdlib/database/snippets.ts` take 260s, several
others 60-120s — multiplied by 80+ tests, this dominates the
macOS doc-tests job wall-time.

`PERRY_NO_AUTO_OPTIMIZE=1` short-circuits the rebuild in
`build_optimized_libs`, returning empty libs. The link path then
falls back to `find_runtime_library` / `find_stdlib_library`
which probe `target/release/` for the prebuilt artifacts.

`scripts/run_doc_tests.sh` now pre-builds runtime+stdlib once with
default features (which is `["full"]`, so every doc-test import
resolves) and exports the env var for all subsequent invocations.

Local verification: language/type_system.ts went from ~30s (cold
auto-optimize rebuild) to 2.5s (cache-hit, link-only). Estimated
macOS doc-tests wall-time reduction: ~25-35 min.

Reversible: env var off → old per-test rebuild behavior.

well-known-binding lookup out of build_optimized_libs so it runs
even when auto-optimize is skipped. Tracked separately.

Net: 86/88 → 87/87 doc-tests passing, with 21 min execute-time

needs HIR extends_expr plumbing + dynamic class registration at the
class declaration site + Function.prototype-assignment modeling, which
is a multi-day class-model restructure. Research findings posted as a
GH comment so the next engineer can pick up from concrete pointers.

* fix(hir,codegen,runtime): #711 — class X extends fn(...) wires parent edge dynamically (v0.5.872)

HIR's extends-clause lowering previously dropped any non-Ident/Member
super-class shape, so `class Lowercased extends String$.pipe(...)` lost
its parent edge and method dispatch on instances couldn't walk through
to inherited methods. The user-visible symptom in Effect@3.21.2 was
Schema.ts__init throwing `TypeError: pipe is not a function` (issue #711).

Three coordinated changes:

1. HIR: new `extends_expr: Option<Box<Expr>>` field on Class. New
   variant `Expr::RegisterClassParentDynamic { class_name, parent_expr }`
   wired into walker traversal and cross-module body scanning.

2. Runtime: `js_register_class_parent_dynamic(class_id, value)` extracts
   a parent class_id from value (ClassRef payload for INT32-tagged,
   ObjectHeader.class_id for POINTER-tagged) and wires the (child,
   parent) edge into CLASS_REGISTRY. No-ops for non-class values, rejects
   self-registration.

3. Codegen: at the class-declaration source position, emits
   `Stmt::Expr(Expr::RegisterClassParentDynamic { ... })` into module.init
   so the extends expression's free variables (imports, top-level let,
   factory functions) are already initialized when we evaluate the
   parent. Codegen of the new variant evaluates parent_expr and calls
   the runtime helper.

New regression test test_issue_711_extends_call.ts covers free-fn
call, member call on Ident, `new` expression, and chained dynamic
extends (parent-of-parent also dynamic) — all byte-identical to Node.

Effect advances past the original pipe-not-a-function throw. A
remaining throw (`value is not a function`) traces to the
`function Base() {}; Base.prototype = X` prototype-assignment pattern
in effectable.ts — Perry has no analogue for that yet. Tracked as a
follow-up still under #711.

* fix(hir,codegen,runtime): #711 part 2 — Function.prototype = X dispatch (v0.5.873)

Effect's internal/effectable.ts declares classes via prototype-object
assignment on a plain function (`function Base() {}; Base.prototype =
CommitPrototype`). Method dispatch on instances of `class Derived
extends Base {}` previously failed because Perry had no analogue for
this pattern — Base isn't a class, so `extends_name` resolved to None
and the parent edge in CLASS_REGISTRY was never registered.

Three coordinated changes:

1. Runtime side-tables: FUNCTION_CLASS_IDS (func bits → synthetic class
   id), CLASS_PROTOTYPE_OBJECTS (synthetic cid → proto ObjectHeader
   address). NEXT_SYNTHETIC_CLASS_ID starts at 0x8000_0000 to avoid
   collision with codegen-assigned ids. New
   `js_set_function_prototype` allocates the synthetic id and binds
   both maps. `js_register_class_parent_dynamic` extends to detect
   closure parent values via `function_class_id` lookup.

2. Method dispatch: both `js_native_call_method` and
   `js_object_get_field_by_name` chain walks now consult
   `class_prototype_object(cur_cid)` and resolve the method as an
   own-property of the proto, called with IMPLICIT_THIS bound to the
   receiver. Matches the JS `Function.prototype.foo.call(this, ...)`
   semantic.

3. HIR + codegen: new `Expr::SetFunctionPrototype` variant emitted
   when `<expr>.prototype = <value>` is detected in HIR's two
   assignment-target lowering paths. The Ident arm of the extends
   clause now falls through to extends_expr capture when the parent
   ident isn't a known class — the common case for
   `class Derived extends Base` where Base is a function.

Regression test test_issue_711_function_prototype.ts covers bare-fn
and Effect's IIFE shapes — both byte-identical to Node. Full
workspace cargo test --release clean (133 buckets).

Effect Schema.ts still throws on a separate pattern (likely

prototype-object blocker.

* fix(codegen): #665 — default-import collision no longer mints phantom cross-class method symbols (v0.5.896)

When two different classes are both default-imported in the same file,
the `class_ids` / `imported_class_prefix` / `imported_class_source_name`
side maps in `compile_module` overwrote each other (last-writer-wins)
while `class_table` kept the first stub (first-writer-wins). The
mismatch produced method symbols mangled with FIRST stub's method list
+ LAST writer's class name + LAST writer's source prefix — names the
linker can't resolve since Phase F only declares each ic's REAL

* fix(codegen,runtime): #665 — setTimeout(fn, delay, ...args) forwards trailing args (v0.5.897)

Existing `"setTimeout" if args.len() == 2` arm only handled the 2-arg
shape; 3+ arg call sites (e.g. `setTimeout(resolve, delay, res)` inside
Promise executors per ECMA-262 §27.5.4.1) fell through to the generic
ExternFuncRef fallthrough and emitted `call @setTimeout(...)` against a
symbol nothing in stdlib defines. Discovering call site:
`RateLimiterMemory.consume()`'s Promise executor in rate-limiter-flexible.

Adds:
- `CallbackTimer::args: Vec<f64>` (empty for 2-arg shape — back-compat).
- `js_set_timeout_callback_args(callback, delay_ms, args_ptr, n_args)`

- `js_callback_timer_tick` dispatch via `match args.len()` to
  `js_closure_call0..js_closure_call9`, clamping at 9 trailing args.
- Codegen `"setTimeout" if args.len() >= 3` arm: alloca a stack buffer

Refs #665. See CHANGELOG.md for full root-cause + scope notes.

* fix(hir): #665 — compilePackages-opted-in packages skip native-instance lowering (v0.5.898)

HIR's `is_native_module` only consulted the NATIVE_MODULES manifest, so
`rate-limiter-flexible` was lowered as a native import regardless of the
user's `compilePackages` opt-in. That cascaded:

  register_native_module(local, "rate-limiter-flexible", ...)
    → new RateLimiterMemory(...) triggers
  register_native_instance(limiter, "rate-limiter-flexible", "RateLimiterMemory")
    → limiter.consume in expr_member::lower_member emits
  NativeMethodCall { module, object: Some(limiter), method: "consume", args: [] }
    → codegen routes to js_native_call_method → no FFI entry → 0.0

So `typeof limiter.consume === "number"`. For genuine native bindings
(req.method on http.IncomingMessage) this zero-arg-getter lowering is
correct; for compile-package-overridden classes it's wrong because
`consume` is a real method, not a getter.

Fix: add a thread-local `COMPILE_PACKAGES_OVERRIDE: HashSet<String>` in
perry-hir, set by the compiler driver via
`set_compile_packages_override(ctx.compile_packages.clone())` before
each `lower_module_full` invocation and cleared after.
`is_native_module` parses the package name (supports `node:` prefix +
`@scope/pkg` scoped form) and returns false when the package is in the
override even if it appears in NATIVE_MODULES.

Validation: rate-limiter-flexible probe now reports `typeof
limiter.consume: function` (was "number"). Workspace tests green.

Refs #665. See CHANGELOG.md for full root-cause walkthrough.

- `v8::TryCatch::new(scope)` → `v8::tc_scope!(tc_scope, scope)`

## Stack-limit override removed

Pre-bump `JsRuntimeState::new` called `Isolate::SetStackLimit` via the
Itanium-mangled `_ZN2v87Isolate13SetStackLimitEm` (since v8 0.106
didn't expose it in the Rust bindings). After the bump, calling that
symbol while the isolate is not entered silently exits the process
with exit code 0 — v8 147's stack-guard aborts cleanly instead of
crashing.

That's what was killing the three parity tests
(test_issue_248_phase2_js_interop, test_issue_248_phase2b_js_callback,
test_issue_255_jsruntime_reentrancy) — every test that loaded a .js
module called js_runtime_init → JsRuntimeState::new → silent exit.

Removed the manual override entirely; v8 147 picks a sane default
stack limit from the calling thread's bounds and deno_core::scope!
pins the isolate properly for each work scope.

feat(wasm): closes #76 — runtime WebAssembly host (PoC, wasmi) (#705)

* feat(wasm): closes #76 — runtime WebAssembly host (PoC, wasmi)

Lets a binary built for `--target macos/linux/windows/ios/android` load
third-party `.wasm` modules at runtime via `WebAssembly.instantiate(...)`
— closing the host-side gap with Node and matching the issue's PoC scope.

Engine: wasmi 0.50 (pure-Rust interpreter), in a separate
`perry-wasm-host` crate so the default Perry build never pulls wasmi in.
Linking is auto-detected when codegen sees any `WebAssembly.*` reference;
the `--enable-wasm-runtime` flag stays available to force-link for
dlopen/FFI scenarios that have no static reference.

Surface (Perry MVP shape; standard async surface tracked as follow-up):
  const bytes = embedWasm("./add.wasm");          // compile-time embed
  const inst  = WebAssembly.instantiate(bytes);   // sync, opaque handle
  inst.exports.add(2, 3);                         // standard JS shape
  WebAssembly.callExport(inst, "add", 2, 3);      // explicit helper
  WebAssembly.validate(bytes);                    // bool

`inst.exports.<method>(...)` is recognised syntactically when the local
was tagged at var-decl time as a wasm instance (init was
`WebAssembly.instantiate(...)`) — this avoids stealing unrelated
`module.exports.foo()` calls from CJS aggregators. `embedWasm("...")`
reads the file at HIR-lower time relative to the importing source and
bakes the bytes into the binary as a `Uint8Array` literal (sidesteps the
in-flight TC39 import-attributes proposal per maintainer preference on
the issue thread).

The `js_webassembly_*` shims in perry-runtime forward to a stable C ABI
on perry-wasm-host. perry-runtime never depends on wasmi at the cargo
level — link-time resolution only. Programs without any `WebAssembly.*`
usage stay exactly the same size (verified: 0.9MB vs 1.9MB on the test).

fix: #733 perry-main stack overflow on `return self(...)` (v0.5.900) (#743)

`transform_async_to_generator`'s inliner unconditionally substitutes
single-Return-of-Call bodies at the call site. For a function whose body
is `return self(args)`, the substituted result is another call to
`self`, which the enclosing `inline_calls_in_expr` immediately re-inlines,
and the recursion is unbounded → perry-main blows its 64 MB Windows
stack.

Two-line repro: `function foo(): any { return foo(); }; foo();`

Surfaced via valibot-visit's transpiled `getSchemaByIssuePath`
recursing through `findAsControlAction` → `schemaForEach`. The user's
exact import (`import {} from "@piying/valibot-visit"` with valibot +
valibot-visit in `compilePackages`) now compiles to a 3.6 MB binary
instead of overflowing during HIR processing.

Fix: add `body_calls_func(body, fn.id)` to `is_inlinable`. Walks
statements/expressions for any `Expr::Call { callee: FuncRef(target) }`
where `target == fn.id`. Closure bodies skipped — a self-reference
inside a nested closure isn't a same-frame inlining target.

`fib(10) === 55` still works: fib's body is `[If, Return(self+self)]`
which had been rejected by other gates anyway (body.len() > 1).

fix(gc): #745 — JSON polyglot RSS regression (v0.5.900) (#750)

* fix(gc): #745 — JSON polyglot RSS regression (v0.5.903)

`gc_bump_malloc_trigger` was ratcheting the bytes-trigger up on every
gc-suppressed parse. For a single 108 MB parse (json_pipeline_full,
v0.5.279's original optimization target) that's correct. For a 50-iter
loop of `JSON.parse + discard` (json_polyglot's ~5 MB parses) it
suppressed GC entirely — the trigger climbed hundreds of MB above the
actual live set before allocation could catch up.

Two guards in gc.rs:

1. GC_TRIGGER_BUMPED — bump the trigger at most once per GC cycle.
   Flag is cleared at the top of gc_collect_inner (covers full,
   minor, manual gc(), and malloc-count trigger paths).

2. GC_PRE_SUPPRESS_BYTES — gc_suppress snapshots arena_total_bytes()
   so the bump can compute actual parse growth. Skip the bump if
   growth is below 32 MB. This cleanly separates json_pipeline_full
   (108 MB parse, bumps) from json_polyglot (~5 MB parse, no bump).

Validation: lazy-roundtrip 250 → 215 MB (-14%), lazy-field-access
407 → 246 MB (-39%) at unchanged wall time. GC fires 2× per polyglot
run vs 0× pre-fix. perry-runtime tests 250/0/0.

* fix(gc): #745 follow-up — preserve test_memory_json_churn (revised guards)

CI run on PR #750 surfaced a regression in
test_memory_json_churn.ts: under all three GC profiles (default,
mark-sweep, gen-gc+wb) the test went from PASS at ~120 MB pre-fix
to FAIL at 461 MB (limit 250 MB). The churn test allocates ~13 KB
per iteration across 5k iterations into a deliberately fragmented
arena where every block holds both live and dead objects — so a
GC cycle sweeps 91-95% of bytes dead but reclaims *zero* blocks,
step-doubles on the productive sweep heuristic, raises the trigger,
and the cascade compounds. The original bytes-bump correctly
deferred GC indefinitely on that shape; my v0.5.900 fix made GC
fire and exposed the fragmentation cascade.

Revised the guards to gate on the suppressed window's actual arena
growth and split tiny-parse vs medium-or-larger parse handling:

  (1) `GC_PRE_SUPPRESS_BYTES` — gc_suppress snapshots arena_total
      so gc_bump_malloc_trigger can compute parse_growth.

  (2) `GC_TRIGGER_BUMPED` — once-per-cycle flag, applied only when
      parse_growth >= 1 MB (the json_pipeline_full and
      json_polyglot shapes). Cleared at the top of gc_collect_inner
      so all collection entry points re-arm. Tiny parses (< 1 MB,
      the churn shape) bypass the flag and bump every call, which
      preserves the pre-fix deferred-GC behavior.

  (3) Step cap at `GC_THRESHOLD_INITIAL_BYTES` (64 MB) — bound the
      bump's effective step so post-73a48ced step-doubling can't
      grant hundreds of MB of headroom per bump.

fix(perry-ext-fastify): #747 + #746 — event_loop + wait_for_promise pump stdlib (v0.5.904) (#751)

The perry-stdlib→perry-ext port (v0.5.572) dropped the
`js_stdlib_process_pending` call that the original
`crates/perry-stdlib/src/fastify/server.rs` had at the top of every
event-loop tick. As a result, any program combining `fastify` with
a perry-ext-* wrapper (ws, net, http, fetch) saw its listener
callbacks stranded the moment `app.listen()` entered its loop —
events accumulated on tokio workers but the JS main thread never
drained the per-wrapper queues. The user's hub reproduced this as
"`wss.on('connection', cb)` never fires" on v0.5.700–v0.5.892, filed
as #746; the underlying defect is in perry-ext-fastify, filed as

1. extern "C" block: declare `js_run_stdlib_pump` (defined in
   `crates/perry-runtime/src/lib.rs:177`).
2. `event_loop`: call `js_run_stdlib_pump()` ahead of
   `js_promise_run_microtasks()`, matching perry-stdlib's order.
3. `wait_for_promise`: same call inside the per-iteration body,
   for parity with `crates/perry-stdlib/src/fastify/server.rs:432`
   (defense-in-depth — the codegen-emitted `await` loop at
   `crates/perry-codegen/src/expr.rs:9500` already pumps stdlib,
   so this only matters for the rare case where a route handler
   returns a Promise resolved by an external mechanism without an
   inner `await` chain).

Validation:

- Fastify + WS combo before fix: `[wss listening]` + `[wss connection
  fired]` never print; after fix: both fire on the next tick.
- Pure-WS minimal repro: already passed on macOS at HEAD (covered
  by the codegen-emitted main event loop's existing pump call). The
  combined fastify+ws path is what the hub actually exercises, so
  this closes #746 in practice.
- Multi-await fastify handler (3× Promise.resolve + reply.code(201))
  returns correct JSON in 4 ms.
- Multi-await perry-ext-bcrypt chain (2× hash + 1× compare inside a
  POST handler) returns correct JSON in 4 ms.
- `cargo test --release -p perry-ext-fastify`: 10 passed.
- `cargo test --release --workspace --exclude perry-ui-{ios,tvos,
  watchos,visionos,android,windows,gtk4}`: exit 0.

pool.exec(...)` chain to stall after the first INSERT, but a
perry-ext-bcrypt chain (same shape, same queue_promise_resolution
mechanism) works fine without the wait_for_promise pump — the
codegen-emitted await loop pumps stdlib on every iteration, so
inner awaits don't strand. The actual #748 root cause needs
reproduction with a real @perryts/mysql + MySQL setup and is left
open.

perf: closes #753 — skip eager init for modules reached only via dynamic import() (#768)

Follow-up to #100/#752. The dynamic-import resolver registered every
target as a regular Import with `is_dynamic: true` and put it in the
eager init chain at program start — functionally correct, but a heavy
locale bundle or optional feature module was paid upfront even when no
dispatch site ever fired.

Reachability classification (compile.rs): fixed-point pass starting from
the entry, propagating Eager across non-type-only static imports and
re-export sources. Everything unmarked is Deferred. Writes the result
to each Module::init_kind (HIR field from #100, no codegen consulted
it before).

Codegen (codegen.rs + expr.rs):
- Entry main filters `deferred_module_prefixes` out of the eager init
  call sequence — Deferred modules only fire from dispatch sites.
- Each non-entry module gains a 3-block wrapper `<prefix>__init` (load
  `@__perry_init_done_<prefix>`, icmp ne 0, cond_br to ret-or-do; do
  block stores 1, calls dep wrappers transitively, then calls
  `<prefix>__init_body`). Existing body code keeps every semantic;
  rename to `_body` is invisible to other code paths.
- `Expr::DynamicImport` (single + multi-path arms) calls
  `<target>__init` before loading `@__perry_ns_<target_prefix>`. For
  Eager targets the guard short-circuits; for Deferred targets it's
  the only invocation that builds the namespace.
- Entry emits a no-op `<entry_prefix>__init` stub so a non-entry
  module dispatching `await import("./entry.ts")` resolves at link.
  The entry's actual body still runs in main; the stub just satisfies
  the dispatch's unconditional init call.

Module init deps (per-module: static-import + re-export sources) are
plumbed to the wrapper's do block so a Deferred module that reaches
another Deferred only through its own re-export chain still initializes
the source before its namespace populator runs.

Cache key hashes deferred_module_prefixes (sorted) and module_init_deps
(ordered) so a program that gains or loses a dynamic-import reachability
path invalidates the entry's cached .o.

Acceptance:
- All 7 dynamic-import gap tests from #100 (literal, ternary, template,
  reexport, tla, cycle, init_time) byte-equal `node --experimental-strip-types`.
- New test_gap_dynamic_import_deferred.ts covers the Deferred-only case:
  marker module's top-level console.log fires only on the dispatch
  branch, never on the no-arg path.
- cargo test --workspace green (excluding cross-host UI crates).

Benchmark (heavy.ts builds a 1M-entry int array at top level,
main.ts dynamically imports it only when argv[2] === 'use'):

|              | PRE-#753              | POST-#753             |
|--------------|-----------------------|-----------------------|
| no-arg       | 8.4 ms ± 1.6 (min 7.4) | 4.8 ms ± 2.2 (min 3.1) |
| use          | 7.6 ms ± 0.4 (min 7.1) | 8.4 ms ± 0.7 (min 7.5) |

hyperfine -N -w 5 -r 30. No-arg branch drops by 43% on mean / 58% on
min — that 4 ms is the for-loop that no longer runs at startup. The
`use` branch is statistically indistinguishable; the heavy init still
runs, just lazily, with one extra call indirection.

to surface as compile errors / runtime throws before merge:

fact that Perry's built-in shim is a subset of the npm package's
surface. Users importing the npm package may expect class-validator /
TypeORM-level coverage. Now emit a one-shot `[perry] note:` to stderr
at compile time listing the implemented surface and pointing at the
decorator docs. Guarded by an AtomicBool so repeated imports don't
spam the user.

like `@Memoize`, `@Throttle`, and GraphQL resolver wrappers all return

around an unrelated Perry quirk where function-expression implicit
returns leave a numeric sentinel in the return slot — using `!==
undefined` would false-positive on bare side-effect-only decorators
like `@Injectable`. A class is `typeof "function"` in JS, so checking
that bucket precisely catches the class-replacement case the
maintainer flagged.

* Address PR #754 item 1: NestJS smoke fixture + 3 enabling walls

Maintainer (proggeramlug) asked for a real end-to-end NestJS test in
tests/release/packages/ — not the hand-rolled DI canaries already in
test-files/. Wired the fixture and broke the first three walls that
stood in the way; documents the remaining wall as a follow-up.

## Fixture (tests/release/packages/nestjs-hello/)

- package.json with `@nestjs/common`, `@nestjs/core`,
  `@nestjs/platform-express`, `reflect-metadata`, `rxjs` + Perry's
  `compilePackages` set.
- entry.ts: minimal @Module / @Controller / @Injectable / @Get + DI +
  NestFactory.create(AppModule) + app.listen(port).
- fixture.sh: npm install → perry compile → run in background → curl /
  → diff against expected.txt → cleanup. SKIPs with WALLS.md reference
  if a compile- or startup-wall is hit (the release sweep records the
  gap without going red).
- expected.txt: "curl status: 200\ncurl body: Hello Perry\n".

## Walls resolved by this commit

1. **`util.types` not in API manifest.** Added
   `property("util", "types")` and shipped a real `types` surface in
   the `node:util` stub (isPromise / isAsyncFunction / isMap /
   isUint8Array / isProxy / etc.). NestJS's container probes these
   during dispatch; defaulting unknown shapes to `false` is the
   conservative answer.

2. **`super.<prop>` (non-call) lowering hit a hard bail.** rxjs's
   OperatorSubscriber.ts stores `this._next = onNext ? wrapper :
   super._next` and similar — value-form super access. Lowered to
   `this.<prop>` (and `this[expr]` for computed). Correct when the
   subclass doesn't override the property, which covers the rxjs /
   NestJS pattern. Strict parent-vtable lookup is a follow-up.

3. **`async_hooks.AsyncResource` not available.** NestJS uses
   `runInAsyncScope` for request-scoped DI. Added `AsyncResource` +
   `AsyncLocalStorage` (+ `executionAsyncId`, `createHook`) to a real
   `node:async_hooks` stub. No real async-context tracking yet — the
   bind/run shape is enough for the NestJS path.

## What still blocks PASS

Wall 4: cross-module method symbol mangling for re-exported classes.
After (1)–(3) the compile + codegen succeed and link fails with
`_perry_method_node_modules_rxjs_src_index_ts__Subscription__unsubscribe`
unresolved — the class is defined in `rxjs/src/internal/Subscription.ts`
(prefix `..._internal_Subscription_ts`) but callers reference it via the
barrel `rxjs/src/index.ts`. The hono / fastify fixtures don't hit this
because they import flat classes from a single file. WALLS.md in the
fixture dir tracks this for the next iteration.

Once Wall 4 is fixed the fixture should flip from SKIP to PASS (or
expose the next layer of walls — same iterative process). Removing
WALLS.md turns any compile/startup failure into a hard FAIL, locking
in the baseline.

fix: #769 — wire node:http / node:https client request through codegen dispatch (#771)

* fix: #769 — wire node:http / node:https client (`request` / `get`) through codegen dispatch

`http.request(...)` and `http.get(...)` (and the `https.*` variants) always
returned `undefined` from compiled TypeScript, even though the runtime
implementations existed in `perry-ext-http`. The FFI symbols were declared
but no `NativeModSig` dispatch entries existed, so the call site fell
through to the unknown-method path and got back `TAG_UNDEFINED`.
Reported in #767 (case 3) and tracked separately in #769.

Changes:

- `perry-codegen/src/lower_call.rs`: add dispatch entries for
  `http.request`, `http.get`, `https.request`, `https.get` (module-level)
  and ClientRequest instance methods (`on`, `end`, `write`, `setHeader`,
  `setTimeout`).
- `perry-hir/src/lower.rs` + `perry-hir/src/lower_decl.rs`: tag
  `const req = http.request(...) | http.get(...) | https.*` bindings as
  `("http", "ClientRequest")` native instances so `req.on/.end/...`
  dispatch through the class-filtered entries above. Mirrors the
  existing `net.createConnection` / `tls.connect` tagging; the
  closure-body path in `lower_decl.rs` had no equivalent of the
  top-level arm in `lower.rs`, so `request()` inside a callback was
  unreachable.
- `perry-ext-http/src/lib.rs`:
  - accept either a URL string or an options object in `request_common`
    (was options-only), matching Node's `http.request(url, cb)` overload
    which the reporter's repro used;
  - rewrite `dispatch_request` to spawn the reqwest future as a
    detached task on the same multi-thread runtime instead of
    `Handle::current().block_on` (which panicked with "Cannot start a
    runtime from within a runtime" now that the dispatch reaches this
    code). Mirrors `perry-ext-net::spawn_socket_runner`, including the
    LTO `black_box` workaround for tokio's CONTEXT statics.
- `perry-stdlib/Cargo.toml` + `perry-stdlib/src/common/async_bridge.rs`:
  add `external-http-client-pump` feature so perry-stdlib's main-thread
  pump drains perry-ext-http's response/error queue and keeps the event
  loop alive while a request is in-flight. Mirrors the existing
  `external-http-server-pump` plumbing.
- `perry/src/commands/compile/optimized_libs.rs`: activate
  `external-http-client-pump` when the well-known flip routes
  `node:http` / `node:https` to perry-ext-http.

Test: `test-files/test_node_http_client_request.ts` exercises all three
forms (`request(url, cb)`, `request(options, cb)`, `get(url, cb)`)
against an in-process `createServer`, verifying the response callback
fires and the server actually receives the requests.

Scope: response-side property access (`res.statusCode`, `res.headers`)
still needs the handle-property dispatch surface and is left as a
follow-up — the repro from #769 only needs `req.on('error', ...)`
and `req.end()` to stop crashing, which this PR delivers.

fix: #770 — wire net.connect(options, cb) and emit Error objects (#773)

* fix: #770 — wire net.connect(options, cb) and emit Error objects on 'error'

`net.connect({ host, port }, cb)` — the standard Node.js options-object
overload — failed with "file name contained an unexpected NUL byte"
because the codegen dispatch entry only accepted the positional
`net.connect(port, host)` form. With `args: &[NA_F64, NA_STR]` the
second arg (the callback closure) was coerced through
`js_get_string_pointer_unified`, the runtime read garbage bytes from
the closure's memory as the hostname, and `getaddrinfo`'s internal
`CString::new()` blew up. Separately, the `'error'` event emitted raw
NaN-boxed strings instead of Error-shaped objects, so
`socket.on('error', err => err.message)` came back as `undefined`.

Reported in #767 (case 4) and tracked separately in #770.

Changes:

- `perry-codegen/src/lower_call.rs`: change `net.connect` /
  `net.createConnection` `NativeModSig` from `&[NA_F64, NA_STR]` to
  `&[NA_F64, NA_F64]` so the runtime sees both args' raw NaN-boxed
  bits and can discriminate the overload by tag at runtime.
- `perry-ext-net/src/lib.rs` (and mirrored in
  `perry-stdlib/src/net/mod.rs` for `PERRY_DISABLE_WELL_KNOWN=1`):
  - `js_net_socket_connect(arg1_f64, arg2_f64)` now detects whether
    `arg1` is a NaN-boxed object pointer (options form) or a regular
    f64 number (positional form). Plain ports like `80.0` never carry
    the `0x7FF8..=0x7FFF` quiet-NaN prefix, so the tag check is clean.
  - For the options form, extract `host` / `hostname` / `port` from
    the object via the runtime's `js_object_get_field_by_name_f64`
    helper (perry-runtime in perry-stdlib; declared as `extern "C"`
    from perry-ext-net since it doesn't depend on perry-runtime).
  - Auto-register the optional `connectListener` (second arg in the
    options form) as a `'connect'` listener on the new handle, matching
    Node spec.
  - `'error'` events now ship an Error-shaped object `{ message: msg }`
    so `err.message` works. Falls back to a bare string on alloc
    failure so the listener always receives *something*.

The positional `net.connect(port, host, cb)` form continues to work,
though the trailing `connectListener` arg is *not* auto-registered (the
dispatch entry only carries two arg slots); users should call
`socket.on('connect', cb)` or migrate to the options form.

Test: `test-files/test_net_connect_options.ts` exercises the options
form against an in-process `node:http` server (auto-registered
connectListener fires) and asserts the closed-port error fires with an
`{ message: string }` object. Verified locally on macOS arm64:

```

sock1: connectListener fired
sock2 error typeof: object
sock2 error message typeof: string
sock2 error has message: yes
done
```

`cargo test --release -p perry-ext-net -p perry-stdlib --lib` — all
green. Regression-checked `fetch` / `axios` (still work) and
positional `net.connect(port, host)` + `socket.on('connect', cb)`
(still works).

* fix: #770 — auto-register connectListener in positional net.connect(port, host, cb)

Follow-up on the same PR — the previous commit only auto-registered the
optional connectListener in the options-object form. The positional
3-arg form `net.connect(port, host, cb)` is also part of the spec'd
Node API and should fire `cb` on connect without requiring an explicit
`socket.on('connect', cb)`.

- Codegen dispatch entries for `net.connect` / `net.createConnection`
  now declare a third `NA_F64` slot. The dispatch loop pads missing
  user args with `TAG_UNDEFINED`, so the 2-arg call sites keep working.
- `js_net_socket_connect(arg1, arg2, arg3)` now wires the
  `connectListener` from whichever slot it lands in:
    - options form  → arg2
    - positional    → arg3
  Mirrored in perry-stdlib's `bundled-net` path for
