fix(codegen): class extending a function base must run the parent constructor (preserve derived identity) (#5613)

* fix(codegen): class extending a function base must preserve derived identity through constructor-return-object

A no-own-ctor derived class whose parent resolves to a plain function
value at runtime (`class D extends <fnValue> {}`, captured by HIR as
`extends_expr`) gets an implicit default derived constructor
`constructor(...args){ super(...args) }`. The inline `new` lowering only
emitted that implicit `super(...)` when the parent could be resolved
statically to a class in `ctx.classes` / `imported_class_ctors`. When the
parent is a runtime function value — e.g. a factory-returned constructor
function that itself returns a `this`-aliasing local — none of those
matched, so no `super(...)` was emitted: the parent function body never
ran on the new instance. Its `this.<field> = …` /
`Object.defineProperty(this, …)` writes were lost, and (when the parent
returns its own `this`) the derived instance was left uninitialized.

Fix: in the no-own-ctor inline-`new` path, when no inherited constructor
was found and the class has a dynamic `extends_expr`, resolve the
decl-time-registered parent value (`js_get_dynamic_parent_value`) and
dispatch it on `this` via `js_fetch_or_value_super`, which binds
IMPLICIT_THIS to the instance for the call. This mirrors the existing
synthesized-default-ctor dynamic-parent super in `codegen/method.rs`
(standalone-symbol path) and the explicit `Expr::SuperCall` dynamic-parent
arm in `expr/this_super_call.rs` — the inline path was the one gap.

Verified against a 12-line repro: a class extending a `$constructor`-style
function base now (a) keeps the derived prototype on the constructed
instance and (b) runs the parent function body first, matching Node.
No codegen/HIR test regressions (perry-codegen 128/128, perry-hir 196/196).

The inline new-lowering's post-super field-initializer re-apply was gated on

zod 4's $constructor) classes never re-applied their own field initializers
after the parent body ran via js_fetch_or_value_super — leaving derived field

fix(codegen): #5437 — inline method-dispatch tower must build args per-case arity, not one global rest decision (#5622)

* fix(codegen): per-implementor arity in idispatch method tower (#5437)

The inline method-dispatch tower (the class-id switch over candidate
implementors of an untyped `recv.method(...)` call) made ONE global
arg-bundling decision for every case. When at least one implementor of
the method name had a `...rest` param, the rest-bundle collapsed all
positional args into a single array passed as arg0 to EVERY case —
including non-rest implementors that declare more positional params. Those
extra params then read uninitialized 0.0.

In the Next.js bundle this dropped `ResponseCache.get(key, gen, context)`'s
3rd param (`context`) to 0.0 (`get` also has rest- and lower-arity impls
LRUCache.get/CacheHandler.get), so `const { incrementalCache } = context`
destructured off the number 0.0 -> incrementalCache undefined ->
"Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'get')" at render.

Build each case's args from the raw user args applying THAT implementor's
own (has_rest, decl_param_count): a non-rest callee gets its positional
params padded with undefined; a rest callee gets the trailing args bundled
at its rest slot. Preserves #235 default-param padding, #672 rest-bundling
and #1758 static-method dispatch, now per-case.

* style: cargo fmt property_get.rs

* perf(codegen): build idispatch impl_meta in discovery loop, avoid ctx.methods rescan (CodeRabbit #5622)

fix(compile): #5621 — route ergonomic camelCase native-library exports to their js_<pkg>_* FFI symbols (#5624)

* fix(compile): #5621 — route ergonomic camelCase native-library exports to their js_<pkg>_* FFI symbols

A `perry.nativeLibrary` package whose TypeScript surface exposes ergonomic
camelCase exports (`requestAdapter`) over snake_case `js_<pkg>_*` FFI
symbols (`js_webgpu_request_adapter`) was not routed to native — the call
silently fell through to the package's `.ts` body (e.g. a `throw`). Perry
only took the FFI-manifest path when the import binding was byte-for-byte
equal to the manifest symbol name, so an ergonomic binding never matched
(`requestAdapter` != `js_webgpu_request_adapter`). This affected
`@perryts/webgpu` and `@perryts/iroh`; `@perryts/storekit` worked only
because it exported the raw symbols verbatim.

Teach the compiler the standard `js_<pkg>_<snake_case(name)>` mapping:

- `ergonomic_export_alias()` (resolve/native_library.rs) derives the
  camelCase export a symbol is expected to back, but only when the symbol
  follows the `js_<pkg>_<snake>` convention for the package (`<pkg>` =
  sanitized last path segment of the module name). Mismatches return
  `None`, so the existing exact-match convention keeps working unchanged.

- The per-specifier import loop (compile.rs) now matches a binding against
  a manifest function either exactly OR via the derivation. On a derived
  match it records the binding → symbol alias in a new per-module
  `import_function_ffi_aliases` map (threaded through CompileOptions →
  CrossModuleCtx → FnCtx as `ffi_aliases`).

- At the call site (lower_call/extern_func.rs), the binding is rewritten
  to its manifest symbol up front, so the `ffi_signatures` lookups hit and
  codegen emits the call (and `declare`) against the real FFI symbol
  instead of the throwing wrapper body / a bare extern.

Tests: unit coverage for the derivation (webgpu/iroh/storekit/hyphenated/
mismatch cases) plus an end-to-end test that links a real one-function
static archive via the manifest's `prebuilt` field and asserts a
camelCase `doThing()` returns the native value (42) rather than running
its throwing `.ts` body.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(compile): address CodeRabbit review on #5621

- Key the FFI alias by the LOCAL binding, not the exported name, so
  aliased imports route correctly (`import { requestAdapter as getAdapter }`
  → call site sees `getAdapter`). Match the manifest against the exported
  name as before.
- Reject ambiguous ergonomic exports: if two manifest symbols derive the

- Restrict alias derivation to genuine snake_case suffixes — a mixed-case

fix(hir): #5579 — fold module-top indirect eval of a declaration-free body to its global completion value (#5627)

* fix(hir): #5579 — fold module-top indirect eval of a declaration-free body to its global completion value

Residual of the #5579 regression batch: the `language/eval-code/indirect`
completion-value cluster. Indirect eval `(0, eval)('<const>')` runs as global
code, but Perry's general indirect-eval path deferred every valid body to the
runtime global-`eval` thunk, which only models the `this`/`globalThis` idiom and
returns `undefined` for everything else. So `(0,eval)('x = 1')` yielded undefined
instead of 1 and never mutated the global `x` — diverging from the script-mode
Node oracle (`vm.runInThisContext`, #5346/#5511).

Perry already models a constant *direct* eval body with a scope-capturing
completion IIFE (#1679). For indirect eval that IIFE is only sound where the
captured enclosing scope already IS the global scope: module top level
(`scope_depth == 0`, no enclosing class / `with` / ESM) under
`PERRY_GLOBAL_SCRIPT_THIS`, where module-top `var`s and `this` are the global
bindings (#5608/#5609). There `try_indirect_eval_general` now folds the body via
the shared `build_eval_completion_iife` (sloppy unless the body opens with its
own Use Strict Directive — indirect eval never inherits the caller's strictness).

The fold is restricted to *declaration-free* bodies. A scope-capturing IIFE
places any `var`/`function`/`class`/`let`/`const` the body declares inside the
wrapper, but real global eval routes `var`/`function` to the global var
environment and `let`/`const`/`class` to the eval's own fresh lexical
environment — and Perry additionally registers class names at module scope, so a
folded `class C {}` would leak `C` to the top level (breaking
`indirect/lex-env-distinct-cls`). A declaration-free body has no such binding to
misplace; it only reads/assigns the globals it names. A new recursive
`eval_body_declares_bindings` scan (through blocks, loops, `try`, `switch`,
`with`, labeled and `if` statements where `var`/`function` hoist) gates this, so
any declaration defers to the runtime thunk as before.

Test262 `language/eval-code/indirect`: +2 (`cptn-nrml-expr-prim`,
`cptn-nrml-expr-obj`) with zero regressions across `language/eval-code` and
`annexB/language/eval-code` (declaration-bearing bodies, incl. the annexB
function-hoisting set, are unchanged). Outside global-script mode (the default,
and every standalone build) behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged.

Regression test: crates/perry/tests/issue_5579_indirect_eval_global_completion.rs
— completion values + global mutation, object identity, always-sloppy `with`/
undeclared-assignment side effects, and that a nested-scope indirect eval does
NOT capture the enclosing function's locals.

fix(regex): accept JS quantified lookaround like (?=x)? (V8 no-op semantics) (#5629)

* fix(regex): accept JS quantified lookaround like (?=x)? (#5437)

A quantifier directly on a zero-width assertion group (`(?=lg)?`, `(?!a)*`,
`(?<=a){0,3}`, …) is valid in V8/JS but rejected by both the `regex` crate
and `fancy-regex` (the lookaround fallback). Perry threw `SyntaxError: invalid
pattern` at regex construction for any such literal.

This bit Next.js hard: the bundled UA-parser table
(`(?=lg)?[vl]k…`, in a chunk every app-route loads at module-init time)
threw at module-eval, aborting the route module's initializer before it
self-registered its exports — so a later runtime `require(<route.js>)`
returned undefined and Next threw 'Cannot find module', turning dynamic/SSR/
API routes into HTTP 500. (A second, unrelated route-init failure — a
'value is not a function' in the app-route-turbo runtime's rJ constructor —
still blocks those routes; this fix removes the regex layer that was masking
it.)

js_regex_to_rust now runs a normalize_quantified_lookaround pre-pass: a
quantifier whose lower bound is 0 (`?`, `*`, `{0,n}`) makes the assertion a
pure no-op and is dropped entirely; a lower bound >= 1 (`+`, `{1,n}`) is
identical to the bare assertion, so the quantifier alone is dropped. The scan
is depth-aware over nested groups, escape- and character-class-aware, and
consumes a trailing lazy `?`. Verified against node's semantics.

* style: cargo fmt regex/grammar.rs

fix(native-abi): #5626 — add `json` manifest param that JSON-serializes objects at the FFI boundary (#5630)

* fix(native-abi): #5626 — add `json` manifest param that JSON-serializes objects at the FFI boundary

#5621 rewrites ergonomic camelCase native-library exports directly to
their `js_<pkg>_*` FFI symbol, bypassing the package's TS wrapper body.
For descriptor-object bindings the wrapper used to do
`JSON.stringify(descriptor)` before handing a `"string"` param to the
native side; with the wrapper gone the live object reaches
`js_native_abi_check_string_ptr`, which validates rather than coerces and
throws `TypeError: Expected string for native string parameter`. This
blocked `@perryts/webgpu` at the first `deviceCreateBuffer(d, { ... })`.

Add a `"json"` ABI param descriptor that moves the marshalling into the
FFI boundary: the call site lowers the argument through `js_json_stringify`
(`JSON.stringify`) and passes the resulting `*const StringHeader` in a
single `string`-shaped ABI slot. The native side reads it with
`read_string` and `serde_json`-deserializes it unchanged — no binding Rust
change beyond the manifest edit. The type is opt-in and param-only, so
existing `"string"` params keep their strict non-string-rejecting check.

- perry-api-manifest: new `NativeAbiType::Json` (parse `"json"`, canonical
  kind `json`, one ABI slot, JS type `any`, valid param, invalid return).
- perry-codegen: `lower_manifest_param` emits `js_json_stringify` + passes
  a `ptr`; verifier accepts the `js_json_stringify` guard for `json`.
- docs: manifest-v1 param-type table + a note on `"json"` vs `"string"`.
- tests: manifest unit test, resolver parse/return-rejection test, and a
  codegen proof-artifact regression asserting the stringify lowering.

perf(net): zero-copy socket read path via reused BytesMut (#5623)

* perf(net): zero-copy socket read path via reused BytesMut

The socket read loop allocated a fresh 16 KiB `Vec<u8>` view per read
(`buf[..n].to_vec()`) to carry each chunk in `PendingNetEvent::Data`.
Read into a reused `BytesMut` with `read_buf` and slice each read out as
a refcounted `Bytes` (`split_to(n).freeze()`), eliminating the per-read
heap alloc + memcpy. The drain handler and `raw_bridge::route_data` only
borrow the chunk as `&[u8]`, so `Bytes` substitutes for `Vec<u8>` with no

fix(runtime): call/apply/bind/Reflect.apply must rebind a concise method's baked `this` (#5632)

* fix(runtime): call/apply/bind must rebind a concise method's baked `this` slot

An object-literal concise method, object-literal accessor, or symbol method is
lowered with `captures_this` and its reserved (last) capture slot baked to the
defining object at construction time, so its body reads `this` from that slot,
NOT from IMPLICIT_THIS. The explicit-`this` entry points (Function.prototype
`call`/`apply`/`bind`, Reflect.apply, and the bound-function trampoline) only
set IMPLICIT_THIS, so the baked slot won the read and the explicit receiver was
silently ignored:

    const proto = { m() { return this.v; } };
    proto.m.call({ v: 7 });   // perry: undefined   node: 7
    proto.m.bind({ v: 42 })(); // perry: undefined   node: 42

This is the exact idiom a schema/validation library's `$constructor` factory
relies on — it installs own bound methods over the prototype's keys
(`inst[k] = proto[k].bind(inst)`) and binds methods in a base constructor
(`this.m = this.m.bind(this)`). With `this` pinned to the prototype, every
nested `inst.clone()`/`inst.check()` dropped the instance, cascading to
mis-constructed values downstream (a large minified ESM CLI bundle surfaced
this as `(boolean).optional is not a function` — a schema var that should have
been an object instance was a primitive).

Fix: add `rebind_explicit_this(target, this_arg)` — clones the target with its
`this` capture slot rebound to the explicit receiver, reusing the existing
`clone_closure_rebind_this` machinery the prototype-walk and accessor paths
already use. It is a no-op for arrow functions (lexical `this` — excluded
explicitly since they also carry the flag), non-captures_this functions (they
read IMPLICIT_THIS already), bound functions, and non-closure values. Applied
at all six explicit-`this` invoke sites: the `call`/`apply` value thunks, the
`.call`/`.apply` method-dispatch arms, the bound-function trampoline, and
Reflect.apply's shared helper.

* test(gap): concise-method explicit-this via call/apply/bind/Reflect.apply

Regression coverage for the rebind fix: object-literal concise methods honor an
explicit receiver through call/apply/bind/Reflect.apply and own-bound-method
shadowing, while arrows keep lexical this and bound functions ignore re-binding.
Byte-for-byte identical to node --experimental-strip-types.

* style: cargo fmt apply-arm rebind in common_methods.rs

* fix(runtime): raise rebind_explicit_this handle floor to 0x100000 (#4740 band); test accessors + symbol methods

CodeRabbit: the [0x10000, 0x100000) native-handle band (Fetch/http/axios/
fastify ids, 0x40000+) is NaN-boxed with POINTER_TAG but not a heap pointer.
The old 0x10000 floor let such a handle reach closure_is_arrow /
clone_closure_rebind_this, which dereference it and SIGSEGV (#4740). Raise the
floor to 0x100000 to match is_closure_ptr's documented band.

Also extend the gap test with the accessor and symbol-method shapes the header
already promised (getter.call, obj[sym].call, Reflect.apply(getter)) — verified
byte-for-byte vs node --experimental-strip-types.

fix(runtime): #5591 — string-coercing a class/object method no longer segfaults (#5633)

* fix(runtime): #5591 — string-coercing a class/object method no longer segfaults

`"" + C.prototype.method` (and template-literal / `+` coercion of any
class or object method) crashed with EXC_BAD_ACCESS. The `+` operator's
fully-dynamic ToPrimitive path (`to_primitive_default_for_add` →
`ordinary_to_primitive_number_for_add` → `call_method_for_primitive`)
bit-casts the operand to an `ObjectHeader` and reads its `valueOf` /
`toString` fields via `js_object_get_field_by_name`. A function value is
a `ClosureHeader`, not an `ObjectHeader`; for a class-method closure the
field read returned a bogus pointer that passed `is_closure_ptr` and was
then *called* → segfault. (Plain function-expression closures happened to
read back as absent, so only methods tripped it.)

Resolve a callable closure's ToPrimitive through the closure-aware path
(`function_to_primitive_for_add`): honor an own/inherited `valueOf` when
it yields a primitive — so `f.valueOf = () => 42; 1 + f` stays 43 — and
otherwise fall back to `Function.prototype.toString` (the function's
source / native form), which is exactly what OrdinaryToPrimitive yields
for a function whose inherited `valueOf` returns the function itself. The
guard mirrors the existing Proxy / Buffer / TypedArray / Date / URL
short-circuits for non-`ObjectHeader` pointer values.

Fixes 26 test262 cases under built-ins/Function/prototype/toString and
built-ins/AsyncFromSyncIteratorPrototype that string-coerce a method via
`assertToStringOrNativeFunction` (the `(no output)` cluster in #5591).

* fix(runtime): #5591 — honor toString in function ToPrimitive (CodeRabbit)

`function_to_primitive_for_add` fell back to `js_jsvalue_to_string` after
`valueOf`, which *stringified* a user `toString` override's primitive
result and never threw on an object result. Per OrdinaryToPrimitive the
`+`/default hint must try `valueOf` then `toString`, returning the first
primitive AS-IS, and throw `TypeError` when both yield non-primitives.

Now resolve `toString` via the closure-aware `call_function_method` and
return its primitive unchanged, so `f.toString = () => 42; 1 + f` is `43`

`TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value`. The trailing

unaffected: their `toString` resolves to `Function.prototype.toString` →
the source / native form.

fix(temporal): #5580 — read era/eraYear for non-ISO calendars in PlainDateTime/ZonedDateTime/PlainMonthDay field bags (#5635)

The PlainDateTime / ZonedDateTime property-bag reader (`read_iso_fields_alpha`,
`read_zoned_bag_alpha`) and `PlainMonthDay.prototype.toPlainDate`'s year-field
reader never read the `era`/`eraYear` keys. For a calendar that uses eras
(gregory, japanese, roc, buddhist, coptic, ethiopic/ethioaa, the islamic
family, hebrew, indian, persian) an `{ era, eraYear, monthCode, day }` bag
therefore reached temporal_rs/ICU4X with no resolvable year and threw
`Insufficient fields` (the dominant intl402/Temporal failure cluster), and a
`with({ era, eraYear })` likewise dropped the era keys. They are now read in
their alphabetical position (right after `day`, before `hour`) for era-using
calendars only, so era-relative dates resolve and a non-finite `eraYear`
rejects with the spec `RangeError`.

Era-less calendars — `iso8601`, `chinese`, `dangi` — still skip the keys
(new `calendar_has_no_eras`), so `from({ era, eraYear, year, … })` ignores them
and a `with({ era, eraYear })` bag stays empty → the `EmptyFieldsIsInvalid`
TypeError rather than an `Unknown era` RangeError. ISO order-of-operations is
unchanged (an ISO bag still observes no era/eraYear gets).

fix(runtime): #5592 — `class X extends <Proxy>` segfault (#5634)

`class X extends <Proxy>` crashed with SIGSEGV at class-definition time. A Proxy
is NaN-boxed as a POINTER_TAG value whose lower 48 bits are a SMALL registry id
in the handle band, not a heap address. During class-parent registration,
`bound_native_callable_module_and_method` checked only `closure.is_null()`
before reading `(*closure).type_tag` (offset 0xc) and `func_ptr` (offset 0) — so
it dereferenced the proxy's ~handle-sized id and faulted.

Classify the pointer through `closure::is_closure_ptr` before touching memory:
it rejects the handle band AND every non-heap address on every platform (the
macOS-only `is_valid_obj_ptr` heap floor would let a `0xf0000`-band id through
on Linux — the #5592 sweep host) before probing `CLOSURE_MAGIC`. The probe then
safely returns `None`, and `extends_target_must_throw` resolves IsConstructor
through the proxy target: a proxy wrapping a non-constructor throws a TypeError
at class-definition time (without reading `.prototype`), and a proxy wrapping a
real constructor is accepted.

Fixes the four test262 cases
language/statements/class/subclass/superclass-{arrow,async,generator,async-generator}-function.js
(previously crashed → "(no output)"); verified byte-for-byte against Node via
the new gap test. The native-module path this probe serves (`class X extends
require('stream').Writable`) is unaffected.

fix(net,http,tls): #1781 — handle SSO short strings in value conversion (#5638)

`JsValue::is_string()` matches the heap `STRING_TAG` only, so an inline SSO
short string (`SHORT_STRING_TAG = 0x7FF9`, length 0..=5) fails the strict
check and falls through every branch. Three value→bytes/string conversion
sites gated their string branch on `is_string()` and therefore silently
dropped short strings:

  - `perry-ext-net` `jsvalue_to_socket_bytes` — `socket.write("hi")`
  - `perry-ext-http-server` `jsvalue_to_body_bytes` — short response bodies
    (`res.end("hi")`)
  - `perry-ext-net` `tls.rs` `as_string` — short `tls.connect` args

Gate each on `is_any_string()` (heap STRING_TAG OR inline SHORT_STRING_TAG)
and materialize through `js_get_string_pointer_unified`, which copies SSO
bytes onto the heap and returns the existing pointer for a heap string, so
the downstream `StringHeader` read is unchanged for both representations.
`is_any_string()` / `is_short_string()` are added to perry-ffi's `JsValue`
to mirror the runtime predicates, and the `is_string()` doc gains the #1781
footgun warning.

The clean non-buffer/non-string reject in `jsvalue_to_socket_bytes` is
preserved unchanged — `js_get_string_pointer_unified` is only reached after
`is_any_string()`, so a non-string heap object is never reinterpreted as a
`StringHeader`.

Surfaced while extending the net zero-copy socket-read work (#5623).

Added a `perry-ext-net` regression test exercising the SSO path
(`socket.write("hi")`, empty string, the 5-byte boundary) plus the heap-string
and non-buffer-object-reject paths; it fails before the fix (SSO → None) and
passes after.

fix(runtime): bind inherited prototype-accessor methods to the receiver (#5637)

When a method call `inst.m()` resolves `m` to an ACCESSOR (getter) installed on
a prototype via `Object.defineProperty(proto, "m", { get })`, the getter must
run with `this === inst` (spec `[[Get]](P, Receiver)`), not `this === proto`
(the object the accessor lives on).

`dispatch_handle`'s two prototype-method resolution paths invoked the getter
with the prototype as the receiver:

  - the `ResolvedMethod::ProtoClosure` walk called the raw, receiver-less
    `js_object_get_field_by_name(proto_obj, key)`;
  - the registry-`None` (`Object.create(objLiteral).m()`) fallback called the
    receiver-less `resolve_proto_chain_field`.

Both now stash the receiver (`accessor_receiver_override` + `IMPLICIT_THIS` —
the mechanism `resolve_inherited_field` / `resolve_proto_chain_field_with_receiver`
already use), so `invoke_accessor_getter` rebinds `this` to the instance.

This surfaced in a large minified CLI bundle built on a schema-validation
library that lazily installs methods such as `describe`/`clone` on the shared
class prototype as accessors whose getter does
`Object.defineProperty(this, k, { value: fn.bind(this) })`. With `this ===
prototype`, the bound method baked `this = prototype` and was cached on the
prototype, so the no-op `clone_closure_rebind_this` (a `.bind()`-bound function
has no `CAPTURES_THIS_FLAG`) could not recover the instance. Every downstream
read of an instance-only field then returned `undefined`
(`Cannot read properties of undefined`).

Verified byte-for-byte against Node for describe/clone/optional/nullable/array/
object parse+safeParse/meta/default/refine method chains, and for an
`Object.create` inherited-accessor method. `cargo test -p perry-runtime
-p perry-codegen` stays green (1079 passed, 0 failed).

fix: #5594 — Annex B.3.3.3 global eval function-declaration binding (#5636)

* fix(hir,runtime): #5594 — Annex B.3.3.3 global eval function-declaration binding

Annex B.3.3.3 (Changes to EvalDeclarationInstantiation): a sloppy *global*
direct/indirect eval whose body contains a block-scoped function declaration
must create a same-named variable binding in the global variable environment,
initialized to `undefined` at instantiation and assigned the function object
when the declaration is reached. Perry folds an eval body into a scope-capturing
arrow IIFE, which trapped the function as an arrow-local, so the binding never
survived the eval (`f is not defined` after `eval('{ function f(){} }')`).

This moves the annexB `language/eval-code/{direct,indirect}` global cluster from
292/469 to 459/469 passing (no regressions across `language/eval-code` and
`language/statements/function`, measured against origin/main).

Three changes:

- perry-hir `const_fold_fn`: before folding a sloppy global (module-top,
  global-script) eval body, rewrite each *nested* (block / `if` / `switch`-case)
  function declaration into a publish to the global var environment. The
  declaration is renamed to a fresh hidden binding (and its body self-references
  with it) so the block-scoped binding stays independent of the published global
  var (BlockDeclarationInstantiation block-scoping invariant), a create-if-absent
  prelude pre-creates the global slot as `undefined` (via `globalThis[...]` so a
  same-named top-level function in the IIFE isn't clobbered), and the value is
  published with a bare assignment when the declaration is reached. The
  B.3.3.3 "would not produce any Early Errors" skip is honored: a same-named
  enclosing lexical (`let`/`const`/`class`/`catch`/`for`-head) binding leaves the
  function unhoisted. Top-level functions and all `var`s stay in the IIFE — their
  EvalDeclarationInstantiation (completion value, CanDeclareGlobal* /
  non-definable-name checks) is already modeled there.

- perry-hir `eval_classifier::const_string_of`: fold constant string
  concatenation (`'a' + 'b' + 'c'`). Test262's procedurally-generated cases split
  an eval body across `+`-joined string literals (one segment per `switch` case),
  so the whole argument is still a compile-time constant the AOT eval fold can
  run instead of deferring to the runtime thunk.

- perry-runtime `js_global_get_or_throw_unresolved`: a global binding whose value
  is `undefined` is *resolvable* — reading it yields `undefined`, not a
  ReferenceError. The field read can't distinguish "absent" from "present, value
  undefined", so confirm the own property exists before throwing.

fix(codegen,hir): cross-module member-new fills captures from the class's decl-site snapshot (#5640)

* fix(codegen): #5437 — cross-module member-new fills captures from decl-site snapshot in the ctor

A function-nested class that captures an enclosing-scope local (e.g. a
hoisted sibling `function r_`) and is constructed via a member-callee
`new ns.C(...)` from a DIFFERENT compiled module routes to the runtime
construct path (`construct_registered_class_ref`) — which supplies NO
capture args, since the captured enclosing local is out of scope at the
construction site and the class can't be resolved statically there.
The synthesized `__perry_cap_*` ctor params then bound to garbage and the
captured local read as a non-callable: Next.js's app-route-turbo `rJ`
constructor (`this.methods = r_(e)`, constructed via
`new w.AppRouteRouteModule({...})` from the app-route template chunk)
threw `TypeError: value is not a function`, so the route module's init
aborted before self-registering its exports and every dynamic/API route
500'd with 'Cannot find module route.js'.

The W6 same-module member-new fix only filled captures from the decl-site
snapshot when the `new` site was statically routed to
`lower_new_member_captured` — the cross-module runtime construct never
reached it. Move the snapshot recovery INTO the synthesized constructor
body: at ctor entry each `__perry_cap_*` param is rebound to
`js_class_capture_value_or(class_id, slot, param)`. The ctor body is
compiled in the class's home module, where `class_name` resolves to its
real `class_id`, so EVERY construction path — inline, same-module member,
and cross-module runtime — recovers the captured value from the class's
own decl-site snapshot. Same-module bare-`new` is unchanged: the live cap
arg equals the snapshot value, so `_or` returns the identical value.

Adds a `fallback: Option<Box<Expr>>` to `Expr::ClassCaptureValue` (codegen
emits `js_class_capture_value_or` when present, plain
`js_class_capture_value` otherwise — the static-method prologue path is
unchanged); the walkers and stable-hash descend it.

* fix(codegen): #5437 — param-first capture rebind + ctor-entry placement

Reworks the synthesized-constructor capture rebind for two correctness
findings on the cross-module member-new fix:

- Param-first recovery: the live new-site cap arg now wins whenever
  present; the decl-site snapshot is consulted only when the param is
  undefined (the cross-module construct signal). Previously the
  snapshot-first js_class_capture_value_or could override a same-module
  new C() whose captured outer was mutated after the class declaration
  (let x="a"; class C{ctor(){this.x=x}}; x="b"; new C() gave "a",
  node gives "b"). New runtime FFI js_param_or_class_capture_value plus
  a prefer_fallback flag on Expr::ClassCaptureValue (default false keeps

perf(net): pool socket read buffers (step 4) (#5642)

* perf(net): pool socket read buffers (step 4)

Add a process-wide freelist of 16 KiB read buffers and route the socket
read loop through it, so steady-state reads reuse pooled capacity instead
of allocating a fresh `BytesMut` on every read.

Step 2 (#5638) reused one `BytesMut` per socket and carved each read off
with `split_to(n).freeze()`, which removed the per-read copy. It did not
remove the per-read allocation: the `Bytes` chunk handed to the 'data'
event is queued and only copied into a JS Buffer on the next main-thread
drain tick, so the chunk — and the buffer's backing storage it shares —
is still alive when the loop comes back to `reserve(16 KiB)`.
`BytesMut::reserve` cannot reclaim shared storage in place, so it
allocated a new 16 KiB block on every read that delivered data, plus one
`with_capacity` per new connection.

The read loop now checks a buffer out of the freelist per read and checks
the post-`split_to` remainder back in. Once a buffer's prior chunk has
drained and dropped, its checkout reclaims the same allocation in place;
the freelist's depth covers the chunks in flight between read and drain,
so steady-state reads reuse pooled capacity and new connections draw from
the same pool. The freelist is bounded (64 idle buffers) to keep idle
memory capped; past the cap, checkout allocates fresh exactly as before.

Behavior is unchanged: checkout always yields an empty buffer with the
same >= 16 KiB writable window, the per-read 16 KiB cap still lives at the
read site (`BufMut::limit`), and the same bytes / 'data' / 'end' / 'close'
/ 'error' events and chunk boundaries are delivered. The freelist is a
`Mutex<Vec<BytesMut>>` so it is sound across the shared reactor's worker
threads (step 3); the lock is held only for the O(1) pop/push, never
across an await.

Step 4 of the 7-step net perf quest in #5419 (steps 1 #5419, 2 #5638,
3 #5488 merged).

  buffer recycles its storage in place (the per-read alloc removed); an
  in-flight chunk's bytes survive recycling; the freelist is bounded.
- New differential test drives the exact pooled read-loop core over a
  real loopback TCP connection across small / 16 KiB-boundary / >64 KiB
  payloads and asserts byte-identical reassembly and the 16 KiB per-read
  chunk boundaries (chunks kept alive to exercise recycle-under-pressure).
- `cargo test -p perry-ext-net`, `cargo check -p perry-ext-net` (clean),
  `cargo fmt --check`, `scripts/check_file_size.sh` all pass.

* perf(net): FIFO read-buffer pool + balance checkin on terminal reads

Address review findings on the step-4 read-buffer pool.

- Make the freelist FIFO (VecDeque, pop_front on checkout / push_back on
  checkin) instead of LIFO (Vec push/pop). A LIFO pool re-hands the
  most-recently-returned buffer immediately, while its just-enqueued Bytes
  chunk is still alive, so reserve(READ_BUF_CAP) cannot reclaim in place and
  reallocates on the hot read path. FIFO cycles the other parked buffers
  through first, giving the chunk time to drain so the reuse reclaims in place.
- Balance checkout() in run_socket_task's terminal read arms: the Ok(0) (EOF)
  and Err(_) paths now checkin(buf) before breaking, matching the success and
  command arms, so a peer FIN or read error no longer leaks pooled capacity.
- Run the pool-data-structure tests against a test-local freelist via internal
  checkout_from/checkin_to helpers instead of the process-wide pool, so the
  pointer-reuse and count assertions can't race concurrent tests.
- Drive the differential read-loop test's writer concurrently with the reader
  and join it after the loop, so a payload larger than the combined OS socket
  buffers can't deadlock.
- Add fifo_lets_in_flight_chunk_drain_before_reuse (passes only under FIFO:
  in-place reclaim by pointer identity) and lifo_reuses_too_soon_and_reallocates
  (shows the LIFO realloc) to lock the freelist ordering in.

perf(ffi): reuse request/response handle ids via a freelist (step 5) (#5643)

* perf(ffi): reuse freed handle ids via a freelist (step 5)

The handle registry minted a fresh id on every register_handle and never
reused one: next_fresh_handle_id only bumped a monotonic counter, while
drop_handle / take_handle removed the map entry but discarded the id. A
process that allocates a handle per unit of work — the HTTP server registers
a request + response handle per request and drop_handles both once the
response flushes — therefore burned through the visible id band (1 ..= 0x40000)
and eventually panicked at the exhaustion check, even though only a handful of
handles were ever live at once.

Add a bounded freelist of reclaimed ids. drop_handle / take_handle park the
freed id after removing it from the map; register_handle pops a parked id
before advancing the counter. Id consumption is now bounded by the concurrent
live-handle count rather than the cumulative allocation count, so a long-lived
server never exhausts the band.

Behavior is preserved. An id is parked only after its entry is removed from
the registry, so a recycled id is never live in two registrations at once;
register_handle inserts the fresh value under the reused id, so a reused
handle carries no prior state and the type-aware downcast keeps a stale
lookup against the old type returning None. The freelist has its own lock,
held only for the O(1) pop/push, and the remove-before-park / pop-before-insert
ordering means an id is never simultaneously on the freelist and live in the
map — sound under the shared reactor (step 3). Past the cap the excess id is
dropped and register_handle falls back to a fresh id exactly as before.

The client-side ClientRequestHandle / IncomingMessageHandle are not dropped
here: JS keeps the req / res objects readable after the request's 'close'
edge (req.method, res.statusCode, res.headers, ...) and there is no GC
finalizer to drop them when JS releases them, so reclaiming them at 'close'
would change observable behavior. The freelist reclaims the ids that wrappers
already free — the HTTP server's per-request handles and every other wrapper
that calls drop_handle / take_handle.

Validation: new unit tests assert a register/drop/register cycle reuses a
freed id, a reused id carries no stale value or type, concurrently-live
handles never share an id, the freelist is bounded at its cap, and a
register/drop churn past the band size keeps fresh-id consumption tiny (the
same loop panics at the exhaustion check without recycling — a fail-before).
cargo test -p perry-ffi (18 passed), cargo check -p perry-ffi (clean, no new
warnings), cargo fmt --check, and scripts/check_file_size.sh all pass;
perry-ext-http-server and perry-ext-http still build.

2 #5638, 3 #5488 merged; step 4 #5642 open.

* perf(ffi): qualify handle-freelist docs; assert id reuse in tests

Address review on the handle-id freelist:

- Docs overstated the guarantee. Recycling does not "never exhaust the
  band": frees past FREE_HANDLES_CAP are discarded and a burst larger than
  the cap still advances NEXT_HANDLE. Qualify the module + FREE_HANDLES docs
  to "while reclaimed ids fit within the bounded freelist", and correct the
  visible band notation to the half-open `1 .. 0x40000` (0x40000 is the
  reserved exhaustion boundary in next_fresh_handle_id, never a returned id).

- The reuse tests (register_drop_register_reuses_a_freed_id,
  reused_id_carries_no_stale_state) passed even when register_handle minted
  a fresh id, so they did not actually verify reuse. They now assert reuse
  via drop_then_register_reusing, which retries until NEXT_HANDLE is observed
  unchanged across a register (a pop, not a fresh mint). Robust to the
  non-serialized registry tests churning the process-wide freelist in
  parallel; a no-reclaim drop_handle parks nothing, so every attempt mints
  fresh and the bounded retry fails the test.

No production behavior change.

perf(ws): SIMD WebSocket frame unmasking (step 7) (#5646)

* perf(ws): SIMD WebSocket frame unmasking (step 7)

Add a portable u64-wide WebSocket frame (un)mask routine to
perry-ext-ws. Each client->server frame is XOR-masked with a 4-byte
key (RFC 6455 §5.3, `payload[i] ^= key[i % 4]`); the new `mask` module
processes the payload in phase-rotated 8-byte words instead of a
per-byte loop, with a scalar fallback for the unaligned head/tail and
correct key-phase carry across calls.

`apply_mask_from` returns the next key phase so a frame split across
multiple buffers unmasks identically to the same payload delivered
whole. Output is byte-identical to the scalar reference for any
length, any key, and any starting phase.

Implemented as a portable u64-wide XOR (no `target_feature`, no
intrinsics, no nightly `std::simd`, no new dependency); the optimizer
auto-vectorizes the hot word loop into wide SIMD stores where
available, and the routine stays buildable on the stable toolchain
and every target.

A property/fuzz test asserts the wide path equals an independent
textbook oracle across random lengths, masks, key offsets, and chunk
split points, including non-4-aligned boundaries where a dropped phase
carry would diverge.

* perf(ws): normalize apply_mask_from return to a 0..=3 key phase

The returned cursor was key_offset.wrapping_add(len), an unnormalized
value (e.g. 103) despite the docs/name describing a key phase. Mask it
mod 4 so the return is a true phase in 0..=3, matching the contract and
preventing unbounded cursor growth across many split-frame chunks.
Behavior is unchanged for callers (the entry path already masks
key_offset & 3); tests assert the normalized contract.

* perf(http-server): response-build fast path (step 6)

The per-response head build runs for every HTTP/1 response a perry server
emits, so the small-response RPS path pays for constant work that can be
precomputed. Add a response_fast module of pure lookups and wire it into the
two hot-path methods plus the standalone flush:

  constant, skipping StatusCode::from_u16's numeric range-check + unwrap_or.
  Uncommon/custom codes keep the from_u16 path.
- apply_default_connection_headers: the `Keep-Alive: timeout=N` value is
  interned for the timeouts servers commonly run with (Node's 5 s default,
  0/10/15/30/60/120 s), so the per-response format! only fires for an unusual

  code uses a precomputed `HTTP/1.1 <code> <reason>\r\n` status line instead

(http1::Builder::serve_connection), so hyper owns the wire writes and already
coalesces; the only hand-rolled wire path (standalone_end) already builds one
head+body buffer and issues a single socket write.

path would have handled differently, so the bytes are byte-identical.

fix(runtime): #5625 — Temporal brand probe must skip header-less typed arrays/buffers (#5650)

`is_temporal_cell_addr` read `GcHeader.obj_type` at `addr - GC_HEADER_SIZE`
without first excluding off-GC-heap, header-less allocations. Small typed
arrays and `Buffer`s are raw-`alloc`'d with NO 8-byte `GcHeader` prefix, so
that back-read lands on unrelated preceding heap bytes — which can
coincidentally equal `GC_TYPE_TEMPORAL` (18). When it did, a method call on
such a typed array (e.g. `<TA>.slice()` / `.subarray()` / `.every()`) was
mis-routed through `temporal::dispatch::call_method`, which then dereferenced
the "cell"'s value box (actually the typed array's `{length,capacity}` words)
as a `Box<TemporalValue>` and segfaulted — surfacing as silent `(no output)`
crashes in the test262 `%TypedArray%.prototype` species-constructor cases.

Reject header-less side-table allocations via `is_offheap_sidetable_alloc`
before the deref, exactly as `crate::date::is_date_cell_addr` already does for
the same reason. A real `TemporalCell` is never registered as a typed array or
buffer, so the guard never rejects a genuine Temporal value.

Fixes the 4 net-new #5579-batch regressions:

fix(regexp): #5586 — RegExp(re) as a function returns the argument unchanged (object identity) (#5647)

ECMA-262 22.2.4.1: when `RegExp` is invoked as a *function* (not `new`) with a
RegExp `pattern` and `undefined` `flags`, and `pattern.constructor` is the
`RegExp` intrinsic, the call returns `pattern` **unchanged** (object identity)
rather than constructing a copy. Perry copied unconditionally, so
`var r = /x/i; RegExp(r) === r` was `false` and a property added to `r` was
invisible through the result.

Three related gaps in the `RegExp(...)` call form, all in test262
`built-ins/RegExp`:

* S15.10.3.1_A1_T1 / _A1_T2 / _A2_T1 / _A2_T2 — identity when flags is
  undefined (or an expression that evaluates to undefined).
* S15.10.3.1_A1_T4 — zero-arg `RegExp()` fell through to the bare `RegExp`
  ident dispatch and produced `null` instead of an empty `/(?:)/`.
* call_with_regexp_not_same_constructor — overriding `re.constructor` makes
  `SameValue` fail, so a fresh copy must be returned.

Implementation:

* HIR: `Expr::RegExpDynamic` gains an `is_call` flag distinguishing the
  function-call form `RegExp(x)` from `new RegExp(x)`. Zero-arg `RegExp()` now
  folds with an `Expr::Undefined` pattern instead of falling through.
* Runtime: new `js_regexp_construct_call` applies the identity shortcut —
  gated on a RegExp pattern, undefined flags, and no own `constructor`
  override — then falls back to the general `js_regexp_construct`.
* Codegen: the call form routes to `js_regexp_construct_call`; `new RegExp`
  keeps `js_regexp_construct` so it always copies.

`new RegExp(re)` and any flag-supplying call still construct a fresh,
independent object. Validated by test-files/test_issue_5586_regexp_call_identity.ts
(byte-for-byte vs Node v26.3.0) and the built-ins/RegExp test262 subset
(cluster now passes, no regressions).

fix(runtime): #5437 — captured-`undefined` tag-loss on Next.js dynamic/API routes (#5648)

`js_class_capture_value_or` substituted the `new`-site appended `fallback`
whenever the decl-site capture snapshot slot was `TAG_UNDEFINED`. That
heuristic was added for the hoisted-class/TDZ case (snapshot taken before the
captured local was assigned, fallback holds the correct later value). But a
capture whose value is *genuinely* `undefined` — the Next.js bundle's
`let t_ = process.env.NEXT_PRIVATE_DEBUG_CACHE ? (...)=>{} : void 0` debug
logger, `undefined` by default — records `TAG_UNDEFINED` in the snapshot,
which is the CORRECT value, not a TDZ artifact.

At giant-module scale the `new`-site appended `fallback` for that same capture
materialized as the tag-stripped raw word `0x0000_0000_0000_0001`
(`TAG_UNDEFINED` = `0x7FFC_0000_0000_0001` with the `0x7FFC` NaN-box tag
stripped by a multi-level capture mis-box). Preferring that corrupt fallback
over the `undefined` snapshot handed `t_` the non-callable `0x1`, so
`null == t_` was false → `t_("...")` was called → "value is not a function"
→ the route's `loadCustomCacheHandlers` init aborted → HTTP 500 on every
API/dynamic route (static routes were unaffected).

Fix: a legitimate captured JSValue is always NaN-boxed (top 16 bits ≥ 0x7FF9)
or a normal IEEE-754 double; a NON-ZERO value with all-zero top 16 bits is a
tag-stripped/mis-boxed raw word that is never a real captured value. When the
snapshot slot is `undefined`/absent and the fallback is such a corrupt word,
keep the snapshot's `undefined` (the authoritative value) instead of the
fallback. A valid fallback over an undefined snapshot still wins, preserving
the hoisted-class/TDZ and require-derived-capture (getSpan) fixes; a
non-undefined snapshot slot still wins over the fallback, preserving W6.

Adds `class_capture_value_or_rejects_tag_stripped_fallback` covering the bug
plus the W6 / TDZ / no-snapshot paths.

fix(ffi): quarantine freed handle ids one tick to close use-after-recycle (stacked on #5643) (#5651)

* fix(ffi): quarantine freed handle ids one tick to close use-after-recycle

The handle-id freelist (the `perf/handle-pool-freelist` work) recycles a
freed id immediately, which reintroduces an ABA / use-after-recycle hazard
for any consumer that resolves an object purely by its bare integer id.

`perry-ext-http-server` hits this: an async request handler can return
before `res.end()`, leaving a stale `res` (a bare tagged handle id)
outstanding. Once that request is finalized its id is freed; with immediate
recycling the very next `register_handle` — the next incoming request's
response — re-occupies the id, and a microtask-deferred `res.write`/`res.end`
from the retired handler then mutates the *new* request's response, bleeding
one request's body into another's. The `Box<dyn Any>` downcast catches
different-type reuse but not `ServerResponse` -> `ServerResponse`. Before the
freelist existed a freed id stayed dead, so the stale write was a safe
no-op; the freelist removed that safety.

Restore it without touching the published i64 handle encoding: a freed id is
parked in a quarantine and only promoted to the reusable freelist by
`drain_quarantined_handles`, which the HTTP pump calls once per tick (at the
top of `js_node_http_server_process_pending`, before the tick's
finalizations). One full tick covers the realistic async-handler shape
(`await`/`fetch`/microtask, then `res.end()`): the stale write runs before
the next drain, and while the id sits in quarantine it maps to nothing, so
that write re-fetches an empty slot and no-ops exactly as before. Fixing it
at the freelist covers HTTP/1, HTTPS, and HTTP/2 in one place, since all of
them free through `drop_handle`. Embedders that never drain simply never
recycle ids (the pre-freelist behavior, safe).

The window is one tick, not unbounded: a write deferred more than a tick past
finalization (e.g. `res.end(); setTimeout(() => res.write(x))`) is a
write-after-end use error Node itself rejects, and closing it generally needs
a per-handle generation that the fixed i64 ABI forbids — out of scope.

Adds a fail-before/pass-after regression test reproducing the cross-request
bleed at the registry layer: reverting the quarantine makes the freed id
reusable within the tick and the test fails on the cross-request mutation;
with the quarantine the stale write hits an empty slot.

* fix(ffi): deadline-gate quarantine for reaper-finalized handles to close long-async use-after-recycle

The one-tick handle quarantine only covers ids whose owner is provably
done writing at free time (an HTTP response past res.end()). The reaper
and closeAllConnections finalize a parked request on peer-disconnect or
server-force-close WITHOUT setting writable_ended, so a handler suspended
on a slow await can resume many ticks later and write through the bare
id after it was promoted and re-minted — a silent cross-request body
bleed that is not a write-after-end.

Add a second deadline-gated quarantine tier (QUARANTINED_UNTIL) holding
(handle, deadline). New drop_handle_until parks an id there;
drain_quarantined_handles drains the one-tick tier whole and promotes
only deadline-gated entries whose deadline has elapsed. The HTTP server
routes a response handle through drop_handle_until with the request's
grace deadline only when finalizing WITHOUT end; ended/synthesized
responses keep the one-tick fast path. The i64 handle encoding is
unchanged.

Regression test: a reaper-finalize-without-end id stays parked across
ticks until its grace deadline, the stale write no-ops against an empty
slot, then the id recycles cleanly once the deadline passes.

fix(net): set TCP_NODELAY on by default; wire socket.setNoDelay (#5658)

* fix(net): set TCP_NODELAY on by default; wire socket.setNoDelay

Node enables TCP_NODELAY on every accepted/connected socket by default
(Nagle off). Perry never called set_nodelay anywhere, so every connection
ran with Nagle on — a Node-parity gap and, via the Nagle/delayed-ACK
interaction, up to ~40ms of added tail latency on small-write keep-alive
request/response. Separately, socket.setNoDelay() from JS was a no-op: the
net dispatch arm returned the handle without touching the socket, silently
dropping explicit calls.

Set set_nodelay(true) at every production accept/connect site in
perry-ext-net and perry-ext-http-server (net server accept, net deferred-
and eager-connect, the TLS connect path before the handshake, the HTTP/1
accept and SCHED_RR fd-inject paths, the HTTPS and HTTP/2 server accept
paths, and the HTTP/2 client connect). The HTTP server paths honor the
existing HttpServer.no_delay option (default true) so noDelay: false is
respected.

Wire socket.setNoDelay([enable]) so it applies TCP_NODELAY to the live
socket: a new SetNoDelay command is sent over the socket's channel and
applied in run_socket_task (which owns the stream), reaching the inner
TcpStream for TLS transports too. The argument is coerced as Node does
(enable === undefined || !!enable), so a bare setNoDelay() enables and an
explicit setNoDelay(false) re-enables Nagle.

Add regression tests that drive the real command loop and dispatch entry
over a loopback connection and observe TCP_NODELAY on the owned socket,
covering the default-on contract, setNoDelay(false)/(true), the argument
coercion, and the dispatch arm end to end.

* fix(net): honor noDelay on the HTTPS and HTTP/2 accept paths

fix(http-server): validate requestTimeout so the deadline cast can't overflow (#5670)

requestTimeout was stored as a raw f64 and later cast straight to u64
to build the in-flight request deadline. Rust's saturating float->int
cast turns a non-finite or oversized value into a garbage deadline:
Infinity becomes u64::MAX (never times out), oversized finite values
likewise. Node rejects those at construction via
validateInteger(value, 'requestTimeout', 0, kMaxRequestTimeout).

Sanitize at every setter path (the createServer option, shared by http
and https, and the http/https property setters) so the stored value is
always a finite, non-negative, integer, MAX_SAFE_INTEGER-bounded ms
count: non-finite falls back to Node's 300s default, out-of-range clamps
to [0, 2**53-1], and the fractional part is truncated. The downstream
cast is then sound regardless of which setter wrote the field, with no
behavior change for valid inputs.

Flagged by CodeRabbit on #5663; pre-existing latent bug, not introduced
by that PR.

* fix(runtime,codegen): #2768 — honor new.target in registered-class constructors

new.target was `undefined` inside a registered-class constructor whenever it ran

- new Ref() (first-class ClassRef value) and the default symbol-call path for a

* fix(codegen): span the super(...) chain for new.target on the symbol-call path

CodeRabbit flagged, and a repro confirms, that the standalone-constructor-symbol

own body never reads new.target but whose super() runs an ancestor that does
(e.g. an abstract-class guard in a base) took the zero-overhead fast path, so
the cell was left unset and the inherited body observed `undefined`:

  class Base  { constructor(){ this.tag = new.target?.name; } }
  class Child extends Base { constructor(){ super(); } }
  new Child().tag  // was "undefined", Node: "Child"

The standalone `<class>_constructor` symbol inlines super() into itself, so an
ancestor ctor reads the same runtime new.target cell. Gate the set/restore on

extends_name — instead of just the leaf. A chain with no reader anywhere keeps
the fast path. Extends reflect-proxy-construct.ts with own-ctor / no-own-ctor /
abstract-base-guard subclass cases (parity vs Node, byte-for-byte).

fix(runtime): #5625 — resolve forwarded grown-array prototype in copyWithin inherited-index reads (#5673)

`Array.prototype.copyWithin` over a receiver with a custom `[[Prototype]]`
(installed via `Object.setPrototypeOf`) nondeterministically produced an
all-holes result instead of copying the inherited indices
(test262 built-ins/Array/prototype/copyWithin/coerced-values-start-change-start.js).

Root cause: `array_custom_array_prototype` decoded the recorded prototype
pointer and dereferenced it directly, without resolving `js_array_grow`
forwarding. When the prototype is a *grown* array (the test's
`longDenseArray()` fills a `[0]` to 1024 elements, reallocating its backing
store), its stored pointer is left FORWARDED: the old location's first 8 bytes
hold the forwarding pointer to the live head, not length+capacity. Reading
`.length` there returns the forwarding pointer's low 32 bits as a garbage huge
value, so `array_has_own_index(proto, idx)` reads unrelated memory and the
inherited-index `HasProperty` check intermittently missed — copyWithin then
deleted the target indices instead of copying. Whether the proto was forwarded
depended on allocator layout, hence the nondeterminism.

Fix: run the decoded pointer through `clean_arr_ptr` (which already follows the
GC_FLAG_FORWARDED chain) before validating obj_type / dereferencing, so we
always operate on the current array head. Both `array_spec_has_index` and
`array_spec_get` route through this helper, so the read and write probes are
fixed together. Normal (non-grown) array prototype inheritance is unchanged.

perf(codegen): size-optimize oversized IR units at -Os instead of -O0 (#5674)

Oversized modules (IR past PERRY_LL_O0_THRESHOLD_BYTES, 6 MB) were compiled
at clang -O0 to dodge the #4880 pathology: a unit dominated by ONE enormous
generated function (a multi-thousand-element data literal lowering to a single
~800k-line function) makes LLVM's -O1+ pipeline super-linear and effectively
never finishes.

But -O0 is the wrong default for the *common* oversized case. A large minified
CLI bundle is tens of thousands of ordinary functions, none individually huge,
and -O0 emits register-pressure-blind, un-folded code: ~30-50% more __text than
-Os for no benefit. That generated code is the overwhelming majority of such a
binary's __text (measured: 253 MB of a 266 MB binary is codegen output, not the
runtime/stdlib), so the opt level on these units dominates final binary size.

Pick the level by average IR bytes-per-function, which cleanly separates the two
regimes (>100x gap): a pathological monolith is megabytes-per-function (the
#4880 400k-element literal is ~9 MB/fn), a real bundle is ~20 KB/fn. Oversized
units at or below PERRY_LL_SIZE_OPT_MAX_FN_BYTES (256 KB) size-optimize at -Os;
denser units keep -O0. A giant-literal unit always has very few, very large
functions and so never reaches the -Os pipeline.

Measured (whole real CLI-bundle IR unit, 15440 functions, ~20 KB/fn):
  -O0 __text 63 MB -> -Os __text 32 MB  (-49%), clang 47s -> 93s.
End-to-end (synthetic 9000-function program): -Os and -O0 produce byte-identical
program output; binary __text 50.7 MB -> 40.7 MB. Small modules (<6 MB IR) are
untouched (still -O3). New escape hatches: PERRY_LL_SIZE_OPT=0/1 forces the
old -O0 / always -Os, PERRY_LL_SIZE_OPT_MAX_FN_BYTES tunes the density cap.

perf(codegen): full-outline the generic property-GET diamond for oversized modules (#5675)

The inline generic property-GET path (`lower_generic_property_get`) expands to
~60 IR instructions across ~13 basic blocks PER property-get site: receiver-tag
routing (SSO / INT32 class-ref / valid-pointer / nullish), a monomorphic inline
cache (shape check + hit/miss), typed-feedback recording, and the nullish-throw.
On a large minified bundle that is the single biggest contributor to generated
`__text` — the dominant component of an oversized binary (a representative bundle
emits 253 MB of codegen `__text`, ~95% of the final binary).

The class-field GET/SET diamonds are already collapsed to one call in
full-outline mode (`js_class_field_get_ic` / `js_class_field_set_ic`, #5334 /
#5391), but the generic-get diamond was not — so it dominated the residual IR.

Add the matching collapse: when `full_outline_ic_enabled()` (oversized modules
only — ordinary programs keep the fast inline PIC), emit a single
`js_object_get_field_ic(obj_bits, key_handle, site_id, cache)` call. The new
runtime helper reproduces the inline diamond's branch ladder exactly, dispatching
to the same runtime entries (`js_object_get_field_by_name_f64`,
`js_typed_feedback_object_get_field_by_name_f64`,
`js_typed_feedback_observe_property_get`, `js_object_get_field_ic_miss`,
`js_throw_type_error_property_access`) — so behavior is unchanged. The only thing
traded away is the inline monomorphic fast-load (every read goes through the

fix(runtime,stdlib): >64-arg dynamic dispatch via ABI trampoline + stream callback-write response bodies (#5676)

* fix(runtime): #5437 — unbounded-arity vtable dispatch + streaming res.write(cb)

Two Next.js app-route blockers, both surfacing only at giant-bundle scale.

1. call_vtable_method capped dynamic dispatch at 64 args. A synthesized
   capture-stashing constructor (synthesize_class_captures appends one
   __perry_cap_* param per captured enclosing local) can have 130+ params —
   Next.js app-route-turbo's route-module class rJ has 134. In release builds
   the debug_assert was compiled out, so a 135-param ctor was transmuted to a
   64-arg fn signature: every param past the 64th read register/stack garbage,
   a captured module-scope function (r_/rQ) arrived non-callable, and
   this.methods = r_(e) threw 'value is not a function' → route-module init
   aborted before self-registering exports → require returned undefined →
   'Cannot find module route.js' → HTTP 500 on every app route.

   New crates/perry-runtime/src/abi_trampoline.rs implements an all-f64
   arbitrary-arity call via an aarch64/x86-64 inline-asm trampoline (first 8
   f64 args in FP registers, the rest spilled to a 16-byte-aligned stack area,
   per the platform C ABI — faithful because every Perry method/ctor param is
   f64). call_vtable_method now builds the positional arg list and dispatches
   through it; MAX_VTABLE_DISPATCH_ARITY=512. Unit tests cover 70-arg ordering
   and stack-spilled args.

2. js_node_http_res_write_with_cb ignored streaming mode. After
   res.flushHeaders() (or a prior streamed write) begins streaming, the
   callback-aware write dispatch arm — used by Next's pipeToNodeResponse
   WritableStream (res.write(chunk)) — still buffered every chunk into
   buffered_body, while res.end() took the stream-finalize path that only
   sends the final .end(chunk) arg and drops buffered_body. The API-route JSON
   body never reached the wire (HTTP 200, 0 bytes). Now routes through
   stream_write first, exactly like js_node_http_res_write.

Result on the Next.js 16 standalone bundle: GET /api/hello 500 → 200 with the
correct {"hello":"world","n":42} body (byte-identical to node); static /,
/about, /counter remain byte-identical.

* fix(runtime): #5437 — use r12 (not rbx) for rsp stash in x86-64 ABI trampoline

`abi_trampoline.rs`'s `call_all_f64_x86_64` stashed the pre-adjust rsp in rbx
across the `call`, declaring `out("rbx") _`. LLVM reserves rbx internally and
rejects it as an explicit inline-asm operand, so the x86-64 build failed:

    error: cannot use register `bx`: rbx is used internally by LLVM and cannot
    be used as an operand for inline asm  --> abi_trampoline.rs:183

This only surfaced on x86-64 CI (the contributor builds on aarch64, which takes
the separate aarch64 asm path). Switch the stash register to r12 — also
callee-saved (so it survives the callee clobbering caller-saved regs) but, unlike
rbx, usable as an explicit inline-asm operand. Verified by cross-compiling
perry-runtime for x86_64-apple-darwin (was: 1 error; now: clean).

perf(codegen): full-outline the instance method-dispatch tower for oversized modules (#5681)

The dynamic instance-method dispatch path (`try_lower_instance_method_call`)
emits, per call site, an own-property override probe followed by a class-id
switch tower: one `icmp` + case block for every class that implements the
method, each calling that class's compiled method directly, with a default arm
that falls through to the by-name runtime dispatcher `js_native_call_method`.
The tower's IR therefore scales with the implementor count — in a large minified
bundle a popular method name is implemented by dozens of classes and called from
thousands of sites, so these towers are a major contributor to generated
`__text` (the dominant component of an oversized binary).

The tower is a compile-time specialization: its default arm,
`js_native_call_method`, already resolves any user-class method by name through
the runtime's (class_id, name) vtable registry (populated by
`js_register_class_method`). So in full-outline mode collapse the whole switch
to that single by-name dispatch, keeping the own-property override probe inline
(an own-method override must still win). The per-site IR drops from ~6 + N blocks
(N = implementor count) to a fixed 3 blocks.

Skipped when any implementor is a `perry_static_*` class-object-static method
(those need `js_class_static_method_call`, which the by-name dispatcher does not
reproduce). Gated on `full_outline_ic_enabled()`; `PERRY_OUTLINE_METHOD_DISPATCH=0`
forces the old inline tower (escape hatch).

Measured (60 classes implementing one method, 4000 dynamic call sites): binary
`__text` 14 MB -> 6 MB (-57%), program output identical.

Validated: across all 252 gap tests, the collapsed path produces output
byte-identical to the inline tower on 250; the 2 exceptions are a
`console.time` wall-clock value (nondeterministic) and a pre-existing
closure-capture bug where the inline tower already disagrees with Node (the
collapse only perturbs the garbage value, turning no correct output incorrect).
A hand-written edge-case test (polymorphic inheritance, inherited methods,
own-property override, rest args, arity padding) matches Node on both paths.
129 perry-codegen unit tests green.

Co-authored-by: Ralph Küpper <ralph2@skelpo.com>

fix(fetch): call linked stdlib fetch constructors directly under external-fetch-symbols (#5687)

The runtime's fetch-constructor wrappers (`call_global_headers_new`,
`call_global_request_new`, and the Blob/File/Response siblings in
`global_fetch.rs`) route through the `GLOBAL_FETCH_*` AtomicPtr registry that
perry-stdlib populates from `js_stdlib_init_dispatch`. When a wrapper observes
its registry pointer null it warns (`js_headers_new is a no-op stub ...`) and
returns `undefined`.

In an `external-fetch-symbols` build, perry-stdlib's `web-fetch` implementations
are statically linked — the same invariant `call_fetch_with_options` already
relies on to call `js_fetch_with_options` directly, and the same one the codegen
fast path uses when it emits a direct `js_headers_new` for a literal
`new Headers()`. Only the registry-backed construction path (a reflective
`new Headers()` / `new Request()` resolved through the class registry, e.g. an
aliased `const K = Headers; new K()`) still went through the AtomicPtr. In a
large auto-optimized binary with bundled runtime copies that wrapper could read
the pointer null even though init had already stored it, yielding a no-op fetch
(a hang on the first request) while the equivalent direct codegen path worked.

Extend the existing `external-fetch-symbols` direct-call pattern to the nine
fetch-constructor wrappers so the registry path matches the codegen path: under
the feature they call the linked `js_*` externs directly; without it they keep
today's registry-load + stub-warn behavior for runtime-only builds. No behavior
change for the default (stub) build.
