feat(fetch): honor AbortSignal — cancel/timeout in-flight requests (#5690)

`fetch(url, { signal })` ignored the signal: `js_fetch_with_options` took only
url/method/body/headers and ran to completion, so neither `controller.abort()`
nor `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` could cancel it. And `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` was
a no-op stub returning a never-aborting signal. Together,
`fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(ms) })` on a slow/held response hung
forever instead of rejecting at the deadline.

This wires AbortSignal through the fetch path:

- `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` (`url/abort.rs`) now schedules a real (unref'd)
  callback timer that aborts the signal with a `TimeoutError` and fires its
  `abort` listeners when the deadline elapses on the main thread.
- The signal reaches the stdlib fetch via a thread-local stash
  (`js_fetch_set_pending_signal`), keeping the 4-arg ABI unchanged. The runtime
  fetch thunk sets it for the dynamic/aliased path; codegen emits it before the
  call for the `fetch(url, { … })` fast path (a new `signal` field on the
  `FetchWithOptions` HIR node).
- `js_fetch_with_options` registers a per-request `tokio::sync::Notify` keyed to
  the signal and `select!`s the request against it; on abort it drops the
  request future (cancelling the in-flight reqwest request) and rejects with an
  `AbortError`. An already-aborted signal rejects up front. The abort reaches
  the request through the runtime: `fire_abort_listeners` calls
  `js_fetch_notify_signal_aborted` on every abort — so there is no per-fetch JS
  listener to accumulate on reused signals.

The pending signal is consumed before the promise is allocated (so a GC during
allocation can't move the TLS-stashed signal). No behavior change for
signal-less fetches; the WASM fetch backend keeps its existing behavior.

Co-authored-by: Ralph Küpper <ralph2@skelpo.com>

perf(fastify): index static routes for O(1) match_route lookup (#5692)

`FastifyApp::match_route` linearly scanned `self.routes` for every request,
calling `RoutePattern::match_path` on each route until a hit — O(N) per request
in the number of registered routes. Most real routes are fully static
(`/health`, `/api/v1/users`, …) and can be matched in O(1) by hashing the
`(method, path)` pair.

Add a `static_index: HashMap<String, usize>` field on `FastifyApp`. `add_route`
inspects the parsed pattern; if every segment is `Segment::Static`, it records
`"{METHOD} {canonical_path}"` → the route's index. `match_route` canonicalizes
the request path the same way and checks the index first (O(1)); on a miss it
falls back to the existing linear scan. The data model is unchanged — routes
still live in `routes: Vec<Route>` and the GC root scanner still walks them — so
the change is purely additive.

Registration and lookup keys both go through one `canonical_path` helper (drop
the query string, keep only non-empty `/`-separated segments), so the index key
can never diverge from `RoutePattern`'s own segment view — which likewise ignores
empty segments — and a route registered with redundant slashes (`/api//users`)
still resolves through the O(1) path. `canonical_path` fast-paths the common
already-canonical case to a single copy, so the lookup stays cheap.

Precedence is preserved exactly. Because the index is consulted before the scan,
a static route is indexed only when no earlier-registered route (another static,
or a parametric/wildcard pattern like `/:slug` or `/static/*`) already matches
the same path; otherwise it is left out so the lookup falls through to the scan
and the first-registered route still wins. Exact-duplicate static keys keep the
first registration (`entry().or_insert`), matching the scan's first-match
behaviour. `match_route` also normalizes the request method to the upper-case
form `add_route` stores, via a `Cow` that only allocates for a genuinely
lower/mixed-case method (requests off the hyper accept loop are already
upper-case), so the fast path stays allocation-free.

Microbenchmark (`match_route` on the last of 64 registered static routes,
release, 1M iterations): linear scan = 3342 ns/lookup → static index =
64 ns/lookup, ~52× faster. The win scales with route count and is largest for
later-registered static routes (the first route was already found in ~one
comparison by the linear scan).

Adds regression tests:
- `static_index_population_and_lookup`: static routes are indexed (parametric /
  wildcard are not), an indexed hit returns the right handler + empty params, a
  query string still hits the index, parametric routes still match through the
  scan, and a method mismatch doesn't short-circuit.
- `static_index_respects_prefix`: a `with_prefix("/api")` app indexes the route
  under its full prefixed path (`GET /api/users`), not the bare path.
- `static_index_preserves_registration_precedence`: an earlier parametric (`/:slug`)
  or wildcard (`/static/*`) route still wins over a later colliding static route;
  the reverse order indexes the static route and wins.
- `static_index_duplicate_routes_keep_first`: exact-duplicate static routes
  resolve to the first registration, not the last.
- `static_index_normalizes_redundant_slashes`: a route registered as
  `/api//users` is indexed under the normalized `GET /api/users` key.
- `match_route_normalizes_method_case`: a lower/mixed-case lookup method resolves
  through both the index and the linear-scan fallback.

perf(fastify): cache the per-request params/query JS object (#5696)

`js_fastify_req_params_object` and `js_fastify_req_query_object` rebuilt a fresh
JS object — a shaped object allocation plus one string allocation per entry — on
EVERY call. A handler that reads `req.params.a` then `req.params.b` (or hands
`req.query` to several helpers) paid the full construction each time.

Cache the built object on the `FastifyContext`. Add two `AtomicU64` slots
(`params_object_cache`, `query_object_cache`): the accessor returns the cached
NaN-boxed pointer on a hit and builds-then-stores on a miss. `0` means uncached
and never collides with a real entry (objects are POINTER_TAG'd, top 16 =
0x7FFD). Each request gets a fresh context (caches reset to 0 in
`FastifyContext::new`, dropped with the context at dispatch tail), so the cache
is naturally request-scoped — no cross-request leak. `AtomicU64` rather than
`Cell` because the handle registry hands out shared `&FastifyContext` and the
type must stay `Send + Sync`.

GC soundness: the cached object is a live heap pointer that a copying GC can
move, so `scan_fastify_roots` now also walks live `FastifyContext` handles and
visits each populated cache slot with `visit_nanbox_u64_slot` — which relocates
the pointer in place AND preserves the NaN-box tag (a raw `visit_i64_slot` would
strip it). Without this, a GC between the first `req.params` build and a later
read would dangle the cached pointer.

Microbenchmark (`js_fastify_req_params_object` on a 2-key params map, release):
rebuild-every-read = 188 ns/op → cached read = 12 ns/op, ~16× faster. The first
read still builds; every subsequent read in the same request is an atomic load.
Single-read handlers are unaffected (one extra atomic load + store).

Adds regression tests:
- `context_object_caches_start_empty`: a fresh context has both caches at 0 and
  the slots round-trip the NaN-boxed bits.
- `req_object_accessors_cache_within_request`: two reads of `req.params` /
  `req.query` return identical cached bits, and the cache holds them.
- `gc_scanner_rewrites_cached_object_slots`: after a minor GC the cache slots are
  relocated to the moved objects and keep their POINTER_TAG — proving the root
  scanner relocates (not just marks) the cache and preserves the tag.

perf(fastify): move per-request headers/body/params into the context instead of cloning (#5691)

`process_request` — the main-thread request pump in perry-ext-fastify — built
the `FastifyContext` by cloning all five `FastifyPendingRequest` fields (method,
path, headers, body, params), even though the context consumes headers/body/
params and they are never read again on the request thread. The three clones — a
`HashMap<String,String>` (headers) + a `Vec<u8>` (body) + a `HashMap<String,String>`
(params) — fired on every request; the header-map clone is O(headers) and is the
largest per-request allocation after the hyper body collect.

Move them out instead: `pending` becomes `mut`, headers/params use
`std::mem::take`, and body uses `Option::take`. method and path stay cloned
because they're still referenced for the route-match pass
(`app.match_route(&pending.method, &pending.path)`). Semantically identical — the
context receives the same data — with three fewer allocations per request.

The context construction is factored into a `build_context_from_pending` helper
so `process_request` and the regression test share a single code path. The test
(`process_request_moves_pending_fields_not_clone`) drives that helper and asserts
both (a) the context receives the original contents and (b) the source `pending`
collections are empty afterward, while method/path survive for the route match;
a clone-based construction would leave them populated, failing the test.

test(fastify): guard per-request context-handle cleanup against regression (#5695)

`process_request` registers a fresh `FastifyContext` in the handle registry for
every request (`register_handle`) and drops it at the end of dispatch
(`perry_ffi::drop_handle`). If that trailing drop were ever removed, every served
request would leak one context — its headers map, body, params, and response
state — into the global registry, growing unbounded under sustained load until an
allocation eventually fails deep in an unsafe FFI path.

The cleanup is already in place, but nothing pinned it. Add a focused regression
test (`context_handle_dropped_after_dispatch`) that asserts the
register → drop → gone invariant: register a `FastifyContext`, confirm it is live
in the registry, drop the handle, and confirm it is gone. A change that removed
the cleanup at the tail of `process_request` would leave the handle live and fail
this test.

Test-only — no production-code change.

perf(fastify): cache the per-request headers JS object (#5697)

`js_fastify_req_headers` rebuilt a fresh JS object (a shaped object allocation +
one string allocation per header) on EVERY call. Handlers commonly read several
headers per request, so each read past the first repeated the full construction.

Cache the headers object on the `FastifyContext`, mirroring the existing
`req.params` / `req.query` caches: add a `headers_object_cache: AtomicU64` slot
(`0` = uncached, else the NaN-boxed object-pointer bits), return the cached
pointer on a hit, build-then-store on a miss, and extend `scan_fastify_roots`'
per-context pass to root the slot with `visit_nanbox_u64_slot` (relocates the
pointer in place AND preserves the NaN-box tag under a copying GC). `ctx.headers`
is set once at context construction and never mutated, so the cache can't go
stale; each request gets a fresh context, so it can't leak across requests.

Microbenchmark (`js_fastify_req_headers` on a 6-header map, release):
rebuild-every-read = 446 ns/op → cached read = 12 ns/op, ~37× faster. The win is
larger than for params/query because header maps are larger. The first read still
builds; later reads in the same request are an atomic load.

Extends the params/query cache regression tests to cover the headers slot —
including `gc_scanner_rewrites_cached_object_slots`, which now also proves the
headers cache is relocated (not just marked) and keeps its POINTER_TAG after a
minor GC.

fix(fastify): bound request-pump re-entrancy to avoid MAX_TRY_DEPTH (#5698)

`js_fastify_process_pending` dispatches each pending request by running its
handler, and a handler that `await`s drives `wait_for_promise` →
`js_run_stdlib_pump`, which re-enters this same pump. Every nested dispatch pushes
another `call_closure2_catching` try-frame (setjmp), so under sustained
awaited-handler load the recursion could blow `MAX_TRY_DEPTH` (128 — "Try block
nesting too deep") and abort the process. The pump had no guard against this.

Add a thread-local `IN_PROGRESS` re-entrancy guard plus a thread-local `DEFERRED`
queue. On a nested entry the pump captures every server's pending requests into
`DEFERRED` (without dispatching) and returns; the OUTER frame drains `DEFERRED` at
the tail of its loop, so every dispatch happens at the outer (bounded) try-frame
depth instead of recursively. A nested entry that occurs during the tail drain is
itself deferred and picked up by the same loop, so depth stays bounded regardless
of arrival timing. WebSocket upgrades keep priority throughout: the tail loop
re-drains each server's upgrades before every deferred request (via the extracted
`drain_server_upgrades` helper), so a long deferred drain can't starve a late
upgrade (#1113).

`DEFERRED` is capped at 4096 entries: a pathological async storm that exceeds the
cap drops the newest pending, whose `response_tx` Drop makes the awaiting hyper
service-fn resolve `Err` → an error response. Memory is bounded (backpressure),
not leaked. The deferred dispatch happens in the same outer pump tick, so an
awaited request observed by a nested pump call is served without waiting for the
next event-loop iteration.

The drain/cap/backpressure logic is extracted into `try_recv_pending_request` and
`drain_server_requests_into_deferred` so it is unit-testable without a runtime.
Adds tests:
- `deferred_drain_respects_cap_and_drains_channel_fully`: over-cap entries are
  dropped, kept entries stay in FIFO order, and the channel is fully drained
  (nothing stranded in the mpsc).
- `deferred_drain_under_cap_moves_all_without_dropping`: under cap, all captured
  in arrival order with no response channel closed.
- `deferred_drain_over_cap_signals_dropped_clients`: a dropped (over-cap) request
  closes its response channel, so the client gets an error response, never a hang.
- `deferred_drain_no_loss_across_servers_and_repeated_passes`: across servers and
  repeated nested-entry drains, every request is captured exactly once in
  per-server FIFO order; a second pass captures nothing.
The full guard → defer → outer-tail-dispatch path is exercised end to end by the
async handlers in `scripts/run_fastify_tests.sh`.

perf(fastify): copy string response bytes directly, skip the String round-trip (#5693)

`jsvalue_to_response_body` handled a handler's string return by going through
`extract_jsvalue_string`:
  StringHeader → js_get_string_pointer_unified → string_from_header
    → String::from_utf8_lossy(bytes).to_string() → .into_bytes()
That is a UTF-8 validity scan plus a `String` allocation (and copy) on the way to
the `Vec<u8>` hyper's body writer actually wants — redundant work, since Perry's
NaN-boxed strings already hold valid UTF-8 and the body writer streams the bytes
out unchanged.

Add a fast path to the `is_string()` branch: read the `StringHeader` directly
(pointer via `js_get_string_pointer_unified`, then `byte_len` and the data
immediately after the header — the same layout `string_from_header` reads), build
a `Vec` with exact capacity, and copy the bytes once with `extend_from_slice`.

The verbatim copy is gated on the string being well-formed UTF-8. Perry strings
are WTF-8 and may carry lone surrogates (marked
`STRING_FLAG_HAS_LONE_SURROGATES`); copying those raw would emit invalid UTF-8 in
the response, whereas the old `from_utf8_lossy` path substituted U+FFFD. So when
that flag is set — and defensively if the pointer accessor ever returns 0 — the
code falls through to the original `extract_jsvalue_string` round-trip, preserving
the prior lossy-but-valid output exactly.

The win is one fewer allocation per text response plus dropping the O(len) UTF-8
scan. Microbenchmark of `jsvalue_to_response_body` on a NaN-boxed string (release,
5M iterations):
  - 16-byte body: 11.6 ns → 5.9 ns  (~2.0×)
  - 1 KB body:    288 ns  → 17 ns   (~16.5×)
The gap widens with body size because the old path's validity scan is O(len)
while the fast path is a single sized copy.

Adds two regression tests:
- `jsvalue_to_response_body_string_fast_path`: small ASCII, multi-byte UTF-8, and
  empty strings round-trip byte-exact through the fast path, tagged `TextOrJson`.
- `jsvalue_to_response_body_lone_surrogate_falls_back_to_lossy`: a WTF-8 string
  with a lone surrogate bypasses the fast path and emits the lossy (U+FFFD),
  valid-UTF-8 form rather than the raw bytes.

test(fastify): drive context_handle_dropped_after_dispatch through process_request (#5700)

The regression test for the per-request context-handle cleanup called
drop_handle directly, so it pinned the handle-registry invariant rather
than process_request's register -> drop lifecycle: it would still pass if
process_request forgot its trailing cleanup entirely.

Drive an actual request through process_request instead. An app with no
routes takes the no-handler path (undefined result -> build_response_body
short-circuits to `{}` with no JS allocation) while still exercising the
full register -> build response -> drop lifecycle. process_request now
returns the context handle it registered (and freed) so the assertion
targets that exact handle, keeping it race-free under parallel test
execution; the live dispatch loop calls process_request as a statement and
discards the value.

Verified by mutation: commenting out the trailing drop_handle makes the
test fail ("FastifyContext handle leaked: still present after
process_request"), which the previous direct-drop_handle version did not.

ci(security-audit): ignore RUSTSEC-2026-0187 (lopdf, transitive, no upstream fix) (#5707)

RUSTSEC-2026-0187 (stack overflow in lopdf via deeply nested PDF
objects) is failing security-audit on every PR. The fix is lopdf
>=0.42.0, but lopdf is transitive via printpdf (perry-ext-pdf), and
printpdf's latest release (0.9.1) still pins lopdf ^0.39 — no actionable
upstream bump exists yet. perry-ext-pdf is a PDF creation API, not a
parser of untrusted PDFs, so the deeply-nested-input surface isn't
reached. Add a tracked --ignore, matching the existing transitive-dep
exceptions; revisit when printpdf moves to lopdf >=0.42.

Co-authored-by: Ralph Küpper <ralph2@skelpo.com>

fix(compile): don't localize panic/unwind symbols on ELF (PIE link break) (#5706)

strip_duplicate_objects_from_well_known_lib force-localizes
rust_eh_personality (and friends) in well-known wrapper archives. The
match is by substring, so it also catches the compiler-emitted
DW.ref.rust_eh_personality. On ELF, --localize-symbol on that breaks its
PC32 relocation:

  relocation R_X86_64_PC32 against undefined hidden symbol
  DW.ref.rust_eh_personality can not be used when making a PIE object

so any Linux compile of a net/stdlib program (e.g. the blocklist /
streams integration tests, and real user builds) failed to link. The
panic/unwind localization exists only for tier-3 Mach-O (-Zbuild-std,
where runtime+stdlib each bundle std's panic runtime -> ld64 duplicate
symbol); ELF tier-1/2 take the panic runtime from prebuilt std, so there
is nothing to dedup.

Fix: split the panic/unwind shims into RUST_PANIC_UNWIND_SYMBOL_PARTS and
skip localizing them for ELF objects (detected by magic bytes, so it is
cross-compile-correct). Allocator-shim localization and the Mach-O
behavior are unchanged. Unit test covers the DW.ref substring match.

Co-authored-by: Ralph Küpper <ralph2@skelpo.com>

fix(codegen): route fastify request/reply `.header()` by receiver class (#5708)

The two `header` rows in `FASTIFY_ROWS`
(`crates/perry-codegen/src/lower_call/native_table/fastify.rs`) both declared
`class_filter: None`: one mapping `request.header(name)` to the 1-arg getter
`js_fastify_req_header`, the other mapping `reply.header(name, value)` to the
2-arg setter `js_fastify_reply_header`.

`native_module_lookup` (`native_module_dispatch.rs`) resolves a native method
in two passes: an exact `class_filter == class_name` pass, then a generic
`class_filter.is_none()` first-match-wins pass. With both rows generic, the
arity-blind generic pass matched BOTH `request.header(name)` and
`reply.header(name, value)` to whichever row appeared first — the request
getter. Result: `reply.header(...)` silently became a no-op, so `Location`,
CSP, and other response headers set via the method form evaporated.

Fastify handler params are already registered by position as
("fastify","Request") / ("fastify","Reply") during HIR lowering
(`pre_scan_fastify_handler_params`). Tagging the getter row `Some("Request")`
and the setter row `Some("Reply")` lets the matcher's exact-class first pass
disambiguate the two by receiver, so each `.header()` call routes to its
correct runtime symbol.

Adds a regression test (`fastify_header_routes_by_receiver_class`) pinning the
dispatch: with both rows generic the reply setter mis-routes to the getter; the
receiver-scoped rows route each correctly.

Co-authored-by: Ralph Küpper <ralph.kuepper@skelpo.com>

fix(stdlib): merge Request headers with init in fetch(Request) (#5704)

* fix(stdlib): merge Request headers with init in fetch(Request)

resolve_fetch_inputs let a Some("{}") headers JSON — which codegen always emits when the init carries no headers — win and wipe the Request own recovered headers. Start from the Request headers and extend() with any init headers (per-key override) so an empty/absent init cannot drop them. Repro: fetch(new Request(url,{headers})) now sends the headers.

* fix(stdlib): lowercase init.headers keys before merging (CodeRabbit)

request_fields.headers are stored canonically lowercased (the Headers
object lowercases keys), but serde_json preserves the JSON casing, so an
init `Authorization` did not override the Request's `authorization` —
both survived and got forwarded. Lowercase init keys (to_ascii_lowercase,
matching the rest of the fetch header handling) before extend. Adds a
regression test for the override.

Co-authored-by: Ralph Küpper <ralph2@skelpo.com>

fix(runtime): preserve generator step-closure this through yield* delegation (#5709)

* fix(runtime): preserve generator step-closure `this` through `yield*` delegation

* fix(runtime): validate closure ptr via is_closure_ptr before header probe

clone_closure_rebind_this used a hand-rolled `ptr < 0x100000` band check
(failing the addr-class lint) and only that band check before the unsafe
CLOSURE_MAGIC read — a mis-boxed POINTER_TAG value above the band (e.g. a
fetch handle or `i32 << 32`) could SIGSEGV the probe (CodeRabbit). Use
is_closure_ptr, which does the handle-band + heap-range + alignment +
CLOSURE_MAGIC checks, and drop the now-redundant inline magic read.

fix(hir): new ClassName(...spread) dropped the spread, passing the array as one arg (SIGBUS) (#5710)

`new S(...arr)` where `S` is a top-level user class was lowered through the
dedicated static-class `new` path, which maps over `a.expr` and DROPS the
`a.spread` marker. The spread collapsed into a single array argument: the
constructor saw `this.dep = arr` instead of `this.dep = arr[0]`, so the first
method call on the field dereferenced an array as the instance and SIGBUSed
(exit 138/139).

This is exactly the NestJS dependency-injection pattern
`new Provider(...resolvedDeps)`, where the container spreads a resolved
dependency array into a provider constructor.

Fix: in `callee_is_generic_construct_shape`, recognize a bare-identifier callee
that names a known user class (`ctx.lookup_class(...)`) as a generic
constructable shape, so spread-`new` on it routes through `NewDynamicSpread`.
That path preserves spread positions as `CallArg::Spread`, allocates the
instance with the class's registered inline-keys shape, and replays the
constructor — producing a result identical to the fixed-arity `new S(arg)`.

Verified against Node: the original repro now prints `direct: hi` / `spread: hi`
(was SIGBUS), plus multi-param/number-field, rest-param, default-param
(under-applied and fully-applied), mixed regular+spread `new M(1, ...tail)`,
`extends` + `super(...args)`, and plain-function spread calls all match Node.
`cargo test -p perry-hir --release` passes with no regressions.

Co-authored-by: Ralph Küpper <ralph2@skelpo.com>

fix(runtime): explicit gc() runs a full collection so dead old-gen objects are reclaimed (#5714)

With generational GC on (the default), `js_gc_collect()` dispatched a MINOR
cycle. The minor sweep intentionally skips dead-old-block reclamation
(`reclaim_dead_old_blocks = false` in `step_sweep`), and large objects (>16KB)
plus minor-GC survivors live in the OLD arena. So dead large/tenured objects
were never returned to the OS by an explicit `gc()`: a large-object allocation
loop grew unboundedly (RSS climbed ~175MB/round with `gc()` between rounds)
instead of plateauing.

Route `manual_gc_collect_now` (the single chokepoint for both the synchronous
`js_gc_collect` path and the deferred flush) through
`gc_collect_full_mark_sweep_with_trigger`, so an explicit `gc()` performs a full
mark-sweep that reclaims dead old-generation blocks. The same allocation loop
now plateaus. Automatic/threshold-driven minor collections are untouched.

Notes:
- V8's bare `gc()` is a scavenge (minor); this makes Perry's explicit,
  user-initiated `gc()` a thorough (full) collection. Gating the full sweep on
  `gc(true)` to mirror V8's minor/major split is a reasonable follow-up.
- A single lone dead large object whose block is the allocator's *current*
  old-gen target is kept mapped + reusable (not returned to the OS until
  reused) — a deliberate allocator trade-off, separate from this change.

fix(hir): report `typeof gc` as "function" so the optional-gc capability guard runs (#5711)

Programs gate the optional `gc()` builtin behind the idiomatic capability
guard `if (typeof gc === "function") gc()` — written that way because Node
only exposes `gc` under `--expose-gc` (where `typeof gc === "undefined"`
otherwise) and Bun behind `--expose-gc` too. See the Node CLI docs, which
show `if (globalThis.gc) globalThis.gc()`.

Perry's `gc()` is ALWAYS a real, callable builtin (a call-intrinsic routed
to `js_gc_collect`), yet the HIR typeof fold deliberately EXCLUDED `gc`
(arm_unary.rs: "gc is excluded — it's undefined in Node without
--expose-gc"), folding `typeof gc` to a non-"function" value. So the guard
was always false: an allocation-heavy program that gates collection on it
never collected and RSS grew unbounded (to ~physical RAM), while an
identical Node run with --expose-gc stayed flat.

Include `gc` in the typeof-"function" fold (matching `setTimeout`,
`queueMicrotask`, etc.). `typeof gc` now reports "function", so the guard
runs the collector and memory stays bounded. Direct `gc()` calls are
unchanged.

fix(hir,codegen): class-expr super() must use in-scope local parent, not same-named module-global class (#5705)

* fix(hir): #5437 — class-expression heritage binds parent Ident to in-scope local, not same-named module-global class

A minified turbopack bundle (Next.js app-page-turbo) declares dozens of
distinct webpack-factory classes under the same single-letter names
(`t`/`u`/`i`). codegen's `super()` resolves the parent via a module-wide
`HashMap<name, &Class>`, which keeps only ONE `t` — so p-queue's
`PQueue extends t` (eventemitter3) resolved `t` to superstruct's
`StructError` base, and `new PQueue()` (AfterContext's
`this.callbackQueue = new (a())()`) inlined StructError's destructuring
constructor on the undefined options arg → "Cannot convert undefined or
null to object" → HTTP 500 on the dynamic page routes.

When a class EXPRESSION's parent Ident is bound by an in-scope LOCAL
(`const t = require('events'); class extends t {}`), route through the
dynamic `extends_expr` parent path so `super()` invokes the lexically
correct local at runtime, instead of the wrong same-named module-global
class. Gated on `!class_renames.contains_key` so the existing
sibling-rename disambiguation still wins; pure module-global heritage
(no shadowing local) is unaffected (`locals.lookup` returns None for a
class name).

* fix(codegen): #5437 — explicit super() prefers dynamic extends_expr parent over same-named module-global class

Companion to the HIR fix: when a class with an OWN constructor calls
`super()` and HIR captured a dynamic `extends_expr` (the parent Ident is
a lexical in-scope local), the codegen SuperCall arm must invoke that
runtime parent value — not the same-named module-global class that
`ctx.classes.get(parent_name)` returns. Force the dynamic-parent dispatch
branch whenever `extends_expr` is set, mirroring the synthesized-ctor
dynamic-parent path already in codegen/method.rs.

* test(#5437): regression for class-expr heritage binding to in-scope local over same-named module-global class

Minimal guard for the Next.js p-queue PQueue HTTP-500: a module-global
`class t { constructor({message}){} }` (destructuring ctor) plus a
function-local `const t = class {…}` that a sibling class expression
`extends t`, constructed via the runtime dynamic path `new (getCls())()`
with no args. Before the fix, super() resolved `t` to the module-global
class and ran its destructuring ctor on the undefined arg → "Cannot
convert undefined or null to object". Fails on the unfixed tree with that
exact error; passes byte-identically to node with the fix.

* fix(hir): local shadow wins over native parent; test uses shared harness (CodeRabbit)

CodeRabbit #2: a lexical local shadowing the parent name must win over the
native/static parent. Both lower_class_decl (class declarations) and the
class-expression arm now compute `locally_shadowed` (`!class_renames &&
ctx.locals.lookup(name)`) and check it BEFORE `native_parent`, so
`const EventEmitter = …; class X extends EventEmitter {}` routes through the
dynamic extends_expr path (the local) instead of recording the native
events parent. ESM imports are not in ctx.locals, so genuine native
subclassing is unchanged.

CodeRabbit #3: the regression test now uses the shared compile-harness
settings (--no-cache, PERRY_NO_AUTO_OPTIMIZE=1, PERRY_RUNTIME_DIR) so it is
deterministic and optimizer-independent (also 374s -> 39s).

* fix(hir,codegen): built-in parent NAME shadowed by a local uses the local (CodeRabbit #1)

Built-in parent names (Error/TypeError/.../Request/Response/Event/
CustomEvent + stream family) are special-cased in SuperCall codegen by
NAME, and `has_extends_expr` can't distinguish a shadowed-local `Error`
(`const Error = class {…}; class X extends Error {}`) from the genuine
built-in (HIR captures extends_expr for both). So a local shadowing a
built-in name ran the built-in initializer instead of the local ctor.

resolves to an in-scope local (`!class_renames && ctx.locals.lookup`),

scope state the heritage routing uses. Codegen excludes
`is_builtin_parent_name` when the flag is set, so super() dispatches the
dynamic extends_expr value (the local). Genuine (unshadowed) built-in
subclassing is untouched — the flag is only ever true for a real local
shadow.

local ctor, while a module-scope `extends Error` still gets the built-in
`.message`.

fix(regex): fold emoji-regex high-surrogate-before-group patterns (#5720)

`emoji-regex` (used by `string-width` for text-width measurement) factors a
shared UTF-16 high surrogate out before a non-capturing group, e.g.
`\uD83C(?:[\uDC04…]|\uDDE6\uD83C[\uDDE8-\uDDEC]|…)` and the ZWJ kiss/family
idiom `\uD83D(?:\uDC8B‍\uD83D)?[\uDC68\uDC69]`.

`fold_surrogate_pairs` only collapsed a high surrogate that was *directly*
adjacent to a low one, so the factored-out lone high surrogate reached the
`regex` crate as a surrogate scalar (`\x{d83d}`) and the whole pattern was
rejected with `SyntaxError: invalid pattern` — even though Node accepts it, so
constructing the regex (and importing `string-width`) threw at runtime.

`distribute_high_over_group` distributes the high surrogate into the following
non-capturing group via the identities `H(?:A|B)` ≡ `(?:HA|HB)` (plain) and
`H(?:G)?L` ≡ `(?:HGL|HL)` (optional group + trailing low unit), then re-folds,
restoring adjacency so each high/low pair collapses to an astral scalar. Only
fires when every alternative is low-surrogate-led and the group is not
otherwise quantified, so patterns that compile today are byte-for-byte
unaffected.

fix(hir): #5588 — reify the full set of Object static methods as first-class values (#5718)

`Object.isExtensible`, `preventExtensions`, `setPrototypeOf`, `seal`,
`isFrozen`, `isSealed`, `is`, `defineProperties`, `getOwnPropertyDescriptors`,
`getOwnPropertySymbols`, and `groupBy` are all installed on the reified
`Object` constructor (global_this/install_static.rs), but the
`outer_is_reified_object_static_value` allow-list in member lowering only
named a subset. Reads of the omitted methods as VALUES (`const f =
Object.isExtensible`, `typeof Object.setPrototypeOf`) collapsed the receiver
to `GlobalGet(0)`, whose intrinsic property path has no value form and yields
`undefined`. The codegen fallback deliberately can't recover these names
because they overlap `Reflect`/`Map` once the receiver is collapsed, so the
fix belongs in HIR: route the reads through the reified `Object` receiver.

Direct calls (`Object.setPrototypeOf(a, b)`) already routed through the
reified receiver and are unaffected.

Fixes 8 test262 built-ins/Object cases (isExtensible/preventExtensions/
setPrototypeOf `name`/`length`/existence + getOwnPropertyDescriptor identity);
no regressions across the 3173-case Object subtree.

fix(hir): #5592 — two anonymous class exprs on one binding + computed-accessor prototype writes (#5717)

Test262 `language/class` tail: `accessor-name-inst-computed-in` (and the
broader pattern of reassigning a binding to successive anonymous class
expressions) failed for two intertwined reasons.

1. ClassId collision. An anonymous `class { … }` assigned to a binding
   infers that binding's name (`C`) as its HIR registration key. A second
   `C = class { … }` inferred the same name, and `lower_class_from_ast`
   dedups by name — so both expressions aliased onto ONE ClassId and the
   second body was silently dropped (`C` kept pointing at the first class).
   Fix: when the inferred name is already a registered class, give the new
   expression a unique registration key (`<name>__anon_dup_<n>`) so it gets
   its own ClassId, and record its real `.name` in a new
   `Module.class_display_names` map so codegen still registers `"C"`.

2. Computed accessors weren't tracked. `get [expr]()` / `set [expr](v)`
   never recorded an accessor name, so `C.prototype.<key> = v` routed to a
   name-keyed prototype monkey-patch (`RegisterPrototypeMethod`, statically
   resolved to the FIRST class) instead of the generic, runtime-evaluated
   setter-invoking path. Fix: flag classes that declare any computed
   accessor (`ClassAccessorNames.has_computed`, propagated to subclasses via
   `extend_from`) and treat `obj.prototype.<x> = v` as accessor-bearing for
   any `<x>`, so the write falls through to the path that evaluates the
   receiver at runtime and invokes the setter on the correct class.

Validated byte-for-byte against `node --experimental-strip-types`: the real
Test262 `accessor-name-inst-computed-in` case passes, as do all 84
`accessor-name-{inst,static}` cases across statements/ and expressions/class.
Adds test_gap_5592_class_expr_rebind_computed_accessor.ts.

fix(hir): a class only shadows a captured outer local when lexically nearer (#5437) (#5724)

Perry's class system is name-keyed + module-global. The lowerer kept a
`forward_class_names` set, inherited into nested function bodies, so a
`class X` declared in the current body could shadow a same-named OUTER
captured local (p-timeout's `class a extends Error` overwriting an
undefined placeholder). That rule was too broad: a class name lingered in
the inherited set while lowering a SIBLING factory, so a deeper nested
closure's bare-ident reference to its OWN captured local resolved to the
sibling-factory class reference instead of the local.

In the Next.js app-page-turbo bundle, a route-render closure read its
captured params local `ej` as the `class ej` (= NextURL) reference. That
class-ref (NaN-boxed INT32_TAG, low32 = class_id 393) flowed into a
WeakMap key and threw "Invalid value used as weak map key", 500ing every
dynamic page route.

Fix: record the scope depth at which each forward class is declared
(`forward_class_decl_depth`). At a bare-ident reference where both a
same-named class and a local exist, apply JS nearest-binding rules — the
class shadows the local only when it was declared at a deeper (nearer)
scope. No local, or unknown class depth, keeps the prior behavior.

Adds test_gap_5437_class_ref_shadows_captured_local.ts covering both the
fixed case (captured local wins) and the preserved case (class shadows an
outer placeholder).

fix(codegen): #5703 — pad under-supplied class-expression static-method calls with undefined (#5719)

* fix(codegen): #5703 — pad under-supplied class-EXPRESSION static-method calls with undefined

A static method of a class EXPRESSION (`var C = class { static m(...) {...} }`)
called with fewer arguments than declared dropped its default-parameter /
array-destructuring prologue. `C.m()` on a class-expression value reaches the
fused get-static-method+call path in
`lower_call/property_get/static_dispatch.rs`, whereas class DECLARATIONS lower
`C.m()` to a `StaticMethodCall` (which already pads missing slots with
`undefined` — #235). The dispatch path forwarded only the supplied args to a
fixed-arity LLVM function, so missing slots arrived as an uninitialized `0.0`
register rather than `undefined`. The callee's default-param prologue
(`if (p === undefined) p = …`) never fired, and array destructuring of the
missing slot (`GetIterator(p)`) threw `TypeError: is not iterable`.

This broke ~61 `language/expressions/class` test262 cases (static methods of
class expressions with default params / destructuring), dominated by static
async-generator methods with an array-destructuring default param. The
maintainer's bisection window pointed at #5662, but that commit only adds a
`RegisterClassCaptures` snapshot under `if !captured_args.is_empty()`; the bug
reproduces with captures disabled, so it is pre-existing in the static-dispatch
path, not a #5662 regression.

Fix: pad the missing positional slots with `undefined` in the static dispatch
path, mirroring the `StaticMethodCall` path — in both the plain-rest and
no-rest branches. Also fix the synthesized-`arguments` branch, which pushed
ONLY the arguments object: a leading real param before the synth `arguments`
slot (`static method(x, _ = 0) { … arguments … }`) received the (empty)
arguments array instead of its argument / `undefined`. It now lowers each arg
once (no double side effects), feeds the leading params their positional values
(undefined-padded), and builds the `arguments` object from all passed args.

Resolves the dominant array-destructuring/default-param cases plus the
`params-dflt-*-meth-static-args-unmapped` and `-ref-arguments` cases; verified
0 newly-broken across `language/expressions/class`. The remaining residuals
(object-rest destructuring with getters/non-enumerable, static setters) are
separate pre-existing issues outside the default-param family.

Regression test issue_5703_class_expr_static_dflt_params (5 cases, byte-for-byte
against node --experimental-strip-types).

fix(hir,runtime): native chained-static-class decorators + reflect-metadata require binding (NestJS bootstrap) (#5721)

* fix(hir,runtime): native chained-static-class decorators + reflect-metadata require binding (NestJS bootstrap)

Two independent bugs that block a NestJS app from booting natively (both
hit at module-evaluation time, before any user code runs).

1. Wall 2 — chained static-class self-alias (`reading 'value'` crash).
   tsc emits decorator-captured classes as `let Logger = Logger_1 = class Logger {…}`.
   The self-alias reference inside a member body lowered to a capture, forcing
   the class onto the per-evaluation `ClassExprFresh` path, whose fresh class
   object never resolved STATIC methods/accessors/descriptors from the class
   registry. So `Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(Logger, 'error')` returned
   undefined and NestJS's decorator (`Reflect.defineMetadata(..., descriptor.value)`)
   threw "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'value')".
   Fix: HIR resolves a class self-alias to `ClassRef` (off the fresh path);
   runtime resolves static methods/accessors/own-descriptors via the registry
   for `ClassExprFresh` heap class objects (guarded for the tagged class-object form).

2. Wall 3 — `require("reflect-metadata")` (`ReferenceError: _req_1 is not defined`).
   `@nestjs/common/index.js` does `require("reflect-metadata")`; the CJS wrap
   hoists it to `import _req_1 ...` + a `return _req_1` shim, but module_decl
   special-cased reflect-metadata with an early return that never bound the
   default-import local. Fix: bind reflect-metadata import specifiers to `{}`
   (the require result is always discarded; perry already provides the global
   `Reflect` polyfill). Bare `import "reflect-metadata"` is unaffected.

Verified on the upstream NestJS typescript-starter: both module-eval crashes
are gone (app advances to the express HTTP-adapter load). cargo test -p
perry-hir + perry-runtime green.

fix(runtime): include the old-gen arena in process.memoryUsage() heapUsed/heapTotal (#5713)

`js_arena_stats` (which backs `process.memoryUsage().heapUsed` /
`heapTotal`) summed only the general/nursery, longlived, and two survivor
arenas — it omitted OLD_ARENA. But large objects (>16KB: typed arrays, big
arrays/strings) are born in old-gen, and minor-GC survivors are promoted there,
so the live/large heap lives almost entirely in old-gen. As a result
`heapUsed`/`heapTotal` collapsed toward 0 (an 80MB array reported
heapUsed=0, heapTotal~4MB) while `rss` (a real OS query) showed ~97MB.

Add the OLD_ARENA region to the walk, mirroring the old-gen phase already in
`arena_in_use_bytes` (walk.rs) so the two accounts agree. Now an 80MB array
reports heapUsed~77MB / heapTotal~82MB.

(Out of scope: gc_malloc/system-malloc'd objects — promises, maps, large
closures — are still not counted, matching the existing accessors; and
external/arrayBuffers remain 0.)

feat(runtime): expose gc() as a callable globalThis property (#5712)

Follow-up to the `typeof gc` capability-guard fix. That change makes the
bare-identifier guard `if (typeof gc === "function") gc()` work, but the
other idiomatic capability-guard forms read `gc` as a VALUE:

  if (globalThis.gc) globalThis.gc();   // Node CLI docs' own example
  global.gc?.();                        // Bun's documented form
  const g = globalThis.gc; g?.();

These all read `globalThis.gc`, which Perry never installed, so they were
`undefined` / no-ops even though `gc()` is callable.

Install `gc` as a real callable property on the globalThis singleton (a
ClosureHeader-backed value, like `setTimeout`/`queueMicrotask`), routed to
the same `js_gc_collect` the bare `gc()` intrinsic uses. Non-enumerable; the
optional Node `force` argument is accepted but ignored (Perry's gc is a full
collection). Now `typeof globalThis.gc === "function"`, `globalThis.gc` is
truthy, and `globalThis.gc()` / `globalThis.gc?.()` / `gc?.()` all run a real
collection.

test: nested object literal must not corrupt an adjacent native (WS) handle (#5701)

Regression guard for a codegen bug present in v0.5.1206: a deeply nested
object/array literal at module scope -- {a:[..],b:[{kind,child:{a:[..],
b:[{kind}]}}]}, an object whose array element holds a nested object that itself
holds an array of objects -- silently broke node:http WebSocket INBOUND
dispatch globally: the upgrade handler's wsId.on("message") never fired while
outbound wsId.send(...) still worked. The literal read back fine; the
corruption hit a neighbouring allocation (the WS client handle). A flat,
single-level literal was unaffected. Fixed after v0.5.1206; this test guards
the regression.

The fixture self-tests in-process: a WS echo server + a ws client that sends
"ping" and expects "echo:ping". A miscompile -> no echo -> hang; a healthy
build -> prints WSOK and exits 0.

feat(fastify): bind with SO_REUSEPORT for cluster workers and the reusePort option (#5699)

A Fastify app under `node:cluster` (`cluster.fork()` workers each
`app.listen(port)`) couldn't scale across workers: the listen path bound with a
plain `TcpListener::bind`, so only the first worker held the port and the rest
failed with `EADDRINUSE`. The runtime's cluster machinery already does
SO_REUSEPORT worker-binding (used by `net` and perry-ext-http-server); this
wires Fastify into it so forked workers share a port (kernel-balanced accepts)
and `cluster.on('listening')` fires.

- Add a `cluster_bind` module mirroring perry-ext-http-server's: a worker bind
  (or an explicit `reusePort` opt-in) goes through socket2 with SO_REUSEADDR +
  SO_REUSEPORT (listen backlog 511, Node's default); other binds keep the plain
  `TcpListener::bind` path.
- Honor an explicit `{ reusePort: true }` listen option — a real Node (`net` /
  `http` `listen`) and Bun (`Bun.serve`) option — in addition to auto-enabling
  it for cluster workers, so a non-cluster program can opt into port sharing
  directly.
- Bind synchronously in `js_fastify_listen`, before registering the server or
  firing the success callback, so a bind failure (e.g. `EADDRINUSE`) reaches the
  `(err, address)` callback as a Node-style system Error
  (`err.code === 'EADDRINUSE'`) instead of being silently dropped inside the
  accept task while the caller is told listening succeeded. Only `from_std`
  stays in the spawned task (it needs the runtime context). The actual bound
  port is now reported for `listen(0)`.

Scope is the SO_REUSEPORT (SCHED_NONE) default; SCHED_RR fd-passing and the
shared ephemeral port for `listen(0)` are the #4962 follow-up, as for the HTTP
listen sites.

fix(hir): #5579 — publish module-top global eval's top-level var/function as configurable global bindings (#5725)

* fix(hir): #5579 — publish module-top global eval's top-level var/function as configurable global bindings

EvalDeclarationInstantiation: a sloppy *global* (direct or indirect) eval whose
body declares a top-level `var` or `function` must create a configurable own
binding on the global object (CreateGlobalVarBinding / CreateGlobalFunctionBinding)
that survives after the eval returns. Perry folds an eval body into a
scope-capturing arrow IIFE, which trapped top-level `var`/`function` as
arrow-locals, so `eval('var x; …')` / `eval('function f(){}')` never published
`x`/`f` to globalThis (test262 reason: "x/f should be an own property"). #5636
already handled *nested* block functions; this extends the same hoist to the eval
body's own top level.

- global_eval_hoist: a top-level `function` is renamed to a hidden binding and
  published with its value at instantiation via `void (f = <hidden>)` (the `void`
  keeps the declaration's empty completion value); a top-level `var x = init`
  becomes a create-if-absent global slot plus `void (x = init)`. A non-simple
  (destructuring) declarator bails the rewrite.
- const_fold_fn: a declaration-bearing *indirect* eval body at module-top global
  with nothing to hoist now still folds to the completion IIFE (running its side
  effects + yielding the completion value) instead of deferring to the runtime
  eval thunk, which returns `undefined` without executing the body. Guarded by
  `eval_body_iife_foldable`, which keeps a class-declaring body on the runtime
  thunk (Perry would otherwise leak the class to module scope —
  language/eval-code/indirect/lex-env-distinct-cls).

fix(runtime): share symbol-keyed metadata by reference across wrappers of one native handle (#5715)

* fix(runtime): #5437 — share native-handle symbol meta across request wrappers (Next.js resolvedPathname)

A native handle (small-id NaN-boxed POINTER, e.g. a node:http IncomingMessage)
carries per-request metadata in the symbol side table keyed by its handle id.
Node shares ONE metadata object by reference across every NodeNextRequest
wrapper that re-news around the same IncomingMessage, so:

 - a wrapper read `req[NEXT_REQUEST_META]` resolves to the shared object, and
 - a write-back `this._req[SYM] = this[SYM]` is harmless when `this[SYM]` is
   the shared object.

In Perry the sharing broke in two ways for a late SSR-bundled wrapper:

 1. WIPE: the bundled wrapper reached the write-back with an *undefined*
    `this[SYM]`, clobbering the handle's existing metadata to undefined and
    losing `resolvedPathname` → Next's `resolvedPathname must be set` invariant.
 2. UNSEEDED READ: the bundled wrapper's own `[SYM]` was never set, so the
    render's `getRequestMeta` read undefined off it even though its `_req`
    handle held the shared meta.

Fix (both gated tightly to native handle-band receivers):
 - set_symbol_property: an `undefined` write onto a handle-band receiver that
   already holds a non-undefined entry is a no-op (never adds information; the
   by-reference object the handle still points at is what Node keeps).
 - js_object_get_symbol_property: on a heap-wrapper side-table miss, fall
   through to the wrapper's `_req` native handle's symbol meta.

Regression tests cover the share, the wipe-guard, and that a plain heap object
setting a symbol prop to undefined still clears it.

* test(symbol): suppress GC in handle-meta-share tests (parallel cargo-test flake)

The two #5437 handle-meta tests compared a heap `meta` pointer that the
GC-rooted SYMBOL_PROPERTIES side table rewrites on a move while the local
stays stale — deterministic serially (how it was validated), but under
parallel cargo-test a sibling allocation triggers a GC mid-test → spurious
`got != meta`. Wrap each body in gc_suppress()/gc_unsuppress() so the
objects can't move; unsuppress before the assert so a panic can't leak
suppression. The symbol-meta fix itself is unchanged.

* fix(runtime): #5437 — GC-invariant handle-meta tests + CodeRabbit fixes

(A) Make the handle-meta-share tests deterministic under parallel cargo-test
without relying on gc_suppress (which only gates gc_check_trigger, not the
1MB block-alloc trigger). Use an immovable NaN-boxed NUMBER for the metadata
value: numbers are never pointers, so the SYMBOL_PROPERTIES side-table
scanner never rewrites them on a GC move -> got.to_bits() == meta.to_bits()
holds across any collection. wrapper_reads_share_underlying_handle_meta also
forces a full gc() up front to compact the arena so its few allocations
can't trip a mid-test block-alloc GC. The metadata tests now use the exact
Symbol.for("NextInternalRequestMeta") symbol (required by the narrowed
guard below).

(B1) req_handle_symbol_fallback (get.rs): drop the is_small_handle pre-check.
is_valid_obj_ptr already rejects handles and accepts a valid heap object even
at a low address; the pre-check wrongly rejected a real low-address wrapper.

(B2) set_symbol_property (properties.rs): narrow the undefined-write no-op to
ONLY Symbol.for("NextInternalRequestMeta") on a handle-band receiver
(resolved+cached once). Any other handle symbol — including clearing it with
undefined — now stores normally. Added a regression test
(undefined_write_clears_non_metadata_symbol_on_handle).

* test(symbol): handle-meta test ids must be < 0x1000 (Linux is_valid_obj_ptr HEAP_MIN)

The handle-meta tests failed ONLY on x86_64-LINUX CI (pass on arm64 + x86_64
macOS — proven via Rosetta). Root: is_valid_obj_ptr uses HEAP_MIN=0x1000 on
Linux but 0x200_0000_0000 on macOS, so synthetic handle ids 0x4321/0x5678/0x6789
(all >= 0x1000) were classified as valid heap objects on Linux, breaking the
handle-band gate. On macOS they're far below HEAP_MIN so the gate worked. Fix:
ids < 0x1000 (matching real tiny native handles), rejected as non-objects on
every platform. Not a GC race (corrects the prior gc_suppress/number-meta theory).

fix(gc): #5476 — reclaim dead old-gen blocks under reclaim pressure on compute-only workloads (#5734)

* fix(gc): #5476 — reclaim dead old-gen blocks under reclaim pressure on compute-only workloads

A workload that churns large temporaries (>16 KB, born directly in the old
arena because they exceed LARGE_OBJECT_THRESHOLD_BYTES) grows the old generation
without ever exercising the nursery. Old-gen reclaim pressure schedules a
budgeted full cycle that *would* return the dead old blocks to the OS, but:

  1. the budgeted stepper is blocked whenever synchronous-only root scanners are
     registered (the common case in a compiled program), and
  2. even when it runs it only advances through bounded mutator-assist steps that
     a compute-only loop never drives to completion — no event-loop safepoint
     ever runs.

Either way no collection completes, so dead old blocks are never reclaimed and
RSS climbs unbounded (the #5476 benchmark reached 1.8 GB RSS / 164 MB live).

Fix: when old-gen reclaim pressure is what's due in gc_check_trigger — a rare
event gated by the ~32 MB growth / 48 MB absolute baseline, so it never fires on
the common nursery-churn path — run a direct full mark-sweep to completion, the
same non-budgeted collection an explicit gc() performs (#5714). The conservative
native-stack scan keeps it safe: anything still referenced from the stack or
registers at the allocation point is retained; only genuinely unreachable old
blocks are returned. A re-entrancy guard prevents a nested trigger from
recursing, and the full cycle's completion rebaselines the reclaim watermark.

Repro (50× new Array(100k) → filter→map→reduce, no gc() calls):
  before: RSS 58→103→149→191 MB, monotonic and unbounded
  after:  RSS 51→66→67→67 MB, stabilizes (matches Node's bounded RSS)

Adds a regression test asserting gc_check_trigger alone drives the old-gen
reclaim cycle to completion (collection runs, dead old bytes freed, live root
preserved) without any host GC step.

feat(runtime): implement process.stdin as a functional raw-mode Readable (#5733)

* feat(runtime): implement process.stdin as a functional raw-mode Readable

Node terminal apps (e.g. ink) read the keyboard through `process.stdin`
using the Readable stream API — `setRawMode(true)` + `on("readable", …)`
+ `read()`, or the flowing-mode `on("data", …)`. Previously `on`/`read`/
`resume` on the stdin stream object were no-op stubs ("encoding-aware
reads remain future work"), so none of that input ever reached JS even
though the raw bytes were arriving on fd 0. Interactive TUIs rendered but
never responded to keystrokes.

Implement a real stdin Readable:

- A dedicated reader thread reads fd 0 one byte at a time into a shared
  buffer and `js_notify_main_thread()`s on each byte so the event loop
  ticks promptly on keypress.
- `process.stdin.on(event, cb)` (2-arg, arity-registered) registers
  `data`/`readable` listeners and starts the reader; `read([size])`
  drains the buffer and returns the bytes as a JS string (stdin is
  `setEncoding("utf8")` in practice) or `null` when empty; `resume()`
  ensures the reader is running.
- Dispatch happens from `js_callback_timer_tick` — the same safe
  event-loop point where timer callbacks fire — NOT from
  `js_wait_for_event` (calling JS from the wait primitive reenters and
  wedges the runtime). Each listener call is wrapped in a
  `RuntimeHandleScope` that roots the closure (and the string arg)
  across the call, mirroring the timer dispatch. `data` listeners get
  the bytes directly; otherwise `readable` listeners are notified and
  pull via `read()`.

The returned string is nanboxed with `STRING_TAG` (not a generic object
pointer) so JS `typeof`/`+`/`!== null` see a real string.

Verified with standalone PTY repros of both the `on("readable")`+`read()`
loop and the `on("data")` flowing path: keystrokes are delivered and
processed (incl. Ctrl-C / backspace handling in the app layer).

fix(object): #5736 — make own_key_present O(1) on wide objects so Object.values/entries aren't O(n²) (#5738)

* fix(object): #5736 — make own_key_present O(1) on wide objects so Object.values/entries aren't O(n²)

A barrel `export *` namespace (or any object grown past ~257 keys) made
`own_key_present` an O(n) keys_array scan. `Object.values` / `Object.entries`
re-check every own key through `own_key_present` (a getter fired on an earlier
value read can delete a later key), so enumerating such an object was O(n²) — the
startup cost jdalton measured as "per-module init scaling" was actually the
entry's `Object.values(mods)` over the star-export barrel namespace.

The read-path getter already maintains an O(1) key→slot index for wide objects
(#5054); `own_key_present` just wasn't using it. Probe that index first: a hit is
O(1), a miss falls through to the existing linear scan (so an absent key, or a
present key whose index entry was dropped as stale, is still answered correctly —
the index revalidates every hit against the live slot). Module init itself was
already cheap (~0.02 ms/module); this removes the quadratic enumeration term.

Repro (K trivial modules behind a barrel, entry does Object.values(mods)):

  | K   | before  | after  |
  | --- | ------- | ------ |
  | 60  | 16.9 ms | 9.8 ms |
  | 120 | 42.0 ms | 10.7ms |
  | 240 | 140.1ms | 12.3ms |   (~11× faster; slope ~3.4 ms/mod → ~flat)

The fix is a no-op for objects below the 257-key wide threshold (the common
case), so normal property access is unchanged. Adds a regression test asserting
own_key_present resolves present keys, rejects absent keys, and Object.values
enumerates every value on a 600-key wide object.

default: `lower_setter_method_with_name` built the `Param` with
`default: None` and emitted no `if (param === undefined) param = <default>`
prologue (only destructuring was handled). So invoking the setter with
`undefined` (`C.a = undefined`) never ran the default expression — test262
`language/expressions/class/scope-static-setter-paramsbody-var-open` left
`probeParams` undefined ("value is not a function").

Fix: mirror the constructor/method path — lower the default via
`get_param_default` in the param loop (BEFORE `define_local`, so the
default's references resolve to the enclosing scope rather than the
param or the body's hoisted `var`s — the separate parameter/body
VariableEnvironment the spec mandates) and prepend
`build_default_param_stmts` to the body. The default's `x` closure then
binds the OUTER `x` ("outside") while the body's `var x = "inside"` closure
binds the body `x`, matching node byte-for-byte. Applies to instance and
static setters alike; affects only setters that actually declare a
default (`build_default_param_stmts` is inert otherwise).

Regression test: class_expr_static_setter_default_param_scope.

fix(temporal): #5587 — validate ZonedDateTime.from options + getTimeZoneTransition direction (#5746)

`ToTemporalZonedDateTime` and `GetDirectionOption` skipped or mis-typed
their argument validation, so several negative test262 cases never threw
(or threw the wrong error type). Three glue fixes, all confined to the
ZonedDateTime paths:

1. ZonedDateTime instance input to `from(item, options)` returned the
   clone immediately without touching `options`. Per spec the options bag
   is still read in order (disambiguation → offset → overflow), so a bad
   options type (TypeError) or value (RangeError) must be observed before
   cloning. Read+validate all three before returning the clone.

2. The string-input branch never read `overflow` (a bad value is a
   RangeError) and validated the options object before parsing the
   string, so an invalid IXDTF string + non-object options threw a
   TypeError instead of the RangeError the spec mandates (string parse
   precedes GetOptionsObject). Structurally pre-parse the string with a
   lenient offset disambiguation to surface the RangeError first, then
   read disambiguation/offset/overflow.

3. `getTimeZoneTransition`'s `transition_direction` threw a RangeError for
   `undefined` and non-object primitives; GetOptionsObject makes those a
   TypeError (the direction option is required). Only a malformed
   string/object value stays a RangeError.

Fixes 12 built-ins/Temporal/ZonedDateTime test262 cases (from/{overflow,
offset,disambiguation}-{invalid-string,wrong-type}, options-wrong-type,
order-of-operations, observable-get-overflow-argument-{primitive,
string-invalid}, getTimeZoneTransition/{options-undefined,wrong-type})
with zero regressions across the 901-case ZonedDateTime subtree.

Refs #5587.

* fix(intl): #5581 — NumberFormat significant-digit formatting of zero infinite-looped

`round_to_significant` rendered a zero value as `("0", "")` and then ran the
min-significant-digits padding loop `while significant_count(int, frac) < min_sig
{ frac.push('0') }`. But `significant_count` of an all-zeros decimal is always 0,
so for any value of `0` formatted with significant digits (or compact notation,
which rounds by significant digits) the loop never terminated — `format(0)` hung.

The hang was latent (every locale, not numbering-specific); the preceding
numbering-system commit merely unblocked the test262 rounding-mode cases far
enough past the digit-set gate to reach `format(0)` and expose it.

Render zero as a single "0" padded to `min_sig` total displayed digits
(ECMA-402 ToRawPrecision: minSig 3 → "0.00") and return early, before the
nonzero-only normalization loops.

Flips the 9 intl402/NumberFormat `format-rounding-mode-*` cases plus
format-significant-digits.js (+10); no regressions across NumberFormat /
DurationFormat / PluralRules.

* fix(intl): #5581 — address CodeRabbit review (increment overflow, currency scale, mantissa carry)

Three correctness findings from CodeRabbit on #5737, each verified byte-for-byte
against Node:

1. roundingIncrement on wide fraction scales / large values. `round_to_increment`
   parsed the scaled integer as `u128`, so `maximumFractionDigits` near its 100
   ceiling (or very large values) overflowed and silently fell back to plain
   fraction rounding, dropping the increment. The scaled integer is now kept as a
   digit string and reduced with small-divisor modular arithmetic
   (decimal_mod_small / decimal_add_small / decimal_sub_small); the increment
   (≤ 5000) and the dropped tail (bounded by the shortest decimal) stay small.
   Parity for halfEven is read off `q mod 2·increment`, avoiding any wide division.

2. Currency increment grid used the default scale. `currency_instance_parts`
   rounded/snapped on the currency's default fraction digits, ignoring
   minimum/maximumFractionDigits — so e.g. 3-digit USD snapped on 0.05 instead of
   0.005. It now uses the resolved width `r.max_frac` (which already folds in the
   currency default plus options) for both the increment grid and the display,
   so grid and precision agree (1.234 → $1.235). Identical to before for the
   default-width common case.

3. Scientific/engineering mantissa carry. The exponent was computed before
   rounding, so a carry (9.9 → 10) emitted `10E0` instead of `1E1`. After
   rounding, a grown mantissa now renormalizes: recompute the exponent from
   msd+1 and reshape the significand — scientific `1E1`, while engineering keeps
   the digit when the new magnitude stays in the same power-of-1000 band
   (`9.9 → 10E0`, `999.9 → 1E3`, `99999 → 100E3`).

NumberFormat test262 unchanged at 158 pass / identical failure set (these cases
have no test262 coverage in the failing set); DurationFormat (92) and PluralRules
(39) unchanged — zero regressions.

  and coerces bool/string per spec, matching the dynamic-dispatch + includes paths
- String.prototype.normalize form (TypeError before the form-validity RangeError)
- String.raw raw[i] / substitution segments

slice: 12 -> 4 failing (remaining 4 are surrogate/observable-order, separate
root); String/prototype/normalize symbol case also fixed. No regressions in the

fix(hir): #5579 — Annex B.3.3.3 direct-eval function-scope block-function hoisting (#5747)

* fix(hir): #5579 — Annex B.3.3.3 direct-eval function-scope block-function hoisting

A sloppy *direct* eval running inside a function routes the var-scoped
declarations of its body into the *enclosing function's* variable environment
(Annex B.3.3.3, EvalDeclarationInstantiation). Perry folds the eval body into a
scope-capturing arrow IIFE, so a block/`if`/`switch`-nested `function f(){}` is
trapped as an arrow-local `f`. When the eval body's function name already binds
in the enclosing function (a parameter or outer `var`), that fresh arrow-local
wrongly *shadows* the pre-existing binding, so a read before the declaration
sees `undefined` instead of the live value (test262
`annexB/language/eval-code/direct/func-*-eval-func-no-skip-param`, 8 cases:
`init = f` read `undefined` rather than the param `123`).

Extend the #5636 global-eval hoist with a function-scope mode: a nested function
whose name is already bound in the enclosing scope is renamed to a hidden
binding (self-references too) and republished to the enclosing binding with a
bare `f = <hidden>` assignment when the declaration is reached — no `globalThis`
create-if-absent prelude (the binding already exists). A nested function whose
name is *not* already bound, every top-level declaration, `var`s, and a `class`
are left exactly as the unmodified fold produced them: the completion IIFE
already models their binding, and a bare assignment for a brand-new name would
leak a sloppy global. The new path is gated on direct (not indirect) eval,
sloppy mode, a non-module-top call site, no enclosing `with`, and the nested
function name being present in `ctx.locals` — so it never touches the cases the
IIFE already handles (`func-init`, `func-existing-*`, `func-update`,
`skip-early-err`, the switch-param family).

annexB + language/eval-code slice: 8 previously-failing no-skip-param cases now
pass, no regressions (the remaining eval-code failures are a strict subset of
the prior set). Adds unit tests for the function-scope hoist and the
nested-function-name collector.

fix(runtime): #5586 — enforce Annex B.1.4 regexp restrictions under the /u flag (#5749)

* fix(runtime): #5586 — enforce Annex B.1.4 regexp restrictions under the /u flag

ECMAScript's Annex B.1.4 regexp leniencies must NOT apply when the `u` flag
is present, but `js_regex_to_rust` silently relaxed them so the patterns
compiled instead of throwing. Adds `has_unicode_forbidden_pattern`, a
single-pass validator (gated on `u`, called from both `js_regexp_new` and

- lone `]` / `}` PatternCharacters and incomplete/standalone `{` quantifiers;
- `-` ranges with a `\d`-style CharacterClassEscape endpoint (`[\d-a]`);
- quantifiers applied directly to a lookaround assertion (`(?=.)*`);
- forbidden IdentityEscapes (`\A`, `\-` outside a class, bare `\x`/`\u`/`\p`/`\k`).

The `v` flag's ClassSetExpression grammar differs, so the structural check is
gated on `u` specifically; the existing legacy-escape check (now also wired
into `compile`) keeps covering `u`/`v`.

fix(async): spec-correct async-generator yield* delegation for return() + non-object next() (#5592) (#5751)

Async-generator `yield *` only implemented the `next()` direction. Three
spec steps were missing, so test262's `yield-star-*` class cases failed:

1. **non-object iter-result** — after `Await(? Call(next, ...))` the spec
   requires `If Type(innerResult) is not Object, throw a TypeError`. Perry
   read `.done`/`.value` off a primitive instead, so `gen.next()` fulfilled
   where it must reject (`yield-star-next-non-object-ignores-then`).

2. **return() forwarding** — `gen.return(v)` while suspended inside a
   `yield *` must forward to the delegated iterator's `return` method
   (spec `yield *` step 6.c): complete with `v` when there is no `return`,
   re-yield on a `{done:false}` result, or complete with the result value
   on `{done:true}`. Perry completed the outer generator directly, never
   touching the inner iterator (`yield-star-{sync,async}-return`).

3. **AsyncFromSync return/throw double-read** — `%AsyncFromSyncIterator
   Prototype%.{return,throw}` do `GetMethod` once then `Call` the captured
   value; Perry re-dispatched by name, firing a `get return`/`get throw`
   accessor twice and diverging from Node's operation order.

Implementation:

- linearize: enforce the Object-check on every awaited delegated pull
  (async generators only — sync `yield *` reads `.done`/`.value` via
  `GetV` and never throws), and record each `yield *` suspend-state
  interval so the `.return()` closure can find the delegated iterator.
- lower/abrupt: in an async generator's `.return()` closure, forward to
  the delegated iterator's `return` (await + Object-check + done dispatch)
  when suspended in a `yield *` interval; otherwise fall through to the
  existing completion path. No-op for sync generators / generators
  without a `yield *`.
- runtime: `async_from_sync_call_raw` invokes the already-fetched
  return/throw method value (with `this = iter`) instead of re-dispatching
  by name.

Fixes 24 of 40 class `yield-star-*` cases (non-object 8, sync-return 8,
async-return 8) across async-gen-method{,-static} and async-gen-private-
method{,-static} (statements + expressions). The remaining `*-throw`
cases need `throw()` forwarding, whose `{done:true}` branch must resume
the outer body after the `yield *` (async-generator dispatch-loop
continuation, analogous to #4374 for sync generators) — left as
follow-up.

have that override honored in two spec-observable spots:

fix(runtime): preserve class refs spread into imported functions (NestJS @UseFilters/guards/pipes) (#5758)

The closure-call dispatcher (`js_closure_call_array` / the per-arity `a()`
marshaller in value_call.rs) unboxes any 0x7FFE-tagged argument to a plain
numeric double — a workaround so v8-bridged integers feed the closure body's
`fadd` arithmetic. But class refs and class-prototype refs are ALSO 0x7FFE
(INT32_TAG)-boxed with the class id in the low 32 bits. So an imported class
passed through a spread call `f(...args)` (e.g. `@nestjs/common`'s
`UseFilters = (...f) => addExceptionFiltersMetadata(...f)`, and the method-

threw "Invalid filter passed to @UseFilters()" at bootstrap and method-level
guards/pipes were silently dropped.

(`class_ref_id(raw).is_some()` — covers class-prototype refs too). A class ref
is never a v8 int32, so arithmetic is unaffected.

now `function`, matching node. `cargo test -p perry-runtime -p perry-hir`

fix(async): #5745 — async-generator yield* .throw() delegation + resume (#5761)

* fix(async): #5745 — async-generator yield* .throw() delegation + resume

When an async generator is suspended inside a `yield *` and `gen.throw(e)`
is called, spec `yield *` step 6.b requires forwarding the error to the
delegated iterator's `throw` method. Perry already forwarded `.return()`
(#5751) but `.throw()` fell through to the outer generator's own catch
routing, so the inner iterator's `throw` never fired, the post-resume
yielded value was dropped, and the delegation loop could not continue.

Unlike `return`, a `throw` whose inner result is `done` does NOT complete
the outer generator — it resumes execution *after* the `yield *` (which may
yield again or run to completion). This needs the async-generator
abrupt-resume continuation machinery that sync generators have (#4374) but
the async path deliberately omitted.

Implementation:
- DelegationRoute records the drive loop's iter-result local (`result_id`)
  and its condition-check state (`resume_state` = the `while` cond state).
- build_yield_star_throw_routes (async only): GetMethod(iterator,"throw");
  if undefined, AsyncIteratorClose the inner iterator then throw a TypeError;
  else await throw.call(iter, e), enforce the Object result, store it into
  `result_id`, set state to `resume_state`, and re-drive a clone of the
  state-dispatch loop. The condition state then reads `result.done` and
  either exits the loop (resuming the outer body past the `yield *`) or
  re-yields `result.value` — reproducing spec operation order exactly.
- Injected into the `.throw()` closure before the catch-routing fallback,
  so it only fires while suspended in a delegation.

Strictly additive and async-only: `delegations` is recorded solely under
`linearize_async_generator()`, so the routes are empty (a no-op) for sync
generators and for async generators without a `yield *`.

* fix(eval,typedarray): #5735 — declaration completion-value (5) + typed-array symbol-key writes

Two coherent test262 clusters from the 2026-06-27 sweep.

## Cluster 2 — declaration completion-value (5 cases, fully fixed)

The completion value of a statement list whose last evaluated statement is a
`function`/`async function`/`generator`/`var` *declaration* must be empty, so it
falls through to the prior statement (`eval("1; function f(){}")` is `1`;
`eval("function f(){}")` is `undefined`; `eval("9; var x = 10")` is `9`).

In global-script mode the eval-fold hoist published these declarations to the
global environment with statements the completion tracker mis-counted:

- A top-level `function` is published via `Object.defineProperty(globalThis, …)`,
  which *returns* `globalThis`. The tracker rewrote that to `__perry_cv = define…`,
  so a declaration-only body yielded the global object. Fix: `void`-wrap the
  defineProperty calls (the publish block is prepended, so an empty completion is
  enough).
- A top-level `var x = init` was rewritten in place to `void (x = init)`, still an
  expression statement, so the tracker wrote `__perry_cv = undefined` and
  *clobbered* a preceding value (`9; var x = 10` wrongly became `undefined`). Fix:
  emit a completion-inert lexical declaration `{ let __perry_eval_void = (x = init); }`
  — a declaration's completion is empty, so the prior value shows through.

Fixes test262 `language/statements/{function,async-function,generators,variable}/cptn-*`
and `language/statementList/eval-fn-block` (all pass).

## Cluster 1 — typed-array symbol-key writes

A Symbol write on a *statically-typed* multi-byte typed array
(`const t = new Float64Array(2); t[sym] = v`) lowered through the width-tracked
native store, which `fptosi`-coerced the NaN-boxed Symbol to index 0 and
*clobbered element 0* instead of storing a symbol property. Fix: route
non-numeric keys on the width-tracked store path to the symbol-aware runtime
dispatcher (mirroring the symmetric IndexGet guard), and make
`js_typed_array_index_{get,set}_dynamic` triage Symbol keys into the symbol side
table.

Note: the two `OwnPropertyKeys/integer-indexes-and-string-and-symbol-keys` cases
remain — they exercise a multi-byte view over a buffer from a discarded temporary
(`new TA(new TA([…]).buffer)`) whose receiver is mis-inferred onto a typed-feedback
array path; that is a separate type-inference issue tracked for follow-up.

fix(deforest): rewrite producer call sites in class member bodies (#5772)

Deforestation promotes an array-producer function (`function f(){ const
out = []; ...out.push(x)...; return out; }`) to take the accumulator as a
synthetic trailing `__deforest_out` parameter, then rewrites every call
site to allocate the array and pass it in.

`detect_producers` scans free functions, module-init, AND class
member bodies (methods + constructors) when deciding whether a producer
is safe to rewrite — a plain `let v = f()` inside a method is a
"supported" call site, so the producer is admitted. But phase 3 only
rewrote call sites in module-init and free functions. A producer whose
call site lived in a class method therefore had its signature rewritten
(gaining the out-param) while the method's call kept its original arity.
Codegen then passes `undefined` for the missing argument, so the body
runs `out.push(...)` / `return out` on a non-array — a SIGSEGV, or a
downstream `TypeError: is not iterable` when the returned value is later
spread / for-of'd.

This is the same arity-mismatch class as the in-closure bail-out
(#5136); there the fix was to drop the producer, but method bodies are
ordinary statement lists we can rewrite rather than bail on.

Fix: make detection, fresh-id seeding, and the phase-3 rewrite all cover
the identical complete set of code bodies — module-init, free functions,
constructors, methods, getters, setters, and static methods:
- `deforest/mod.rs` (phase 3): rewrite call sites in every class member
  body, not just module-init + free functions.
- `deforest/detect.rs`: extend the three safety scans (funcref misuse,
  unsafe call sites, in-closure usage) to getters/setters/static methods
  so admission and rewrite stay symmetric.
- `deforest/walk.rs` (`max_local_id`): include getter/setter/static-
  method locals so the synthetic-id seed can't collide with a local
  already living in those bodies.

Adds a regression test: a producer called via `let v = helper()` inside
a class method is deforested AND its call site is rewritten to pass the
accumulator (arity matches the rewritten producer).

fix(runtime): #5591 — method-dispatch depth guard leaked across longjmp throws; Uint8Array/Buffer dynamic callbacks silently no-op'd (#5775)

* fix(runtime): #5591 — method-dispatch depth guard leaked across longjmp throws; Uint8Array/Buffer dynamic callbacks silently no-op'd

Two root causes behind the test262 `%TypedArray%.prototype.{every,some}`
callbackfn-not-callable failures (and a broader correctness gap):

1. **Depth-guard leak across `longjmp`.** `js_native_call_method` is wrapped in
   a RAII `CallMethodDepthGuard` (a stack-overflow backstop for circular module
   init). Perry's exceptions unwind with `setjmp`/`longjmp`, which does NOT run
   Rust `Drop`s — so every exception thrown from inside a method call and caught
   by an outer `try` skipped the guard's decrement, leaking one count per
   throw/catch. After `MAX_CALL_METHOD_DEPTH` (512) such cycles the guard
   tripped *permanently* and every subsequent method call returned the empty
   null-object fallback instead of dispatching, so a method that should throw
   (or compute) silently no-op'd. This is the cumulative pattern test262's
   `every`/`some` suites hit (~11 `assert.throws` per typed array across all
   constructors). Fix: snapshot the depth at each `try` (`js_try_push`) and
   restore it on the unwind (`js_throw`), mirroring the existing shadow-stack /
   async-context restores.

2. **Uint8Array/Buffer dynamic dispatch skipped callback validation.** A
   `Uint8Array` / `Uint8ClampedArray` / Node `Buffer` reached via the dynamic
   `(ta as any).method(...)` path routes through `dispatch_buffer_method`, whose
   match only implements the Node `Buffer` API surface; the inherited
   `%TypedArray%.prototype` iteration methods (`every`/`some`/`map`/`forEach`/
   `find`/`reduce`/…) fell through to the catch-all and silently returned
   `undefined` — never validating the callback nor iterating. Fix: delegate
   unclaimed methods on a uint8-backed view to the shared
   `dispatch_uint8_buffer_method` (which validates callbacks and reads the typed
