fix(hir): clear callee marker when lowering short-circuit/conditional operands (#5784)

Calling a native builtin reached through a short-circuit or conditional
expression — `(K || JSON.parse)(x)`, `(K ?? B.method)(x)`, `(c ? a : JSON.parse)(x)`,
`(0, JSON.parse)(x)` — threw `TypeError: value is not a function` when the
builtin branch was taken.

Root cause (perry-hir): lowering a call sets `ctx.lowering_call_callee` before
lowering the callee so a DIRECT intrinsic call (`JSON.parse(x)`, `Date.now()`)
takes the fast path — the member-tail reroute-undo collapses the receiver to a
bare `GlobalGet(0)` and codegen emits the intrinsic. But a binary/logical/
conditional/sequence expression in callee position is ITSELF the callee; its
operands/branches are values, not the immediate callee member. The marker
leaked through `lower_bin_expr` / `lower_cond` / `lower_seq` into those operands,
so a nested builtin-namespace member (`JSON.parse`) was collapsed to the
value-less intrinsic form `PropertyGet { GlobalGet(0), "parse" }` (the namespace
name dropped). That form has no value materialization and lowers to `undefined`,
so the short-circuit/conditional result threw when called. Stored-then-called
(`let g = K || JSON.parse; g(x)`) and direct calls were unaffected because the
marker was correctly false / true there.

Fix: save/clear/restore `lowering_call_callee` around lowering the operands in
`lower_bin_expr` (`||`/`??`/`&&`/all binary), `lower_cond` (ternary), and
`lower_seq` (comma). A nested *call* operand re-sets the flag for its own callee,
so direct intrinsic calls keep their fast path.

This is the runtime shape behind axios's `transformRequest` (`(K || JSON.parse)`)
and other `(x || nativeBuiltin)()` call sites.

Adds an integration test covering `||`/`??`/`&&`/ternary/comma callees with
native builtins, plus user-fn-via-`||`, stored-then-called, and direct-call
(must keep working), run under a wall-clock timeout.

fix(regex): #5586 — \s NEL, lone surrogates, unknown Unicode 16 scripts, large quantifiers, (?:(?=X))? normalization (#5781)

* fix(regex): #5586 — \s NEL, lone surrogates, unknown Unicode 16 scripts, large quantifiers, (?:(?=X))? normalization

Addresses the five root causes behind the built-ins/RegExp test262 failures
tracked in #5586:

1. `\s`/`\S` outside a character class: Rust's `\s` includes U+0085 NEL via
   the Unicode `White_Space` property; ECMAScript's `\s` explicitly excludes it.
   Rewrite standalone `\s`/`\S` to an explicit character class that matches JS
   semantics exactly.

2. Lone-surrogate `\uXXXX` escape outside a character class: `regex` rejects
   bare surrogate code points. Emit a never-matching class instead (`[^\s\S]`)
   since lone surrogates cannot appear in valid UTF-8 strings.

3. Unknown Unicode 16.0 scripts and `Changes_When_NFKC_Casefolded`: `regex-syntax`
   v0.8.x does not yet include Beria_Erfe, Sidetic, Taiyo, Tolong_Siki, Script=Unknown,
   or the `Changes_When_NFKC_Casefolded` binary property — it rejects them as a hard
   SyntaxError. Substitute a never-matching class (positive form) or always-matching
   class (negated form) so the pattern compiles.

4. Large braced quantifiers (e.g. `/b{9007199254740991}/`): ECMAScript allows
   quantifier counts up to 2^53−1; `regex-syntax` uses `u32` internally and
   rejects values > u32::MAX as a parse error. Clamp counts to 65535 before
   passing to the Rust engines.

5. `(?:(?=X))?` pattern: a non-capturing group whose sole content is a single
   lookaround assertion, with a quantifier on the outer group. `fancy-regex`
   rejects this form. Extend `normalize_quantified_lookaround` to detect and
   normalize the `(?:LOOK)Q` wrapper in addition to directly-quantified
   lookaround groups.

* fix(regex): update lone-surrogate test to expect never-match output

`\uD800` (lone high surrogate) outside a char-class is now rewritten to
`[^\s\S]` (never-match) by `js_regex_to_rust`. The old assertion expected
the pass-through `\uD800x`, but leaving a lone surrogate verbatim causes
Rust's Unicode-only `regex` crate to reject the pattern at construction
time. Never-match is the correct safe fallback: lone surrogates cannot
appear in any UTF-8 string, so the pattern legitimately never matches.
Update the unit-test assertion and add a comment explaining the JS↔Rust
impedance (WTF-8 lone-surrogate matching is a known categorical gap).

fix(regex): don't recompile a cached pattern just to re-validate it (#5777)

`js_regexp_new` validated every pattern by compiling it with BOTH the `regex`
and `fancy-regex` engines (to decide whether to throw `SyntaxError`) — and did
so BEFORE consulting `REGEX_CACHE`. So a regex literal evaluated in a hot loop
recompiled its automaton on every single call even though `get_or_compile_regex`
had already cached the compiled form from the first call.

This is pathological for large patterns. string-width's `emojiRegex()` returns
a fresh `/…/g` literal (12807 chars, a huge alternation) on every text
measurement; ink's flexbox `calculateLayout` measures every cell, so the splash
render sat at ~99% CPU for minutes rebuilding the same automaton thousands of
times.

Fix: skip the expensive validation compile when `(pattern, flags)` is already
in `REGEX_CACHE`. A cached pattern is by definition compilable, so the
"both engines fail → throw" branch can never fire for it. The cheap JS-syntax
checks (`has_invalid_repeated_quantifier`, the `/u`-flag legacy-escape checks)
still run on every call, and `get_or_compile_regex` below returns the cached
`Arc<Regex>` as before — each `RegExp` object still gets its own fresh header
(and thus its own `lastIndex`). Uncached patterns are validated exactly as
before.

Adds an integration test asserting a repeatedly-compiled literal keeps matching
correctly, that two regexes from the same pattern keep independent `lastIndex`,
that flags stay part of the cache key, and that invalid patterns still throw on
every call. The test runs under a wall-clock timeout so a regression to per-call
recompilation fails fast.

fix(http): implement IncomingMessage.pipe() so node-fetch/gaxios bodies flow (#5787)

A client `http.IncomingMessage` (response) had no `.pipe()` method. Calling
`res.pipe(dest)` fell through to `undefined` and forwarded zero bytes, so any
library that reads a response body by piping it — node-fetch
(`res.pipe(new PassThrough())`), and gaxios/Got built on top of it — got a dead
body stream: `response.text()` / `.json()` never settled and the request
promise hung forever.

This blocked real startup paths: a connectivity-preflight that does two gaxios
GETs hung indefinitely (socket ESTABLISHED, response received but never read to
completion), wedging the flow that depended on it.

Fix: implement `IncomingMessage.pipe(dest)` in perry-ext-http — store the
destination, forward the response body to it via `dest.write(chunk)` and
`dest.end()` (mirroring the existing zlib `js_native_call_method_str_key`
forwarding), for both the buffered and streaming response paths, and return
`dest` (Node's pipe-returns-the-destination contract). Stored destinations are
GC-scanned. `dispatch_http` routes the `"pipe"` method to it.

Adds a regression test (`incoming_message_pipe.rs`) that does
`http.get(...).pipe(new PassThrough())`, asserts the full body arrives and the
destination is returned, under a wall-clock timeout so a regression of the hang
fails fast. `cargo test -p perry-ext-http` green (24/0).

fix(streams): drive pull when draining a ReadableStream body into a Response (#5776)

`new Response(stream)` / `new Request(url, { body: stream })` materialize the
body at construction via `drain_readable_into_bytes`. That function snapshotted
only the chunks already queued at the synchronous call instant and force-closed
the stream. Data enqueued in `start(controller)` survived (already queued), but
anything produced by a `pull(controller)` callback — sync OR async — was
dropped: `maybe_pull` defers the pull to a microtask that hasn't run yet, and
an async pull defers its `enqueue` further (past `await`). So `.text()` /
`.arrayBuffer()` / `.json()` returned an empty body.

The canonical victim is axios's fetch adapter: when `onDownloadProgress` is
set it wraps the response body in `trackStream` — a new ReadableStream whose
async `pull` does `await reader.read()` on the original body — then does
`await new Response(trackStream(body)).text()`. The empty body left the read
(and thus the request) promise unsettled, hanging apps at startup.

Fix: `drain_readable_into_bytes` now loops — collect queued chunks, then drive
the source (`maybe_pull_force`) + run the microtask queue so the (possibly
async) pull's `enqueue`/`close` land — until the stream reaches a terminal
state. An idle counter plus an absolute iteration cap (mirroring the
`await_maybe_promise` pump used for `node:stream` consumers) bound the loop: a
genuinely live source still awaiting external I/O can't be drained
synchronously here and falls back to whatever has arrived. Bodies whose data
was already queued in `start()` are byte-for-byte unaffected.

`maybe_pull_force` is a `maybe_pull` variant that ignores the
highWaterMark/read-request gate, so a `highWaterMark: 0` stream — which has no
parked reader on this drain path — is still driven to completion instead of
draining empty.

Adds an integration test (`response_stream_body_pull.rs`) covering start-,
sync-pull-, async-pull-, highWaterMark:0-, and trackStream-shaped bodies across
`.text()`/`.arrayBuffer()`/`.json()`. It runs the compiled program under a
wall-clock timeout so a regression of this hang fails fast instead of stalling
CI.

fix(runtime): #5779 — rouse a parked tokio worker before the main thread idles so in-process server+fetch can't deadlock (#5795)

Perry runs JS on the main thread (not a tokio worker); it parks on the
event-loop condvar while the shared multi-thread runtime drives async I/O.
For an in-process loopback request the response is handed back to the hyper
serve task via a oneshot::send fired from res.end() in the main-thread pump.
When the runtime has gone fully idle (every worker parked, reactor in kevent)
that remote worker-unpark can be lost: the serve task strands, the response is
never written, the in-process fetch() never settles, and the main thread —
having already shipped its half — re-parks. Permanent deadlock (the #5779
sequential in-process server+fetch hang; sample confirms main + all workers
parked, one in kevent).

Fix: perry-runtime gains an opt-in idle-kick callback (js_register_idle_kick)
invoked from js_wait_for_event on the pre-sleep slow path only (never the hot
NOTIFIED fast path). perry-stdlib registers a kick that, when async client work
is in flight, schedules a task on the shared runtime so a worker is roused to
drain the stranded task; its own completion notify then wakes the main thread.
The kick task does real work (a release atomic store) — an empty spawn(async {})
was measured not to reliably rouse a parked worker (8/8 deadlocks) whereas a

fix(json): serialize int32-tagged numbers instead of emitting null (#5796)

JSON.stringify dropped every int32-tagged value to `null`. An int32 is
NaN-boxed (INT32_TAG = 0x7FFE), so its bits ARE an IEEE NaN; with no int32
branch in `write_number`, it fell into the `is_nan()` -> "null" arm. Numeric
literals dodge this because codegen stores them as plain f64 doubles, but
values produced as int32 -- notably integer columns from the better-sqlite3
binding (`sqlite_value_to_jsvalue` boxes SQLITE_INTEGER as `JSValue::int32`)
-- serialized as `null`. This silently corrupted every integer crossing
JSON/IPC: a Drizzle/better-sqlite3 `SELECT id, ...` row reached an Electron
renderer as `{ id: null, ... }`.

Fix: decode INT32_TAG in `write_number` (the central numeric funnel that
stringify_value, object fields, array elements, and both shape fast-paths
all route through) before the NaN check, mirroring the BigInt funnel above.

Adds regression tests for int32 object fields and array elements.

Reported on the electron-compat stress test (integer PRIMARY KEY / integer
columns return null in Drizzle SELECT results once serialized over IPC).

Co-authored-by: Ralph Küpper <ralph@skelpo.com>

fix(runtime): decode int32 operands in the dynamic arithmetic helpers (#5798)

The dynamic `+`/`-`/`*`/`/`/`%` runtime helpers performed the raw f64 op on
their operands. An int32 is NaN-boxed (INT32_TAG = 0x7FFE), so its f64 bits ARE
an IEEE NaN; doing `a + b` on it propagates the tag through the FPU (ARM64 keeps
the NaN payload) and returns the *boxed operand* instead of the result.

The most visible symptom: a better-sqlite3 integer column read through the
`any`-typed path made `n + 100 === n` (and the same for every integer column).
`-`/`*` happened to work only because codegen eagerly coerces operands for the
unambiguous numeric operators; `+` stays boxed (it may be string concat) and
routes the raw int32 into `js_dynamic_string_or_number_add`, whose numeric
fallback returned the operand's NaN-boxed bits for an int32 instead of its value.

Fix: decode int32 operands to their plain-double value before the f64 op, in
`js_dynamic_string_or_number_add` and the five `js_dynamic_{add,sub,mul,div,mod}`
helpers (shared `numify_arith_operand`). Plain doubles and real NaNs pass through
unchanged. Adds regression tests.

Same INT32_TAG-not-decoded class as the JSON `null` bug; surfaced on the
electron-compat stress test (math on sqlite integer columns silently wrong).

fix(regex): skip redundant pattern validation on a RegExp cache hit (#5808)

`js_regexp_new` ran three JS-syntax validation checks
(`has_invalid_repeated_quantifier`, `has_unicode_forbidden_legacy_escape`,
`has_unicode_forbidden_pattern`) on EVERY call, before the `if !in_cache`
gate that already skipped the expensive both-engines recompile (#5777).

These checks are not actually cheap: `has_invalid_repeated_quantifier`
does a `pattern.chars().collect::<Vec<char>>()` (a ~51 KB allocation for a
12,807-char pattern) plus an O(n) scan. The common `string-width` /
`emoji-regex` npm packages construct a fresh ~12,807-char `/…/g` literal on
every measurement, and a layout pass can call them thousands of times, so
this re-validation — not the already-cached compile — became the top hot
frame in profiles.

Move all three checks inside the existing `if !in_cache { ... }` block (with
`in_cache` computed first), so the whole validation block is skipped on a
REGEX_CACHE hit. This is safe: regex validity is a pure function of
(pattern, flags); an invalid pattern throws before `get_or_compile_regex`
can cache it; and both writers of REGEX_CACHE (`js_regexp_new` and
`regex/compile.rs`) run these exact checks before populating the cache, so
any cache hit is provably valid. Invalid patterns are never cached, so they
remain cache misses and still throw SyntaxError on every call.

* fix(runtime): truly-async consumption of live Node Readable streams

Consuming a live Node `Readable` via `for await...of`, `Readable.prototype.toArray()`,
or the async helpers (`forEach`/`reduce`/`find`/`some`/`every`) returned an
empty/partial result or hung. The async iterator block-drained the stream's
buffered macrotask queue (a sync-over-async drain) instead of truly suspending
the consumer: it returned wrong results for live (socket/`setImmediate`-fed)
sources whose data had not buffered yet, and spun the event loop synchronously,
re-entering unrelated macrotasks.

Rewrite `ns_readable_iterator_next` to be genuinely async — suspend on a pending
promise resolved by persistent `data`/`end`/`error` listeners, backed by a
per-iterator queue, with no premature EOS and no block-drain. Route `toArray`
through `js_array_from_async` (the same pending-promise iterator `for await`
uses). Make the consume helpers truly async via a `.then` chain that awaits each
(possibly-async) callback, wired by `register_consume_arities`. Lazy
`map`/`filter`/`flatMap` keep their existing settle path.

* fix(runtime): address CodeRabbit review on async stream consumption

Live Node Readable async-iteration edge cases flagged on #5810:

- async_iterator: hold pending next() pulls in a FIFO queue instead of a
  single slot, and settle EVERY outstanding pull on data/end/error/return.
  A second next() while the queue was empty previously overwrote the first
  promise (left pending forever); return() dropped its pending slot without
  settling it.
- async_iterator: await promise-valued chunks on the pending data path via
  js_promise_resolve_with_promise adoption (js_promise_resolve does not
  assimilate thenables), matching the queued path so a promise chunk no
  longer leaks as { value: Promise, done:false }.
- iter_helpers: route every early settle of the consuming helpers
  (find/some/every short-circuit, callback throw, rejection, reduce-empty)
  through a shared cleanup that calls iterator.return() first, releasing the
  persistent stream listeners/queues.
- iter_helpers: register an abort listener for the consuming helpers and for
  toArray so a per-call/inherited signal that aborts mid-consumption rejects
  with AbortError and closes/cancels the iterator instead of leaving the
  promise pending.

fix(zlib): buffer decompressed output for a late-attaching stream consumer (#5809)

* fix(zlib): buffer decompressed output for a late-attaching stream consumer

perry-ext-zlib's handle-stream (gunzip/inflate/etc.) drains decompressed
output through a deferred event queue in js_ext_zlib_process_pending.
Previously a Data event was DROPPED when no 'data' listener was attached
at drain time, and an End event REMOVED the stream and its listeners.

A consumer that attaches on('data')/on('end') a tick LATE -- e.g. code
that awaits before reading the stream (the common
stream.pipe(zlib.createGunzip()) then read-after-await pattern used by
node-fetch/gaxios for gzipped HTTP bodies) -- then found the decompressed
output already discarded and the stream gone, so it never received data
and the read hung.

Mirror Node's paused-Readable buffering: buffer Data output
(output_buffer) when there is no consumer, mark End as deferred
(end_buffered) and keep the stream alive, and flush_buffered(handle)
re-queues the buffered Data then the deferred End once a 'data' listener
or pipe attaches. Consumers already present at drain time are unaffected
(direct delivery).

* fix(zlib): order late-flushed buffered output + cap abandoned ended streams

Addresses CodeRabbit review on #5809:

- flush_buffered now splices the buffered Data (then deferred End) ahead
  of any newer pending events for the same handle instead of pushing to
  the FIFO tail. Without this, a consumer that attaches after a mid-stream
  write would receive the older buffered bytes after the newer queued
  chunk (process_pending drains FIFO). New event_stream_handle +
  insert_buffered_ahead helpers serialize per stream.

- The deferred-End path now caps how many never-consumed end_buffered
  streams are retained (MAX_BUFFERED_ENDED_STREAMS) and evicts the oldest
  excess, so an abandoned handle (ends but never gets a 'data' listener or
  pipe) can't pin its buffered output for the process lifetime.

- Add focused unit tests for the insert-ahead ordering and the eviction
  cap.

* fix(zlib): bound buffered output bytes + fix reentrant-flush drain ordering

Addresses CodeRabbit's second review on #5809:

- Bound retained buffered BYTES, not just the ended-stream count. A
  never-consumed stream (or a decompression bomb fed incrementally with no
  listener) could grow `output_buffer` without limit. Add a per-stream cap
  (64 MiB) enforced before appending: a no-consumer stream that would exceed
  it is treated as abandoned and dropped (buffer freed) rather than grown;
  plus a global cap (256 MiB) tracked via a running `buffered_output_bytes`
  total that evicts the oldest no-consumer buffers first. A stream with a
  consumer never buffers, so this never penalizes a live consumer. All stream
  removals route through `drop_buffered_stream` so the total stays in sync.

- Handle reentrant flushes during an in-progress drain. `process_pending`
  took a snapshot of the queue (`mem::take` into a local vec); a callback
  firing mid-drain that attached a late consumer spliced the older buffered
  bytes onto the shared queue for the NEXT tick, behind a newer same-handle
  event still in the current snapshot -> newer delivered first. Drain one
  event at a time from the shared `VecDeque` instead, so a reentrant
  `flush_buffered` splice lands ahead of newer same-handle events still
  queued for this drain. Lock is held only to pop, never across a callback.

- Tests: reentrant-flush ordering, per-stream byte-cap drop, global byte-cap
  eviction, and byte accounting. Caps are parameters on the helper so tests
  exercise the policy without allocating hundreds of MiB.

* fix(zlib): tombstone evicted streams + bound drain loop per CodeRabbit feedback

- `drop_buffered_stream` now inserts into `evicted_streams` when it removes
  a stream, so late consumers attaching after a per-stream/global byte-cap
  eviction receive a terminal error event instead of hanging forever.
- `flush_buffered` checks the tombstone when the stream is absent: consumes
  it, queues `ZlibEvent::Error`, and notifies the main thread.
- `js_ext_zlib_process_pending` now snapshots `initial_count` at entry and
  drains at most that many events per call, preventing a write/flush loop
  from starving the event loop indefinitely.
- Tests: `drop_buffered_stream_leaves_tombstone`,

* feat(compile): support eval-mode worker_threads Workers (inline source)

`new Worker(source, { eval: true })` — where the first argument is JS SOURCE,
not a filename — failed codegen with "worker_threads Worker target was not
compiled". The WorkerNew lowering only handled file-path workers (resolving the
filename to a compiled module via dynamic_import_path_to_prefix); an inline
source string has no corresponding module, so nothing was registered.

way, so it could not be compiled at all.

code, materialize it to a content-addressed `.js` file under the system temp
dir and feed that path through the existing file-worker machinery — the worker
then compiles as a normal module. Detection: the resolved value contains a
newline. A worker filename (path or URL) is always single-line, so a newline is
an unambiguous "this is source, not a path" signal with no false positives.

`parallelMap([1,2,3,4], n => n*2)` compiles and runs → `[2,4,6,8]`. Adds a unit
test for the content-addressed materialization.

fix(codegen+hir+runtime): #5587 — Temporal subclass dispatch, cap writeback in inlined scope, Duration f64 precision (#5820)

* fix(codegen+hir+runtime): #5587 — Temporal subclass dispatch, cap writeback in inlined scope, Duration f64 precision

Three bugs fixed in the Temporal subclass test262 gap (#5587):

**Bug 1a — class capture stash must come AFTER constructor body**
`synthesize_class_captures` was inserting `this.__perry_cap_<id> = param`
immediately after the `super()` call. If the constructor body later ran
`++called`, the stash recorded the PRE-mutation value. Fixed by appending
the stash statements at the END of the constructor body (after all user
code but still after `super()`).

**Bug 1b — cap writeback uses wrong local ID after module-level inlining**
`emit_class_capture_writeback` extracted the outer-scope local ID from the
`__perry_cap_<id>` name suffix, then did `ctx.locals.get(&id)`. When the
enclosing function is inlined at module level, Perry alpha-renames every
local — `called` might be id=2 inside `check()` but id=9 in module-init.
The suffix lookup (`ctx.locals.get(&2)`) returns `None`, silently skipping
the writeback. Fix: accept `new_args: &[perry_hir::Expr]` and use the
position of the cap arg in the `New` node's args to find the current-scope
id via `LocalGet(id)`. Call sites updated: `new.rs` passes `args`;
`new_dynamic.rs` and `proxy_reflect.rs` pass `&[]` (suffix fallback).

**Bug 2 — Duration add/subtract/round diverges from ECMAScript f64 rounding**
ECMAScript spec coerces Duration fields through ℝ(𝔽(·)) after arithmetic,
so sub-float64 precision is lost. `temporal_rs` operates in i128 and stores
exact results (e.g. `MAX_SAFE + (MAX_SAFE - 1) = 18014398509481981`).
`toString()` then printed `PT18014398509.481981S` while the `microseconds`
getter showed `18014398509481980` (because `i128 as f64` rounded). Added
`f64_round_duration()` applied after `add`, `subtract`, and `round` so the
stored value equals the spec's ℝ(𝔽(·))-rounded result.

Regression tests: 6 tests in `crates/perry/tests/issue_5587_temporal_subclass.rs`
covering Duration subclasses, PlainDate subclasses, aliased heritage,
no-ctor subclasses, the module-level-inlining capture writeback case,

fix(runtime): #5588 — fix 6 built-ins/Object test262 failures (seal + proxy) (#5823)

* fix(runtime): #5588 — fix 6 built-ins/Object test262 failures (seal + proxy)

Two distinct bugs fixed:

1. proto_dispatch misfire on Function-family constructors during `new`
   (`seal-arrowfunction`, `seal-asyncarrowfunction`, `seal-asyncfunction`,
   `seal-generatorfunction`, `seal-asyncgeneratorfunction`):

   `Object.seal(new (Object.getPrototypeOf(fn).constructor)())` retrieves
   the %Function% or %GeneratorFunction% constructor and passes it to
   `js_new_function_construct`. Because these closures share the builtin
   noop thunk *and* have `builtin_closure_length` set (the gate for
   `try_dispatch_value_called_proto_method`), proto_dispatch fired on the
   newly-allocated receiver object — looked up "Function" / "GeneratorFunction"
   as an own method on it and threw "X is not a function".

   Fix: exclude these three constructor names from proto_dispatch. The noop
   thunk then returns `undefined`, `new` falls back to the allocated receiver
   object (per spec semantics), and `Object.seal(obj)` succeeds.

2. IsCompatiblePropertyDescriptor rejected generic descriptors on accessor props
   (`proxy-with-defineProperty-handler`):

   `Object.seal` on a Proxy drives `{configurable:false}` (a *generic*
   descriptor — no get/set and no value/writable) through the defineProperty
   trap. The invariant check compared `desc_is_accessor` (false) against
   `current.is_accessor` (true for an accessor target prop) and returned false,

hir: prealloc closure-capture boxes for lets nested in Try/If (array destructuring) (#5859)

compute_prealloc_for_hoisted_closures collects the function-entry
prealloc-box set via collect_top_level_let_ids_stmt, which only matched
top-level `Stmt::Let`. But array-destructuring bindings
(`let [a, b] = expr`) lower through the iterator protocol wrapped in a
`Try` (iterator close), so their leaf `let`s live inside the Try body /
its `if`s — never at the statement top level. A hoisted function
declaration capturing such a binding was therefore omitted from the
prealloc set: the closure captured the un-boxed, not-yet-assigned slot
and read `undefined` instead of the current value (e.g.

handler saw k === undefined and took the wrong branch).

— the constructs the destructuring lowering emits — when collecting
hoisted-let ids. Loops are intentionally not recursed: a per-iteration
`let` needs a fresh box per iteration, not a single function-entry
prealloc.

whenever B wasn't `Any`. But these can yield the LEFT operand (`A || B`
→ A when A is truthy; `A && B` → A when A is falsy), so when A and B
have different types, typing the result as B is unsound.

`let r = arr || 99` inferred `r: number`, so `lower_truthy` took the
numeric `fcmp one <v>, 0.0` path and read the NaN-boxed array pointer as
NaN → false. `!r`, `r ? _ : _`, and `Array.isArray(r)` (const-folded
from the static type) were all wrong, though the stored value was the
correct array (value ops `r[0]` / `r === arr` / `r.length` were fine).
Any truthy heap value (array/object/string) was affected.

Fix: trust the right operand's type only when both operands share a
type; otherwise return `Any` (dynamic ToBoolean / isArray path).
Preserves #3527 (right = Any → Any) and same-type precision
(`x || 0` → number, `maybeArr || []` → array).

transform(async): CPS async class methods, capturing-closure fns, and nested async closures (#5854)

* transform(async): CPS async class methods, capturing-closure fns, and nested async closures

The async_to_generator pre-pass ran the per-function CPS marking over
`module.functions` only, and bailed to the synchronous block-wait fallback for
several async-function shapes instead of transforming them to a suspending
state machine:

- async class methods (in `module.classes[*].{methods, static_methods,
  computed_members}`) were never marked at all;
- top-level async fns whose body contains a capturing closure hit a
  per-function bail;
- any module containing a capturing class hit a module-level bail;
- async closures nested inside a non-matching (non-async) closure were
  collected but never rewritten.

On the block-wait fallback an `await` runs the awaited work to completion
synchronously from the caller, so such functions cannot interleave with other
tasks; an `await` on a promise resolved only by a later callback/microtask

owned by the wrapper, so the runner does not settle it); the handler slots

* fix(runtime): promise combinator/finally reactions must not clobber the inline handler slot

promise_resolve_for_combinator, stream adapters) and js_promise_finally's

* fix(runtime): #4873 — Object.setPrototypeOf spurious TypeError on even-length prototype chains

PR #5857's required cargo-test check was failing (deterministically, also on
main's nightly runs for 5+ days) on
bare_new_message_channel_delegates_to_worker_threads, unrelated to the
Intl.NumberFormat changes in this PR. Root-caused and fixed here so the PR
can go green rather than merging past a real regression.

js_object_set_prototype_of's Floyd's tortoise-and-hare cycle-detection walk
guarded the *second* hare hop within an iteration against landing on null,
but not the *first* hop when `hare` had already reached null on a previous
iteration (hare moves 2 steps per tortoise's 1, so it reaches null first on
even-length chains). Advancing a null hare called
js_object_get_prototype_of(null), which throws "Cannot convert undefined or
null to object" — a spurious TypeError on a perfectly valid
Object.setPrototypeOf/__proto__ write whenever the target's prototype chain
had an even hop count to null.

`new MessageChannel()` delegating through the worker_threads factory builds
exactly such a chain (2 hops), reproducing it deterministically. Fixed by
checking `hare == null` before every advance, not just the inner one.
Verified against 0/1/2/3-hop prototype chains and confirmed cycle detection
still throws correctly; full perry-runtime suite (1108 tests) and both
issue_4873_message_channel_global_new.rs tests pass.

fix(transform): switch inside async/generator state machines miscompiled (#5885)

* fix(transform): #5868 — switch inside async/generator state machines miscompiled

Two defects, one shared fix:

1. yield/await inside a case body was silently lowered to 0: the
   linearizer had no Stmt::Switch arm, so the switch fell to the
   catch-all, was emitted unsplit inside one state, and codegen's
   fallback lowered the residual Expr::Yield to 0.0. async f(x){
   switch(x){ case 1: return await g() } } resolved to 0 without
   suspending; a generator yield inside a case vanished.

2. a loop-level continue inside a yield-free switch in a CPS'd loop
   survived as a raw Stmt::Continue the dispatch loop ignored, so the
   iteration's remainder ran anyway.

New desugar_switch_to_ifs (break_continue.rs): discriminant temp +

storing it the same way as the array case.

are inherited from Object.prototype, not own. Partial fix for

two separate implementations, both limited to real Arrays and arguments
objects: the generic thunk path silently returned an empty list for anything
else, and the direct-dispatch path (hit by a literal `fn.apply(...)` call

bug. Both now fall back to a generic Get("length") + indexed-Get walk

fix(link): #5892 — keep perry_ffi test shims out of production ext archives (#5911)

perry-ext-http and perry-ext-http-server compiled their test_async_shims
modules (synchronous perry_ffi_* stand-ins for unit-test linking) into the
production staticlib archives: the mod declaration was missing the
#[cfg(test)] gate that perry-ext-net already has. The shims' own comment
says 'Test-only; never shipped.' — but they shipped.

Those shims define the same #[no_mangle] C symbols as perry-stdlib's real
perry-ffi async bridge, with catastrophically different semantics:
perry_ffi_spawn_blocking_with_reactor/spawn_blocking run the closure
inline (no runtime context, no pump/wait-driver registration) and
perry_ffi_spawn_async is a no-op that silently drops the task. Whenever
the linker resolves these from an ext archive instead of libperry_stdlib.a
(single-pass archive scanning: the reference and the shim live in the same
archive), the #5831 current-thread runtime is never driven: the wait-driver
never registers, js_wait_for_event falls back to the 1 s condvar park, and
any program with in-process server+client I/O parks forever. This is the
cargo-test hang in issue_4903_listen_callback_deferred (#5892) that has
blocked nightlies and release tags since #5831 merged; the auto-opt path
was immune because strip-dedup (#5000/#5685) localizes duplicate wrapper
globals.

Gate both modules with #[cfg(test)], matching perry-ext-net. Validation on
the hang-lab branch (debug/5892-hang-lab): ungated cargo-test loop hung on
iteration 1 in three consecutive runs; with the gate, single-run repro +
6/6 cargo-test iterations clean (run 28669296187).

fix(link): #5920 — dedup wrapper-bundled perry-runtime in wrappers-first links (#5921)

* fix(link): #5920 — dedup wrapper-bundled perry-runtime in wrappers-first links

Well-known wrapper staticlibs (perry-ext-http, …) bundle a full copy of the
perry_runtime codegen unit. In the wrappers-BEFORE-stdlib link shapes
(prefer_well_known_before_stdlib: the out-of-tree prebuilt path and the
auto-optimize archives-fresh fast path), that copy became the
first-definition winner for every extern runtime symbol the user object
references — while perry-stdlib's own code kept using ITS bundled runtime
copy through LTO-promoted `.llvm.` internal names. The process then ran two
disjoint copies of the runtime's mutable globals (event-pump wait-driver
slots, NOTIFIED, microtask queue, exception state): spawn() registered the
wait-driver in stdlib's copy, js_wait_for_event read the wrapper's
never-written copy, parked on the condvar fallback, and every spawned task
starved. First compile of a program worked (full auto-optimize rebuild links
wrappers after stdlib); every recompile with warm archives hung. Same family
as #5892/#5911 (cargo-test shim flavor) — this is the perry-compile flavor,
still live with #5911's gate in place.

Fix: in the wrappers-first shape, drop a wrapper's bundled perry_runtime-*
member before the wrapper-globals localization pass, under the evidence-based
rule (v0.5.331 standard): only when the stdlib archive bundles the same
codegen unit (stdlib packaging renames members to
`perry_stdlib-<h>.<original>.rcgu.o` — matched by name containment; same
crate+cgu hash ⇒ same rlib input), and no sibling member references a symbol
only the doomed member defines (a sibling depending on one of the copy's
LTO-promoted internals keeps it — fail-safe). The standalone runtime archive
linked after stdlib keeps filling DCE gaps as before. Non-fatal throughout:
any ar/nm failure falls back to the untouched archive.

Repro (issue #5920, now a test): an in-process node:http server + a
fire-and-forget fetch().then() with an interval watchdog — compile the same
source twice, run both binaries. Pre-fix the second binary ticked to the
watchdog FAIL with the fetch never resolving; post-fix both pass and the
second link logs `dropped 1 bundled perry-runtime member(s)` with ld64
duplicate-symbol warnings down ~4x.

Fixes #5920.

fix(transform): #5925 — keep comma-sequence operands ahead of hoisted awaits (#5926)

The plain-async pre-pass hoists every nested await into a
`let __await_N = await <operand>;` above the containing statement. For a
comma sequence that moved the awaited operand's evaluation above the
sequence's earlier operands: `this.l = new L, this.p = await this.l.start()`
evaluated `this.l.start()` while `this.l` still held its pre-assignment
value (null) — a TypeError under perry where node prints the result.
Minifiers comma-fold consecutive statements, so any
`const x = new X(); const y = await x.m();` pair in bundled async code hits
this. Conditional branches (#342) and logical RHS (#5434) already have
dedicated lifts for exactly this class of unsound hoist; Sequence had none.

Fix: `lift_sequence_with_await` — when a sequence contains an await, lift
the non-final operands to statements (each recursively hoisted, preserving
evaluation order) and continue with the final operand as the expression
value. Wired into both `hoist_awaits_in_expr_full` (nested sequences) and
`hoist_awaits_avoiding_top_level` (statement-position sequences, re-processed
so a final-operand await stays directly handled). The generator yield hoist
(generator/hoist_yields.rs) has the same latent gap for yield-in-sequence;
left as a follow-up per #5925.

Fixes #5925.

fix(hir): #5912 — new URL()/TextEncoder()/etc. ignore lexical shadowing (#5913)

* fix(hir): #5912 — new URL()/TextEncoder()/etc. ignore lexical shadowing

`new URL(...)` (and URLSearchParams/URLPattern/TextEncoder/TextDecoder)
were dispatched by bare identifier name with no check for whether the
name actually resolves to the global constructor or is shadowed by a
local function/class — unlike sibling well-known constructors
(Function, Object) in the same match, which already guard on
lookup_local/lookup_func/lookup_class.

Real packages ship their own tolerant polyfills under these names
(found via @mixmark-io/domino's lib/URL.js, which defines
`function URL(url) { ... }` and calls `new URL()` with zero args
against its own constructor) and hit perry's native WHATWG URL
constructor instead, which requires at least one argument.

The same unguarded name match also existed in a second, independent
spot: `static_receiver_class` (used to decide whether `.toString()` /
`.toJSON()` / `JSON.stringify()` on a receiver should route through
the native Date/URL fast paths) classified any `new URL(...)` — or a
local typed as `URL` — as the native type by name alone, so even after
fixing the construction site, printing/serializing a shadowed
instance still silently substituted native URL output.

Fixes both sites by checking `lookup_local`/`lookup_func`/
`lookup_class` before applying the native lowering, matching the
existing shadowing-guard pattern used elsewhere in expr_new.rs.

* fix(hir): #5912 CodeRabbit follow-up — globalThis escape hatch, alias, imported bindings

Three issues from CodeRabbit's review of the initial fix:

1. Real regression: the static_receiver_class shadowing guard collapsed
   `new globalThis.URL(...)` and bare `new URL(...)` into the same
   class_name capture, so a locally-shadowed URL made even the explicit
   globalThis-qualified form misclassify as "Object" and lose the
   native fast path. Track which callee shape matched and only apply
   the shadow check to the bare-identifier form.

2. Coverage gap: `const MyURL = URL; new MyURL()` bypassed the
   shadowing guard entirely via the resolve_class_alias branch, which
   runs before the later callee_local_at_entry/lookup_func/lookup_class
   checks. Added the same shadowing check there, against the
   ALIAS-RESOLVED name (aliases are name-keyed, not scope-aware).

3. Coverage gap: an imported binding shadowing one of these names
   (`import { URL } from "./polyfill"`) wasn't covered by the
   lookup_local/lookup_func/lookup_class triplet. Added
   lookup_imported_func alongside it in expr_new.rs (module-level
   registry, safe to query fresh — unlike lookup_local, this one isn't
   subject to the scope-stack-disturbance issue callee_local_at_entry
   exists to avoid, so no special snapshotting needed).

static_receiver.rs's own guard now calls the existing
`shadows_unqualified_global` helper (already covers all four cases)
instead of reimplementing three of them by hand.

Extended the regression test with both the globalThis-escape-hatch and
alias cases; both match node byte-for-byte.

fix(compile): #5918 — import_function_prefixes collides on exported name across unrelated imports (#5919)

import_function_prefixes (imported name -> source module prefix,
consumed by ExternFuncRef codegen to form perry_fn_<prefix>__<name>)
was populated by inserting BOTH the exported/origin name and the local
alias for every renamed Named import. Per the #35/#321 precedent in
the same function, a renamed import's ExternFuncRef in the HIR always
carries the LOCAL name (unique per import site) -- the exported_name
insert only ever mattered in the no-rename case (local == exported).

Running it unconditionally meant: when two DIFFERENT import statements
in the same file rename to different locals from modules whose ORIGIN
export names happen to collide (common with short, minifier-style
names -- "a"/"b"/"c" -- which is exactly what esbuild's chunk-splitting
produces), the second insert silently overwrote the first's entry.
The overwritten entry could be a completely unrelated LOCAL alias from
an earlier import, repointing that alias's ExternFuncRef at the wrong
module entirely.

Confirmed via a real-world source compile of sst/opencode
(compilePackages: ["*"]): remeda's real dist/chunk-*.js build output
has this exact shape, and nearly every remeda function transitively
imports the four affected chunks, so this single bug blocked the
entire package.

Fix: only insert under exported_name in the local_name == exported_name
case; the aliased case inserts under local_name only, keeping every
key in the map unique per file (local identifiers can't collide with
each other within one file; export names from different origin
modules can and do).

Added a 4-file regression test reproducing the exact collision shape,
lifted from remeda's real build output. Verified test_gap_renamed_
class_export_namespace.ts, test_issue_836_zod_class_reexports.ts, and
test_issue_678_reexport_default.ts (the existing tests covering this
same code path) are unaffected.

fix(ext-http): #5892 — keep in-flight client requests visible to the exit gate (#5929)

The main reqwest dispatch path (dispatch_request) and the Expect:
100-continue path never created a ClientInflightGuard — only the
agent-socket path did. spawn_blocking_with_reactor's EXT_BLOCKING gate
drops the moment the outer closure returns (it only spawns the detached
task), so between that and the task's first push_event the whole
exchange was invisible to js_stdlib_has_active_handles. An in-process
server+client program whose server just close()d could observe an
all-zero gate while the response sat unread in the socket and clean-exit
before 'response' fired — the write_end_callbacks CI failure ('status
200' missing, exit 0) that kept full cargo-test red after the #5892
hang fixes landed.

dispatch_request_over_socket), covering dispatch until the response
fully streams or errors; js_http_has_pending covers the drain after.

Regression test: with the inline test shims and an entered (but not yet
driven) current-thread runtime, dispatch_request returns with the task
spawned but never polled — the guard must already be up, the exit-gate
union (inflight || pending events) must stay nonzero until ResponseEnd
is queued, and the guard must release once the response streams.

fix(transform): await/yield in loop condition/update runs per iteration (#5934)

* fix(transform): #5933 — await/yield in loop condition/update runs per iteration

The async hoist's single pre-loop hoist ('safe-but-incomplete
approximation' per its own comment) evaluated a loop condition's await
ONCE: async drain loops (while ((v = await q.next()) !== undefined))
never re-awaited — truthy first value spun forever on stale state, falsy
never entered. do-while additionally evaluated the condition before the
first body run. Generators had the sibling defect at the linearize
layer: while (yield ...) cloned the condition, embedded yield included,
into the cond state where codegen lowers residual yields to 0.0.

Restructure instead of hoisting out, preserving break/continue:
- while (C) -> while(true){ let t = C; if (!t) break; body } (continue
  re-enters at the condition evaluation, per spec);
- do B while (C) -> first-iteration flag + while (first || C) (body
  precedes first condition eval; continue falls through to the eval);
- for (init; C; U) keeps the For: awaited C -> body-top check with the
  condition slot emptied; awaited U -> body end with every loop-level
  continue prefixed by it (new shared prefix_loop_continues, same
  descent scoping as the #5868 helpers).
Linearize gains the three guarded yield-twin arms for direct
generators, normalizing synthesized condition evals through
hoist_yields_in_stmts.

e2e: crates/perry/tests/issue_5933_loop_condition_await.rs (7 scenarios
byte-for-byte vs node --experimental-strip-types).

* review(coderabbit): bail the awaited-update move when a continue sits inside try/finally

A continue inside try{..}finally{..} is an abrupt completion: the
finally must run BEFORE the loop update, and a finally that overrides
the continue (return/throw) means the update must not run at all —
prefix_loop_continues would insert the update ahead of the finally.
New stmts_have_continue_inside_try_finally detector; both the async
hoist and the linearize For arms keep the PREVIOUS lowering for that
shape (never worse than before), including the linearize arm GUARD so
a fully-bailed For cannot re-match its own desugar (infinite
recursion). continue inside the finally block itself, or under a try
without finally, still gets the prefix — new e2e covers the
try-without-finally path.

fix(compile,codegen): #5922/#5924/#5927 — namespace-reexport member resolution collisions (#5923)

* fix(compile,codegen): #5922 — namespace-reexport member prefix collision

`import { Context } from "effect"` (named import of a value the source
module re-exports as a namespace via `export * as Context from
"./Context.js"`) registered every member of the target namespace into the
flat `import_function_prefixes` map, keyed only by the member's bare name.
When two such namespace-reexport targets imported into the same file
export a member with the same bare name (e.g. `Context.a` and `Option.a`,
both reached through effect's barrel), the second registration silently
overwrote the first.

perry already has the fix for this exact class of collision (#680):
`namespace_member_prefixes`, keyed by `(namespace_local, member_name)`.
The plain `import * as X` branch already populates it; the
named-import-of-namespace-reexport branch did not. Fixed by registering
there too, and by teaching `expr/static_method.rs`'s
`namespace_imports.contains(class_name)` branch (the actual codegen
consumer for uppercase-receiver forms like `Context.a()`) to consult
`namespace_member_prefixes` before falling back to the flat map — mirroring
the pattern `namespace_call.rs` and `property_get.rs` already use for
lowercase-receiver call/read forms.

Found via a real-world source compile of `sst/opencode`, whose
`provider.ts` does `import { Effect, Layer, Context, Schema, Types } from
"effect"` — the last remaining pair of undefined symbols after #5918/#5919.

* fix(compile,codegen): #5924 — namespace-reexport origin-name collision

Follow-up to #5922/#5923: fixing `import_function_prefixes` alone wasn't
enough for a real-world `sst/opencode` compile. `import_function_origin_names`
(issue #678's symbol-suffix-override map for re-export renames) has the
same flat, bare-name-keyed structure and independently broke the same
real code.

`import { Effect, Layer, Context, Schema, Types } from "effect"` processes
five namespace-reexport targets into one file's shared maps. `Effect`
re-exports something named `Service` under a rename, so its turn inserts
`import_function_origin_names["Service"] = "<effect's internal origin
name>"`. `Context` directly exports its own `Service` (no rename needed),
so its turn inserts nothing — the earlier (wrong) entry survives. Codegen
then resolves `Context.Service(...)` (a real call in opencode's
`provider.ts`: `class Service extends Context.Service<...>()(...)`) via
the contaminated flat entry, producing an undefined
`perry_fn_..._Context_ts__<wrong-suffix>` symbol at link time.

Fixed by adding `namespace_member_origin_names`, a per-namespace-scoped
companion map mirroring #680's `namespace_member_prefixes` — but
unconditionally populated for every namespace member (not just renamed
ones), since a sparse map would still fall through to the contaminated
flat map for unrenamed members. Consulted by every codegen site that
builds a `perry_fn_<src>__<suffix>` symbol for a namespace-member access
(`expr/static_method.rs`, `lower_call/namespace_call.rs`,
`expr/property_get.rs`) via a new `import_origin_suffix_ns` helper.

* fix(compile): #5927 — plain-import-vs-namespace-member flat map collision

Third companion to #5918/#5922/#5924. A PLAIN named import's bare name and
a NAMESPACE MEMBER's bare name share the same flat
`import_function_prefixes`/`import_function_origin_names` maps. A plain
import has no other resolution path (a bare call has no namespace to
scope against), so it must always win — but namespace processing's
unconditional `.insert()` could silently overwrite it depending on
import-statement order.

Found via a real-world `sst/opencode` compile: `provider.ts` does
`import { omit } from "remeda"` (plain) and `import { Context } from
"effect"` (namespace-reexport), and effect's real `Context.ts` also
exports a member literally named `omit`. `Context` is imported after
`omit` in source order, so Context's registration silently overwrote
remeda's — the bare `omit(...)` call then resolved against Context.ts's
prefix combined with remeda's origin-name rename, producing an undefined
symbol request.

Fixed by using `.entry().or_insert()` instead of `.insert()` for BOTH
namespace-processing branches' flat-map writes (plain `import * as X`
and the named-import-of-namespace-reexport branch). Plain imports keep
their unconditional `.insert()`, so they always win regardless of
processing order: if a namespace claims an empty slot first, the plain
import's later unconditional insert still overwrites it; if the plain
import claims it first, the namespace's `or_insert` sees the slot taken
and skips. Namespace-member resolution is unaffected since the three
real consumers (`expr/static_method.rs`, `lower_call/namespace_call.rs`,
`expr/property_get.rs`) already prefer the namespace-scoped maps from
#5922/#5924 and never need the flat-map fallback for genuine namespace
members.

Verified both import orderings against Node with new regression
fixtures.

* style: rustfmt property_get.rs import list

CI's `cargo fmt --all -- --check` flagged the import_origin_suffix_ns
addition from the #5922/#5924 fix — rustfmt wraps differently than the
manual edit did.

* fix(link): #5928 — fixed-point dedup for shared deps across well-known libs

Companion to #5920/#5921. `strip_bundled_runtime_from_well_known_lib` only
targets `perry_runtime-*` codegen-unit members. Programs linking multiple
well-known libraries that each independently bundle a full "shared tokio"
HTTP-client stack (e.g. both `http` and `fastify` need tokio/hyper_util/h2/
rustls/reqwest/ring) still collide on every OTHER shared transitive
dependency those libraries have in common with `libperry_stdlib.a` — even
`std`/`core`/`alloc` themselves. macOS's current linker has no
`-multiply_defined suppress` / `-ld_classic` escape hatch anymore (verified
obsolete on current toolchains via direct testing), so these surface as
hard `ld: duplicate symbol` failures.

Adds `strip_bundled_shared_deps_from_well_known_lib`, applying the same two
safety rules as the runtime-specific function (stdlib bundles the identical
codegen unit; no other kept member depends on a symbol only the
duplicate-candidate provides) to every member, not just `perry_runtime-`
ones. A naive one-shot widening is NOT safe — candidates can depend on each
other (e.g. hyper_util's object referencing a symbol only tokio's object
defines, both bundled in the same well-known lib and both initially
flagged removable) — so this is a fixed-point iteration: each round
recomputes undefined-symbol references from the shrinking kept-set and
protects any still-needed candidate, repeating until stable.

Verified against `issue_5920_wrapper_bundled_runtime_async_starvation`
(passes) and a real-world `sst/opencode` compile: fully eliminates
duplicate symbols for simpler well-known libs (ioredis/net/ws went from
hundreds of duplicates to zero); substantially reduces them for the
largest, most interconnected pair (http+fastify, both needing the full
HTTP-client stack) though Rule 2 conservatively protects more members as
a single archive's internal dependency graph grows, so this specific
combination is improved but not fully zero yet.

Note: `strip_bundled_runtime_from_well_known_lib`/this function require
`llvm-objcopy`/`llvm-nm`/`llvm-ar` (via `PERRY_LLVM_OBJCOPY`/`PERRY_LLVM_NM`/
`PERRY_LLVM_AR` env vars or `PATH`) to actually run — without them they
silently no-op (each wrapped in `.unwrap_or_else` with a "(non-fatal)" log
line), producing a much later, confusing "N duplicate symbols" `ld`
failure with no indication dedup was skipped. This cost significant
debugging time this session before being traced to a missing local LLVM
toolchain install — worth a louder diagnostic in a follow-up.

fix(runtime): #5437 — async-step result-promise identity + reaction preservation restore Next.js SSR statics (0/8→5/8) (#5932)

The #5854 CPS transform made the whole Next.js render chain suspend as
async-step state machines. At that scale three promise-machinery bugs
surfaced and deadlocked even the static routes (0/8). Fixing them restores
the 5 build-prerendered + API routes to byte-identical vs node (0/8 → 5/8).
The 3 request-time dynamic RSC renders remain blocked on a separate
structural issue (React's server render not yielding the shell under the
full transform — a transform-side follow-up, not addressed here).

- async-step result-promise orphan (async_step.rs): a machine entered via
  js_async_first_call nulls its trap_next (#691); the chain's pending-promise
  arm then registered resume thunks whose captured trap_next was null, so
  js_async_step_done's reuse gate failed and minted a FRESH result promise,
  orphaning the one the caller awaits -> the awaiter hangs. New
  then_backpatch_result allocates the result explicitly, back-patches the
  thunks' captured trap_next (capture slot 1) to it, and attaches handlers
  WITHOUT a chained next (a chained next would self-resolve a mid-chain
  await -> "Chaining cycle detected"). Applied at all 3 chain thunk-path sites.

- resolve-with-promise reaction clobber (then.rs): js_promise_resolve_with_promise's
  slow path OVERWROTE inner's inline on_fulfilled/on_rejected to install its
  forwarders — clobbering a reaction already registered there (e.g. an
  async-step awaiter's resume thunk from an earlier `await inner`), so when
  inner settled only the forwarder fired and the awaiter hung. Register the
  forwarders as an OVERFLOW reaction instead; both fire when inner settles.

- microtask cycle guard (microtasks.rs): propagate_callback_result rejected
  `result == next` as a chaining cycle unconditionally. In the async-step
  steady state js_async_step_done already resolved that result before the
  thunk returned it, so `next` is already settled and re-resolving it with
  itself is a harmless no-op, not a cycle. Only reject when `next` is Pending.

- req.read Buffer default (perry-ext-http-server/request.rs): js_node_http_im_read
  always returned a string; Node's req.read() returns a Buffer by default
  (string only after setEncoding). Next.js App Router's Readable.toWeb / the
  Web Request body reader require Buffer/Uint8Array chunks — a string chunk was
  dropped, so request.json() saw {}. Return a Buffer by default, string when an
  encoding was set (mirrors emit_data_to_listeners).

Validated: boots + 5/8 byte-identical vs node v26 (/, /about, /counter,
/api/hello GET+POST). Runtime-only; independent of the CPS transform.

fix(runtime): #5893 — class setter .length ignores default params (#5939)

A setter with a defaulted formal param (`set m(x = 42)`) must report
`.length === 0` (defaults do not count toward a function's length), but
`class_accessor_function_value` hardcoded the reflected setter value's
length to 1, ignoring defaults. Reading
`Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(C.prototype, 'm').set.length` therefore
returned 1 instead of 0.

Fix: codegen now registers each setter's default-aware spec length
(`spec_function_length`) against its accessor func_ptr via
`js_register_closure_length`, and `class_accessor_function_value`
consults `lookup_closure_length` for the raw setter pointer, falling back
to the fixed 1/0 when no registration exists (native / cross-module
accessors). A plain `set m(x)` still reports 1; getters stay at 0.

Fixes test262 language/{statements,expressions}/class/setter-length-dflt.

fix(runtime): #5893 — reading a private method as a value then calling it (#5944)

Reading a private method off an instance (`const f = this.#m`) must yield
the OWNER class's method function; calling it (`f.call(o)`) runs that body
with the supplied `this` and performs no brand check (the brand check
already happened at the read site). Perry's bound-method dispatch instead
re-resolved `#m` on the CALL-TIME receiver's own class — a plain object has
no `#m`, so `f.call({...})` threw "#m is not a function".

Fix: in `dispatch_bound_method`, when the bound method name is `#`-prefixed
and the captured receiver is the owner class's prototype-ref (the canonical
private-method-value marker), resolve the method in the OWNER's vtable chain
and invoke it directly with the call-time `this` (IMPLICIT_THIS), bypassing
the receiver-class by-name lookup. Public-method dispatch is untouched (the
new path is gated on the `#` prefix).

Fixes test262 language/{statements,expressions}/class/elements/private-method-get-and-call.

fix(runtime): #5909 — JSON.stringify(toJSON-returns-cycle) throws instead of SIGSEGV (#5954)

`SerializeJSONObject`'s circular-reference detection only pushes the object
pointer onto `STRINGIFY_STACK` once `depth > MAX_FAST_DEPTH` (128) — a
performance gate that assumes a shallow structure cannot be cyclic. But the
two object toJSON-result branches serialized the substituted value via the
depth-0 `stringify_value` entry, resetting depth to 0 on every re-entry. A
`toJSON` that returns a structure re-entering an object still open in the walk
(`obj.toJSON = () => circular; circular.prop = obj`) therefore recursed
forever without the depth ever reaching 128, overflowing the native stack
(SIGSEGV, no output) instead of throwing the spec TypeError.

Fix: thread the current depth into both object toJSON-result walks
(`stringify_value_depth(result, …, depth + 1)`), matching the shape-template
path that already did this (stringify.rs:1573). Depth now accumulates across
the toJSON recursion, so the `depth > MAX_FAST_DEPTH` push engages, the
already-open pointer is found on the stack, and `Converting circular structure
to JSON` throws. The compact-array path already pushes unconditionally, so
value-tojson-array-circular was unaffected.

test262 built-ins/JSON: value-tojson-object-circular now passes; JSON slice
15 → 14 fail, zero regressions. Verified nested objects / arrays, class
`toJSON`, Date `toJSON`, and plain circular detection still behave.

fix(runtime,codegen,hir): #5898 — mutating array methods throw on frozen/non-writable length (#5953)

Three spec-conformance gaps in `Array.prototype` mutators that perform
`Set(O,"length",…,true)` (ECMA-262 §23.1.3.*) and so must throw a TypeError
when that set fails:

1. `arr.push()` with no items was lowered to a bare `length` read in the HIR
   local-array fast path, eliding the mandatory `Set(O,"length",…)` step. A
   frozen array or one whose `length` is non-writable therefore silently
   no-op'd instead of throwing. Route the zero-arg case through the native push
   dispatch (`js_array_push_guard`) so the guard fires.
   (push/set-length-zero-array-is-frozen, ...-length-is-non-writable)

2. The codegen inline dense-push fast path (`apush.inbounds`) wrote the element
   and bumped length directly, checking only the GcHeader FORWARDED bit — it
   skipped the integrity flags. An empty array frozen via `Object.freeze([])`
   (capacity present, in-bounds store) was mutated without throwing. Load the
   GcHeader `_reserved` u16 and bail to `js_array_push_f64` (which throws /
   applies descriptors) when FROZEN|SEALED|NO_EXTEND|ARRAY_DESCRIPTORS is set.

3. The generic array-like `Set(O,"length",…)` helper (`al_set_length`, used by
   the borrowed-receiver mutators pop/shift/push/unshift/splice/…) called the
   by-name setter, which silently no-ops for a frozen array / non-writable
   `length` / callable receiver. Detect that failure and throw, matching
   Throw=true. (shift/throws-when-this-value-length-is-writable-false — the
   function-receiver sub-case.)

regressions across pop/shift/push/unshift/splice/sort/concat/slice/reverse.

fix(runtime): #5961 — URLSearchParams methods reachable through dynamic access (#5964)

The native URLSearchParams is an ordinary object (class_id == 0,
`_entries`/`_owner` slots — the shape try_read_as_search_params guards on)
whose method surface existed only via static type-directed lowering
(perry-codegen url_main.rs). The moment the receiver's static type was lost
(`any`, heterogeneous containers, bundled/minified code where inference
can't track the value) the generic dynamic paths found nothing:
`typeof sp.append` read `undefined` and `sp.append(...)` threw

builder does eleven `url.searchParams.append(...)` calls — works extracted,

  `url_search_params_method_value` (bound-closure thunks for property
  reads, receiver carried in a GC-traced nanboxed capture). `get` and
  `toString` rebuild their boxed results here — the raw natives return
  `*mut StringHeader` for the static path. `has` boxes a real boolean.
- object/native_call_method.rs: dispatch arm for the covered names before
  the generic field-scan (fused `inst.m(...)` calls resolve here, not via

fix(runtime): #5894 — exact BigInt-vs-large-Number comparison (Number.MAX_VALUE) (#5974)

Comparing a BigInt with a Number whose magnitude reaches 2^1023
(e.g. 1n >= Number.MAX_VALUE) round-tripped the Number through
js_bigint_from_f64, which overflows the fixed 1024-bit two's-complement
BigInt: MAX_VALUE's top magnitude bit lands on the sign bit and reads
back as negative, so 1n >= Number.MAX_VALUE wrongly returned true.

bound the comparison is decided by the sign of y alone. Add that
short-circuit in bigint_cmp_f64 before the (lossy) f64→BigInt conversion.

remaining bigint-and-number-extremes assertions use BigInt literals near
2^1024 that exceed the fixed 1024-bit BigInt width (a separate
architectural limit). No regressions (built-ins/BigInt unchanged).

fix(gc): compiled programs never GC'd on nursery pressure (P0) + copied-minor weak-slot semantics (#5977)

* fix(gc): copied-minor must not evacuate through weak target slots; repair + tombstone on the fast path

The copied-minor scan visited weak target slots (WeakRef referent,
WeakMap/WeakSet entry key, FinalizationRegistry record target) with the
full-strength visitor — evacuating THROUGH them and thereby strengthening
the weak edge — and the fast path never ran the after-mark tombstone pass
at all (it bypasses cycle.rs's WeakProcessing subphase). Net effect: weak
entries never tombstoned and FinalizationRegistry never fired while
copied-minor was the operative cycle.

The scan now records weak slots without evacuating (mirroring the
mark/barrier/heap-snapshot paths' is_weak_target_trace_slot skip), repairs
already-forwarded targets in place, and re-repairs all recorded slots
after the final drain (a target moved via a strong edge AFTER its weak
slot was scanned still needs the forwarding address). The fast path then
runs process_weak_targets_after_mark before the from-space flip, gated on
a new weak-holder latch so programs that never allocate a weak container
skip the full arena walk. The eligibility checker skips weak slots too —
weak-only reachability imposes no copy constraint.

Three unit tests, negative-controlled: the dead-target tombstone test
fails on the unfixed collector and passes with the fix; the live-target
repair tests guard the two-phase rewrite.

* fix(gc): P0 — nursery allocation trigger never fired in compiled programs; run the direct synchronous minor when the budgeted stepper is scanner-blocked

Since the budgeted-GC slicing (897f50c8b, 2026-05-30), gc_check_trigger
routed ArenaBytes/MallocCount pressure exclusively through the budgeted
mutator-assist stepper — and registered_root_scanners_block_budgeted_gc
holds for the LIFE of every compiled program (codegen registers
synchronous-only root scanners at startup), so the stepper could never
start a cycle and the assist step no-op'd forever. A compiled program
churning small allocations ran ZERO collection cycles: 4M small objects
grew RSS to 1.9 GB, and a weak-only-reachable WeakRef target was never
collected. #5476 had patched the identical hole for the OldReclaim
trigger only.

When a nursery-churn trigger is due and the budgeted machinery is
structurally unavailable, gc_check_trigger now runs the direct
synchronous minor (gc_collect_minor_with_trigger, made pub(super)) under
ManualGcScanGuard::force_full_scan — mirroring the OldReclaim arm: the
conservative native scan retains values mid-construction at the
allocation point, which also makes copied-minor ineligible for that
cycle, so the non-moving minor runs (no relocation hazards). The
post-cycle policy re-baselines GC_NEXT_TRIGGER_BYTES as usual.

Probe (4M small allocations): before — 0 cycles, 1.93 GB RSS,
deref still-alive; after — 14 cycles, 539 MB RSS, deref cleared.
Adds the compiled-binary e2e pinning the trigger contract; the full GC
unit suite (386 tests) is green.

* fix(gc): array higher-order methods re-derive element pointers through rooted handles

Every callback-looping array method (forEach/map/map_discard/filter/find/
findIndex/findLast/findLastIndex/some/every/flatMap/reduce/reduceRight)

safepoint-driven copying cycle) does not.

sub-array) is held in a RuntimeHandleScope root, and the header + element
base are re-derived per access. Per-iteration cost is a TLS handle read +
an offset add, dwarfed by callback dispatch.

allocation pressure; output matches node --expose-gc byte-for-byte.

fix(intl): ToObject primitive options in SupportedLocalesOf (#5995)

ECMA-402 SupportedLocales step 1.a is `? ToObject(options)`. When options is
a non-object primitive (Boolean/Number/String/Symbol/BigInt), ToObject boxes
it into a wrapper whose prototype chain reaches Object.prototype, so reading
`localeMatcher` fires an Object.prototype getter for that key exactly once.

Perry read option keys directly off the raw value, so a primitive options
argument yielded every-key-absent and never consulted the prototype chain —
the getter was never called (`called === 0`).

Box a non-object primitive into a fresh empty object before the localeMatcher
read (null is still rejected first). An empty object carries no own option
keys, so the read resolves through the prototype chain, matching the boxed
wrapper the spec observes.

Intl.ListFormat, and Intl.RelativeTimeFormat (3 cases).

fix(runtime): js_dynamic_mod preserves sign of zero (fmod semantics) (#5999)

js_dynamic_mod computed the remainder with the closed form
a - (a / b).trunc() * b. That drops the sign of a zero result:
-1 % -1 evaluates to -1.0 - (1.0 * -1.0) == +0.0, but JS % is C fmod,
whose result takes the sign of the dividend, so -1 % -1 is -0. The same
closed form also returned NaN for x % Infinity (should be x).

This surfaced as a regression once a compound assignment on a
separately-declared int-valued local (var x; x = -1; x %= -1) started
routing through js_dynamic_mod:

  language/expressions/compound-assignment/mod-whitespace.js

which asserts x %= -1 is -0.

Rust's f64 % f64 is fmod, so replace the closed form with a % b. It
matches the spec on the sign of zero, on x % Infinity == x, and on
Infinity % y / x % 0 == NaN.

Verified on an internal Linux sweep host: mod-whitespace passes; the
compound-assignment and modulus slices are 100% (0 runtime-fails).

fix(runtime): guard URLSearchParams shape probe against non-object receivers (#5997)

PR #5964 made native URLSearchParams methods reachable through dynamic access
by probing the receiver in js_native_call_method for the method names
append/set/get/has/delete/toString. That probe masks the receiver bits into
an *ObjectHeader and calls shape_is_url_search_params, which reads class_id /
keys_array / length at ObjectHeader offsets.

But the receiver may be any pointer-tagged value, not an ordinary object. A
Date value is a pointer to a GC_TYPE_DATE_CELL, whose bytes at those offsets
are garbage. Reading keys_array as a pointer and dereferencing its length
segfaulted -- so any two Date.toString() calls (the probe fires on toString)
crashed:

  language/expressions/addition/S11.6.1_A2.2_T2.js

(the test does date.toString() + date.toString()).

allocation is GC_TYPE_OBJECT. A Date cell (GC_TYPE_DATE_CELL), array, buffer,
closure, etc. now returns false immediately instead of reading ObjectHeader
fields off a foreign layout. This protects every caller of the shared probe,
not just the new toString arm.

Date.toString()+Date.toString() no longer segfaults, and URLSearchParams
dynamic get/toString/size still work. The addition slice is clean; the

fix(runtime): dispatch user-assigned callable methods on exotic receivers (#6004)

A callable stored as an own property of a RegExp / Date / Error object was
never invocable as a method: `var r = /x/; r.f = function(){...}; r.f()` threw
`TypeError: f is not a function`, and the same shape borrowing a builtin —
`reg.toLowerCase = String.prototype.toLowerCase; reg.toLowerCase()` — threw
too. These exotic objects keep their dynamic (expando) properties in a
side-table, not in the ObjectHeader field map, so the field / vtable /
prototype dispatch in `js_native_call_method` never saw them and fell through
to the "is not a function" catch-all.

Before the final throw, look the method name up in the exotic-expando table for
a RegExp/Date/Error receiver; if it resolves to a callable, invoke it with the
receiver bound as `this` (via IMPLICIT_THIS, matching the existing
closure-field dispatch path).

Fixes test262 built-ins/String/prototype/{toLowerCase,toUpperCase,
toLocaleLowerCase,toLocaleUpperCase}/*_A1_T14 (String.prototype case-mappers
borrowed onto a RegExp receiver) with zero regressions across the
Array/Object/String/Proxy/JSON/Function built-ins slice.

fix(runtime): proxy [[Get]] forwarding for numeric keys and proxy prototypes (#6005)

Two related bugs on the proxy get path:

1. A computed read on a statically-known proxy — `proxy[10]` — lowers to
   `js_proxy_get(proxy, 10.0)`, handing the get trap the raw number. `[[Get]]`
   is defined over an already-computed property key, so the trap must see the
   canonical string `"10"`; a trap comparing `key === "10"` silently missed and
   the read returned `undefined`. Apply `ToPropertyKey` at the top of
   `js_proxy_get` (numeric `10` -> `"10"`), short-circuiting keys that are
   already a string (the common `proxy.foo` case) or a symbol so the conversion
   only runs for the numeric / object-index forms.

2. `Object.create(proxy).x` records the proxy as the object's prototype. When
   resolving the inherited read, `resolve_inherited_field` took the proxy's
   small fake pointer — which lives in the proxy id band and passes the loose
   `is_valid_obj_ptr` heap-range check — and dereferenced it as an
   `ObjectHeader`, a SIGSEGV. Detect a proxy prototype first and route the
   inherited read through the proxy's `[[Get]]`, binding the original instance
   as the receiver.

Fixes test262 built-ins/Proxy/get/trap-is-null-target-is-proxy; no regressions
across the built-ins/{Array,Object,Proxy} slice (the inherited-field hot path
is unchanged for non-proxy prototypes).

fix(runtime): enforce preventExtensions/seal on function objects (#6007)

`Object.preventExtensions(fn)` / `Object.seal(fn)` set the NO_EXTEND / SEALED
flag in a function's GcHeader (functions are GcHeader-backed closures), and
`Object.isExtensible` correctly reported `false` afterwards — but the
property-write path never consulted the flag, so `fn.newProp = v` still created
the property.

In `ordinary_set_with_receiver`'s closure branch (the `[[Set]]` path that
materializes a new own property on a function), check the closure's GcHeader for
`OBJ_FLAG_NO_EXTEND` / `OBJ_FLAG_SEALED` before creating a NEW own property. If
set, the set fails (OrdinaryDefineOwnProperty returns false — silent in
non-strict, TypeError in strict via the existing `js_put_value_set` strict
handling). An existing own key can still be updated; only new-key creation is
blocked.

Fixes test262 built-ins/Object/preventExtensions/15.2.3.10-3-{3,13}; no
regressions across the built-ins/{Object,Array} slice.

fix(runtime): latch array iterator done state after exhaustion (#6008)

An array iterator (`arr.values()` / `.keys()` / `.entries()`) re-read the
backing array's length on every `.next()` and never latched "done": once
exhausted, pushing a new element and calling `.next()` again resurfaced the new
element. Per spec (22.1.5.2.1) the iterator sets `[[IteratedArrayLike]]` to
undefined when it finishes, so it stays done.

On the exhausted branch (`idx >= len`), clear the backing-array field to
`undefined`, and short-circuit to `{ value: undefined, done: true }` when that
field is already undefined. Elements added while the iterator is still live are
unaffected — only additions AFTER exhaustion stay invisible.

Fixes test262 Array/prototype/{values,keys,entries}/iteration-mutable.

fix(runtime): #6006 — content-validate shape transition-cache edges (stale-pointer false match) (#6012)

* fix(runtime): #6006 — content-validate shape transition-cache edges (stale-pointer false match)

The shape transition cache (`transition_cache_lookup`) validates a hit by raw
pointer equality — `entry.prev_keys == prev_keys && entry.key_ptr == kp` — but
`prev_keys` and `key_ptr` are plain `usize` addresses that the GC does NOT
track or relocate (only `next_keys` is a scanned root, stored via
`runtime_store_root_usize_slot`). When the GC frees a keys_array and later
recycles that same address for an unrelated array, a stale cache entry
pointer-matches falsely: the object then adopts the cached `next_keys` shape
and writes the value at the cached `slot_idx`, which belongs to a *different*
shape. The keys_array ends up looking correct (`Object.keys` is fine) but the
value slots are mis-placed, so property reads return `undefined` for the
mis-slotted keys.

This only bites at scale, where GC actually recycles keys_array addresses —
a large app's dynamically-grown objects (e.g. an HTTP header set built by
repeated `obj[k]=v`) silently lose values past a leading prefix. Observed on a
13 MB bundle: authenticated-request headers (`Content-Type`, `anthropic-beta`,
`anthropic-version`) became `undefined`, dropped from serialization, and the
request went out with a partial header set — server rejects, breaking the whole
authenticated path. Every isolated reproduction passed (no GC pressure → no
address reuse → no false match).

Fix: `transition_edge_places_key` — before trusting a cached edge, content-
validate that `next_keys[slot_idx]` actually string-matches the key being
stored. A genuine transition always places the key there; a recycled-address
false match never will, so the lookup returns `None` and the caller falls back
to the correct slow path. Guards all three fast-write callers through the one
`transition_cache_lookup` choke point.

Regression test `transition_cache_lookup_rejects_slot_key_mismatch` inserts an
edge whose target slot holds a different key (target_len matches, so only the
content check can catch it) and asserts the lookup rejects it, plus that a
genuine edge still hits. Fails without the fix, passes with it. Full
perry-runtime suite green (1153 tests).

Fixes #6006.

* fix(runtime): #6006 — also require exact target length on transition-cache edges

Strengthen `transition_edge_places_key`: a single-key transition edge always
produces a target shape of exactly `slot_idx + 1` keys, so require
`next_keys.length == slot_idx + 1` (not just `slot_idx < length`). This also
rejects the "shared target grew in place after caching" case — where the
cached `target_len` still matches `slot_idx + 1` but the actual `next_keys`
array has since been extended by a sibling object, so the fast-return would
adopt it as a smaller shape and leave `field_count` behind the real key count
(keys present, values undefined).

Adds `transition_cache_lookup_rejects_grown_shared_target` covering exactly
this: cache a 1-key edge, grow the shared target in place to length 2, and
assert the lookup now rejects it (falls back to the correct slow path). Fails
without the exact-length check, passes with it. Full perry-runtime suite green.
